**SHELL PAKISTAN LIMITED**  
**Tax Periods: January 2020 to December 2022**  
**Subject: Response to Hearing Notice – Show Cause Notice Dated August 29, 2023**

**Mr. Muhammad Yousuf Bukhari**  
Deputy Commissioner (Unit–21)  
Sindh Revenue Board  
2nd Floor, Shaheen Complex  
M. R. Kiyani Road, Karachi

**Dear Sir,**

We write in response to your notice dated May 3, 2025, issued in continuation of the Show Cause Notice dated August 29, 2023, for the above-mentioned tax periods. As noted, your office has issued a corrigendum revising the applicable Sindh Sales Tax (SST) rate from 10% to 13%, thereby recalculating the alleged short payment to Rs. 46,803,148. We are grateful for the extension granted to our client for compliance until May 13, 2025.

At the outset, we wish to correct a significant misstatement in the subject notice. It has been recorded that our client, during the course of the hearing, identified that the applicable SST rate should be 13% instead of 10%. This is factually incorrect. It was, in fact, your good office that acknowledged during the hearing that the application of the 10% rate in the original Show Cause Notice was a clerical oversight on the part of the previous officer. We respectfully request that the record be rectified to reflect this correction accurately.

More importantly, our client has already submitted comprehensive reconciliations and supporting documentation substantiating the discharge of sales tax liabilities across all relevant jurisdictions—namely, Punjab, Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT)—on the basis of revenue attribution. These reconciliations were submitted via our letter bearing reference DST 1189 dated February 10, 2025 (attached again herewith as Annexure ‘A’) and were further discussed in detail during multiple in-person hearings held before your good office, attended by the client’s authorized representatives.

Despite these extensive submissions, the current notice not only reiterates the earlier allegations but also seeks additional documentation in the form of bank statements and remittance application/approval forms—documents that have no direct relevance to the discharge of sales tax liabilities under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011. The payments in question are already evidenced through provincial tax returns and reconciliation statements, which are the primary and legally recognized documents for substantiating jurisdictional tax compliance. We respectfully request clarification as to the statutory basis for requiring such additional documentation, especially when your office has already been provided with full and verifiable evidence of compliance.

Furthermore, it is pertinent to bring to your attention a critical legal undertaking made by the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) before the Honourable Sindh High Court during the hearing of a constitutional petition. In its written submission, SRB categorically affirmed that sales tax paid to other provincial jurisdictions would be duly acknowledged and credit allowed—subject to the condition that the taxpayer provides appropriate supporting documentation. Our client has fully complied with this condition by repeatedly submitting reconciliations and accompanying provincial sales tax returns. The continued disregard of these documents and the consequent demand for the gross amount of sales tax—without granting proportionate credit—is contrary to the express commitment made by SRB before the Honourable High Court and undermines the principle of fair administration and lawful conduct by public authorities.

In light of the above, and in the interest of justice and consistency with SRB’s own representations before the judiciary, we respectfully urge your good office to withdraw the impugned Show Cause Notice and acknowledge the duly discharged tax liabilities by our client in accordance with applicable law. We remain available to provide any further clarification, if required, and remain committed to resolving this matter amicably, fairly, and in accordance with law.

Yours faithfully,  
**Zuhair Ahmed Minhas**  
Senior Manager

**cc:** Ms. Komal Ali  
Tax Lead  
Wafi Energy Pakistan Limited  
Shell House, 6, Ch. Khaliquzzaman Road, Karachi

Dear Sir,

We write with reference to your notice dated May 3, 2025, issued in continuation of the Show Cause Notice dated August 29, 2023, pertaining to the above-referenced tax periods. Through the subject notice, your good office has issued a corrigendum correcting the applicable rate of Sindh Sales Tax (SST) from 10% to 13%, thereby recalculating the alleged short payment to Rs. 46,803,148. At the outset, we express our sincere appreciation for granting our client an extension for compliance until May 13, 2025.

We would, however, like to correct a significant factual inaccuracy recorded in the said notice. It has been stated that during the hearing, we, on behalf of our client, pointed out that the correct rate of SST was 13% instead of 10%. This assertion is grossly incorrect. In fact, it was your good office that acknowledged during the hearing that the original application of a 10% SST rate was an inadvertent error committed by the previous officer while issuing the show cause notice, and that the correct rate should have been 13%. This admission was made by your good self and not by us, and we respectfully request that the record be amended accordingly.

Furthermore, our client has repeatedly and in good faith furnished a detailed reconciliation of the sales tax payments made across all relevant jurisdictions—including Punjab, Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Islamabad Capital Territory—on the basis of revenue allocation ratios, consistent with their business operations and service footprints. These reconciliations were submitted along with supporting documentation, including tax returns filed in those jurisdictions, through our letter bearing reference DST 1189 dated February 10, 2025 (attached again herewith as Annexure ‘A’), and were further explained during multiple in-person hearings attended by the client’s representatives before your good office.

Despite these efforts, the current notice reiterates the same allegation of short payment and further requests the submission of bank statements and remittance approval/application forms—documents which have no direct bearing on the discharge of sales tax liabilities and which are not statutorily required under the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 for substantiating inter-jurisdictional sales tax payments. We respectfully request your good office to justify the basis and necessity for such additional documentation when statutory compliance has already been demonstrated through verifiable provincial tax returns and reconciliations.

More critically, we would also like to draw your attention to a binding commitment made by the Sindh Revenue Board before the Honourable Sindh High Court during the hearing of a constitutional petition, wherein SRB categorically submitted in writing that it would allow input tax credit or acknowledge sales tax payments made to other provincial jurisdictions, provided that the taxpayer submits appropriate supporting documentation. Our client has fully complied with this condition by furnishing the requisite reconciliations and supporting tax filings. However, by continuing to charge the gross amount without granting due credit for sales tax already paid to other jurisdictions, your good office’s action stands in direct contradiction to the categorical statement filed by SRB before the Honourable Court. This not only undermines the sanctity of SRB’s own representation before a constitutional forum but also offends the principle of legitimate expectation and fair administrative conduct.

In light of the above, we respectfully urge your good office to withdraw the impugned show cause notice and conclude the matter in recognition of the documented and bona fide discharge of tax obligations by our client. We remain available to provide any further clarification your office may require and are committed to concluding this matter through constructive and lawful engagement.

Yours faithfully,  
**Zuhair Ahmed Minhas**  
Senior Manager

**cc:** Ms. Komal Ali  
Tax Lead  
Wafi Energy Pakistan Limited  
Shell House, 6, Ch. Khaliquzzaman Road, Karachi

## 1. Constitutional Jurisdiction Issues under Articles 137, 141 & 142  
**Argument:** The province may have exceeded its constitutional mandate by taxing services rendered outside its territorial boundaries. Under Article 141, a Provincial Assembly can only make laws for its province (no extra-territorial application). Article 142(c) reserves “sales tax on services” to provinces, but only for services within their jurisdiction【15†L155-L163】. ENI contended that Sindh’s attempt to tax services performed by foreign affiliates (outside Pakistan) violates these provisions by effectively reaching beyond Sindh. 

**Order’s Handling:** The Order-in-Original summarily dismissed this objection, asserting that Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011 (SSTSA 2011) is intra vires the Constitution. It emphasized that **provinces have exclusive authority to tax services** after the 18th Amendment【16†L205-L213】. However, the order did not specifically address ENI’s point about territorial nexus – i.e. whether the **service was sufficiently connected to Sindh** to fall within provincial taxing power. This lack of a reasoned rebuttal is a weakness. The adjudicating officer failed to engage with ENI’s claim that Sindh was taxing an “extra-provincial” activity (services of foreign entities)【15†L155-L163】. 

**Appeal Angle:** ENI can argue the order **glossed over the territorial limits** on Sindh’s taxation authority. Superior courts have upheld provincial sales tax laws generally, but only so long as the taxable service **occurs within or has nexus to the province**【17†L239-L247】. The appeal can emphasize that the order never established *how* these foreign-provided services were rendered or consumed “in Sindh,” nor cited any legal provision deeming them as such beyond a conclusory reference to the SSTSA. This leaves a jurisdictional void to exploit. If the nexus was not proven (e.g. if services were performed abroad with only indirect benefit in Sindh), ENI can invoke Articles 137/141/142 to challenge the **legislative and adjudicative competence** for this levy.

## 2. Misclassification and Tariff Heading Errors  
**Argument:** The order demands tax on services described only in vague terms (“technical assistance/consultancy”) without identifying a specific taxable category under the Second Schedule of SSTSA 2011. Proper classification of the service is crucial to determine taxability, applicable rate, and any exemptions. ## 3. Reverse Charge Mechanism & Lack of Territorial Nexus  
**Argument:** Even if the services are taxable in nature, SRB was obligated to show that the *reverse charge* provisions apply – i.e. that the services, though provided by a foreign associate, were received or consumed within Sindh. Section 3(2) of SSTSA 2011 (read with Section 9(2)) requires a **territorial nexus**: services originating outside Sindh are taxable **only if received in Sindh** and taxable as per the Act. The department cannot have it both ways: if they assert the amounts were payments for taxable services, then those amounts should be treated as *net of tax* (since no SST was included). The inconsistent use of a tax-inclusive formula reflects an overreach to maximize compatibility with the SCN figures, rather than a sound application of law. An appellate forum could question the **accuracy and legality of the Rs.172.3 million calculation** on this basis.

- **Acknowledgment of Additional Amount Beyond SCN:** A striking aspect of the order is its reference to an **additional Rs.53,098,088 tax** that was not part of the show-cause notice. ENI’s records showed total payments of Rs.1.734 billion (Jan 2017–Dec 2018), higher than the Rs.1.498 billion inferred from financial statements【1†L30-L38】. The adjudicator notes this difference and states it was *“not covered in the instant SCN,”* yet **“gives an opportunity”** to ENI to voluntarily deposit the extra Rs.53 million (the tax on the differential), or else face recovery proceedings【25†L155-L163】. This is procedurally improper. By doing so, the officer ventured beyond the scope of the SCN (which defines the case to be answered) and effectively attempted to **amend the demand without a proper notice**. ENI can argue that this conduct amounts to *undue pressure* and is indicative of an overzealous approach. In law, any amount not charged in the SCN cannot be recovered unless a separate notice is issued, and mentioning it in the order cannot cure that defect. This overreach could be cited to cast doubt on the entire proceedings – it shows the officer was considering liabilities outside the notice, which is a breach of due process. At the very least, it underlines that the quantification in the SCN was based on incomplete data, further supporting that the case was not properly investigated before issuance. 

- **Willful Default vs. Minimal Penalty:** The order finds *“willful default on the part of M/s ENI is duly available on record”*【3†L192-L200】 yet imposes only a 5% penalty (Rs.8.617 million) under Section 43(3) – which is actually the penalty for default **without fraudulent intent** (typically 5% of tax). If truly willful (deliberate evasion), the law allows much heavier penalties (up to 100%). This inconsistency suggests the officer was unsure of the gravity of ENI’s “offense.” ENI can leverage this in appeal: the officer’s own reasoning is contradictory – alleging willful non-payment (a strong accusation) but then choosing the nominal 5% penalty as if it were a routine lapse. This could support ENI’s position that it acted under a bona fide interpretation (reimbursements not taxable) rather than an intent to evade. It undermines the narrative that ENI willfully defied the law. 

**Appeal Angle:** These inconsistencies and errors collectively weaken the order’s defensibility. ENI should compile them to argue that the order is **not the result of a careful, impartial adjudication**, but rather a flawed attempt to penalize the company by any means:

- The use of an incorrect formula (tax fraction) can be challenged as *ultra vires* the tax charging section, potentially invalidating the quantification【25†L143-L151】.
- The handling of the additional amount is a clear procedural fault – ENI was never given notice to defend that portion, violating Article 10A of the Constitution (due process) and Section 47 requirements for a proper show-cause. This alone could be cause for setting aside that portion (and since that portion wasn’t formally added, it shows the lack of clarity in the order).
- Highlight to the appellate authority that such flaws, when viewed together, show a **failure to establish the case with certainty**. Tax demands must be made on the basis of consistent legal reasoning and correct facts; any significant doubt should be resolved in favor of the taxpayer. Given the multiple doubts (what was the real taxable amount? was the service within jurisdiction? was it even a service?), the safest course is to **quash the order in its entirety**.

## Conclusion and Recommended Strategy  
In light of the above, ENI has a strong basis to contest the full Rs.172.36 million demand (along with surcharge and penalties). The appeal should systematically attack the order on **jurisdictional, factual, and procedural grounds**, as outlined:

- Emphasize the constitutional boundary issue and the lack of analysis on whether the services were **truly within Sindh’s taxing jurisdiction**.
- Underscore the failure to **identify the exact taxable service** and to apply the correct legal provisions (reverse charge conditions, notifications, etc.), which calls into question the legitimacy of the tax assessed.
- Drive home the point that **what ENI paid for were not taxable services at all, but intra-group reimbursements** – a position supported by contracts and case law【25†L111-L117】【23†L747-L755】. The adjudicator’s silence on binding precedents (like 2022 PTD 576) is a key point of law in ENI’s favor.
- Highlight **procedural unfairness**: the way the case was initiated and handled (no prior audit, use of Rule 3(10), demand beyond SCN, etc.) violated ENI’s rights and the prescribed process, warranting relief.
- Point out the **internal contradictions and errors** in the order’s reasoning and calculations, which make the conclusions unreliable.

By presenting these arguments under clear headings (jurisdiction, classification, taxability, evidence, legal precedent, procedure, quantification), ENI can give the appellate forum a comprehensive view of the order’s weaknesses. Each weakness, on its own, provides a ground to reduce or annul the demand; collectively, they paint the impugned order as **legally unsound**. 

**References:** Case law and statutory interpretations will be crucial. ENI should attach or quote the relevant portions of the Sindh High Court judgment (2022 PTD 576) about reimbursements【25†L95-L103】, the Supreme Court’s observations on what constitutes consideration【23†L747-L755】, and any constitutional case upholding provincial tax jurisdiction with caveats (to contrast how ENI’s case differs). These references, along with the documented record from the OIO (e.g. the order’s own text acknowledging the reimbursement nature and additional amounts), will reinforce the appeal. 

In conclusion, the goal is to convince the appellate body that **the entire Rs.172 million assessment is ill-founded** – whether on constitutional grounds or on the simpler basis that ENI never received a taxable service in the first place. The multitude of legal and factual deficiencies in Order-in-Original 2824/2025 provide ample room for relief, ideally a full nullification of the tax demand and associated penalties. Each of the above points should be developed in the appeal to maximize the chances of a favorable outcome for ENI.

---

**GROUNDS OF APPEAL**

The Appellant respectfully submits the following grounds of appeal against the Order-in-Original No. 2824/2025 dated May 8, 2025, passed by the Deputy Commissioner (Unit-24), SRB. These grounds are raised independently and without prejudice to one another:

1. **That the impugned Order-in-Original is legally unsustainable and factually misconceived, having been passed without due appreciation of the Appellant’s submissions, supporting documentation, and settled legal principles.**

2. **That the learned adjudicating authority erred in holding the services received from foreign affiliates as “taxable services” without identifying any specific classification under the Second Schedule to the Sindh Sales Tax on Services Act, 2011.** The demand is premised on a sweeping and unsubstantiated assumption of taxability, in violation of the statutory requirement for precise service classification.

3. **That the order is ultra vires the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, particularly Articles 137, 141 and 142(c), insofar as it seeks to tax international transactions that do not have a sufficient territorial nexus with the Province of Sindh.** The learned officer failed to establish that the impugned services were rendered, provided, initiated, or consumed within the province, a prerequisite for invoking provincial taxing powers under Section 3(2) of the Act.

4. **That the application of the reverse charge mechanism under Section 9(2) of the Act was both factually and legally flawed, as the order does not establish that the foreign-provided services were consumed or utilized in Sindh.** Mere registration or presence of the Appellant in Sindh does not, in and of itself, create the requisite taxable nexus.

5. **That the adjudicating authority failed to examine the detailed contractual agreements, sample invoices, and supporting documents placed on record, which clearly demonstrate that the inter-company charges were in the nature of intra-group cost allocations without any element of profit or commercial consideration.** Such transactions fall outside the purview of taxable services, both under the Act and established jurisprudence.

6. **That the impugned order disregarded binding judicial precedents, including the judgment reported as 2022 PTD 576 (Sindh High Court), and various Supreme Court rulings which have categorically held that cost reimbursements, particularly those without any value addition or profit motive, do not constitute consideration for a taxable service.** The complete omission to address these precedents renders the order legally deficient.

7. **That the show cause proceedings were initiated in violation of due process, as no prior audit, inquiry, or investigation was conducted under Sections 23 or 52 of the Act.** The reliance placed on Rule 3(10) of the Special Procedure (Withholding) Rules, 2014, in the absence of any ongoing statutory proceedings, is procedurally flawed and legally untenable. Consequently, the imposition of penalty under Section 43(11A) is also without lawful basis.

8. **That the quantification of the alleged tax liability is erroneous and based on an arbitrary methodology, including the application of an incorrect tax fraction (11.5%) to values which were not grossed up for tax.** Furthermore, the attempt to enlarge the demand beyond the scope of the original show cause notice by including additional amounts is procedurally impermissible and reflects a lack of judicious application of mind.

9. **That the imposition of penalty under Section 43(3) of the Act is unjustified, as the Appellant acted in good faith, based on a reasonable interpretation of the law, supported by judicial guidance.** No evidence was adduced to demonstrate willful default or deliberate non-compliance that would warrant penal consequences.

10. **That the impugned order is otherwise arbitrary, excessive, passed in disregard of the principles of natural justice, and liable to be set aside in the interest of equity, fairness, and lawful administration.**

---

# Tax Risk Assessment for EEDD–Engro Split Contract

## Background Summary

Excelerate Energy Development DMCC (EEDD) – a UAE-based subsidiary of US company Excelerate Energy LP – currently has a single time-charter contract with Engro Elengy Terminals (Engro) for a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU) deployed in Pakistan【19†L229-L238】【19†L252-L259】. Under the original contract (a “wet lease”), Engro pays EEDD a daily fee that covers two components: (1) **FSRU charter hire** and (2) **Operation & Maintenance (O&M) services** performed by EEDD’s crew【21†L158-L166】. The entire payment has historically been treated as a royalty, subject to a 12% withholding tax under the Pakistan–UAE tax treaty per a 2018 Advance Ruling【20†L59-L67】【20†L69-L72】. 

Now, EEDD and Engro propose **splitting this single contract** into separate agreements – one for the **FSRU charter hire** (lease of the vessel) and one for **O&M services** – to segregate the payments【21†L168-L172】. This restructuring can yield tax benefits (e.g. potentially exempting the charter hire fee from Pakistani tax if treated as business profits) but also raises a number of **tax risks**. Below, we detail the key tax risks of the split arrangement and recommend mitigation steps, structuring options, and internal planning actions.

## 1. Key Tax Risks in the Proposed Contract Split

### Permanent Establishment (PE) Risk for EEDD in Pakistan

**Risk:** The O&M services may create a **Permanent Establishment (PE)** of EEDD in Pakistan, exposing EEDD’s income to Pakistani corporate taxation. Under the original wet-lease, EEDD’s continuous operation of the FSRU in Pakistani waters with on-site personnel could already constitute a PE (even if the Advance Ruling initially did not treat it as such). With a dedicated O&M contract, EEDD’s provision of services on the FSRU (a fixed location at Port Qasim for 15 years【28†L103-L110】) makes the PE risk more explicit.

If EEDD is found to have a PE, **Pakistan can tax the business profits** attributable to that PE under domestic law (29% corporate tax on net profits, or minimum tax on gross turnover)【5†L14-L22】. In fact, Pakistani tax authorities have broad anti-avoidance powers to **treat an arrangement as a PE** if the substance of the deal indicates a local presence fulfilling the contract【11†L118-L123】. There is a risk that by splitting the contract (clearly delineating a service component), the FBR (Federal Board of Revenue) will assert that EEDD **has had a PE all along** (given the “wet lease” nature) and seek to tax **past and future income** on that basis【19†L164-L169】. This could mean reopening up to 6 years of assessments to recharacterize EEDD’s Pakistan-source income as PE-attributable business profits【19†L163-L169】, rather than treating it as royalty. The outcome would be potential additional tax liability (if 29% of profit exceeds the royalties already withheld) and penalties.

**Implications:** With a PE, EEDD’s Pakistan-sourced O&M income would no longer be protected by the “no PE, no tax” rule of tax treaties. Instead, Pakistan would impose either regular corporate tax on **net profits** or a **minimum tax on gross receipts**. Under domestic law, payments to a non-resident’s PE for services incur **9% withholding tax on gross fees** (as an advance tax)【5†L10-L18】. The final tax on the PE’s profits would be the higher of: (a) 29% corporate tax on net income, (b) 9% of gross (minimum tax), or (c) 17% of accounting profit under the Alternate Corporate Tax regime【5†L14-L23】. In essence, the PE’s income is fully taxable in Pakistan, potentially at a higher effective rate than the current 12% gross withholding. EEDD would also face compliance obligations (registering the branch/PE, filing returns, etc.).

### Classification of FSRU: Machinery vs. “Industrial, Commercial & Scientific (ICS) Equipment”

**Risk:** The nature of payments for the FSRU charter hire may be disputed – i.e. whether they constitute **royalties for the use of industrial, commercial, or scientific (ICS) equipment** (taxable in Pakistan) or simply business income from leasing **machinery** (not taxable in Pakistan absent a PE). The 2018 Advance Ruling explicitly classified the full FSRU lease payment as a **royalty** under Article 12 of the Pakistan-UAE tax treaty【20†L59-L67】. This classification hinged on treating the FSRU as “industrial or commercial equipment” whose use or right-to-use is being paid for by Engro.

If the contract is split, EEDD intends to argue that the **FSRU charter is not a royalty** payment but rather a **lease of machinery/plant**, falling under business profits. In support of this, one can note that an FSRU is an active, operational unit (regasifying LNG) – effectively **machinery that performs a task** – rather than passive equipment that Engro simply uses. In other words, “equipment…does nothing by itself, whereas machinery operates to perform a process”【4†L1-L9】. On this logic, the FSRU charter payments should be viewed as **operating lease income** from provision of a complex machine, not as consideration for the use of “ICS equipment” in the sense intended by the treaty. If successful, this reclassification means the charter hire fees would be treated as **business profits** of EEDD, taxable in Pakistan only if EEDD has a PE (which EEDD would argue it does not, for the charter-only contract).

The risk is that **Pakistani authorities may reject this re-characterization**. They may maintain that the FSRU lease is a royalty payment for use of equipment, given that Article 12 of the treaty (and domestic law) explicitly covers rentals of industrial or commercial equipment as royalties. The FBR could continue to impose withholding on the charter hire fee as a royalty despite the contract split. In effect, the split itself doesn’t change the physical reality that Engro is paying to utilize an asset (the FSRU), which traditionally falls within the royalty definition. Thus, there is a **tax risk if EEDD unilaterally treats charter fees as non-taxable** while FBR views them as royalties – leading to potential under-withholding and disputes.

**Implications:** If the **FSRU charter fees are treated as royalties**, Pakistan can tax them (subject to treaty limits). Under the Pakistan–UAE treaty, royalties paid to UAE residents can be taxed up to **12%** (the rate applied under the Advance Ruling)【20†L69-L72】. Under domestic law (absent treaty benefits) royalties to non-residents are taxed at **15%**. Successfully classifying the FSRU lease as non-royalty business income would mean **0% Pakistani tax on that portion** (since EEDD has no PE for mere leasing). However, if FBR disagrees, Engro could be held liable for withholding (12–15%) on charter payments. This classification issue thus directly affects the **withholding tax obligations and cash flows** of the project.

### Pakistan–UAE vs. Pakistan–US Treaty Applicability (Beneficial Ownership Issue)

**Risk:** The **applicable double tax treaty** could change due to **beneficial ownership** concerns. EEDD is a UAE resident entity, so the Pakistan–UAE DTT would normally apply. However, if Pakistani authorities assert that EEDD is **not the “beneficial owner”** of the income from Engro (but rather a conduit for its US parent), treaty benefits under the Pakistan–UAE treaty could be denied【4†L21-L25】. In that case, Pakistan might apply the Pakistan–US DTT (since the ultimate parent Excelerate Energy LP is US-based) or just domestic law.

The concern arises because **EEDD passes most of the charter revenue to its parent (EELP)**, retaining only a small margin【4†L16-L24】. If EEDD is deemed to lack control and economic benefit in its own right (i.e. merely collecting and remitting funds), it might not qualify as the beneficial owner of the income【4†L11-L19】. Pakistani authorities could argue that the **UAE entity is interposed solely to obtain treaty benefits**, and that the real lessor/service provider is the US company. 

If the Pakistan–UAE treaty is disallowed, the **fallback is the Pakistan–US treaty**【4†L25-L33】. The Pakistan–US treaty has *no provision for equipment royalties* (it only recognizes royalties for intellectual property like patents, trademarks, etc.). This means a payment for equipment use (like an FSRU) **would not enjoy a specific reduced treaty rate**. In practice, Pakistan could then tax the charter hire fee at the full domestic rate of 15% (since the treaty doesn’t prevent it)【4†L27-L34】. In addition, under the Pakistan–US treaty, technical service fees are not separately addressed – they too generally fall under business profits or Independent Personal Services articles, requiring a PE to tax. But if EEDD’s UAE residency is disregarded, one could contend the **US company has a PE via the FSRU and crew in Pakistan**, exposing the income to full taxation on a net basis【4†L61-L67】.

**Implications:** Losing UAE treaty protection would likely **increase the tax burden**: for example, royalty withholding would jump from 12% to **15%**【4†L27-L34】, and Pakistan could more aggressively assert PE taxation. Additionally, the shift in treaty brings uncertainty – the Pakistan–US treaty’s protections (e.g. no tax on business profits absent PE) might not help if a PE is found or if Pakistan simply recharacterizes the income. In summary, **treaty shopping/beneficial ownership challenges** could invalidate the expected treaty benefits of the new structure.

### Withholding Tax Obligations Under Different Scenarios

**Risk:** The contract split alters the **withholding tax (WHT) obligations** for Engro, and missteps could lead to non-compliance. Under the single contract (with the Advance Ruling), Engro has been deducting **12% WHT on the gross payment** (royalty) to EEDD【20†L69-L72】. Going forward, Engro must handle two payment streams:

- **Charter Hire Payments:** If treated by EEDD as non-taxable business income (no PE), Engro might **not withhold any tax** on these. This is a significant change, and if the FBR later deems these payments taxable (e.g. as royalties or PE income), Engro could be held liable for the unpaid withholding, plus penalties. On the other hand, if Engro continues to withhold 12% (or 15%) as a precaution, EEDD would face excess tax or need to claim refunds if its position is that no tax was due. There is thus a risk of **disagreement on whether to withhold on charter fees** in absence of a clear ruling.

- **O&M Service Fees:** These will almost certainly be viewed as Pakistan-source service income. If EEDD has a PE for O&M, Pakistan’s law requires Engro to withhold **9%** of the gross service fee under section 152(2A) of the Income Tax Ordinance【5†L10-L18】. This 9% is an *advance* tax – not a final amount – and is adjustable against the PE’s eventual tax liability. If EEDD instead opts for the **gross basis taxation** (discussed below), the withholding might need to cover the full final tax (15%). Engro needs to know whether to apply 9% or 15% on the O&M payments, depending on EEDD’s election. 

The **risk** is if the parties fail to coordinate, Engro could under-withhold (e.g. only 9% while EEDD misses the 15% election, making the tax due higher) or over-withhold unnecessarily. Additionally, if Pakistan–UAE treaty benefits remain in play for services (though the treaty offers no reduction for PE-attributable FTS), Engro might need to consider any treaty rate (likely none, as Article 13 of the Pak-UAE treaty effectively defers to PE taxation for services)【3†L131-L139】.

**Implications:** Ensuring **correct withholding** is critical to avoid interest and penalties. Potential scenarios include: **(a)** Charter hire deemed non-taxable – **0% WHT** (requires strong support for Engro to refrain from withholding); **(b)** Charter hire taxable as royalty – **12–15% WHT** (depending on treaty) on that portion; **(c)** O&M via PE – **9% WHT** (advance) on service fee【5†L10-L18】; **(d)** O&M with gross-tax option – possibly **15% WHT** if structured as a final tax【5†L42-L50】. Engro, as the withholding agent, carries the obligation and needs clarity on which rates apply under what conditions. Any misalignment (e.g. EEDD claiming treaty exemption while Engro withholds, or vice versa) could lead to cash flow issues and disputes.
