### Advance Ruling Validity Risk

**Risk:** The 2018 **Advance Ruling (AR)** obtained by EEDD will **no longer protect the new arrangement**, and changing the contract could even invalidate the ruling retroactively if tax authorities determine that the facts are materially different or were misrepresented. The AR had concluded that EEDD’s income *“is taxed in Pakistan regardless of PE”* and that the FSRU lease payments are royalties under the Pak-UAE treaty【20†L59-L67】. That ruling was **binding on the tax authorities** (FBR) with respect to the specific transaction **as long as the facts remained as presented**【4†L37-L45】. However, by **splitting the contract**, EEDD is effectively deviating from the scenario on which the AR was based.

Once the facts change, the AR’s applicability **falls away going forward** – FBR is no longer bound by it for the restructured contracts【19†L160-L168】. Moreover, if the authorities believe that **the original ruling was obtained on incomplete or inaccurate facts**, they may **declare the Advance Ruling “null and void ab initio”** (from the beginning)【4†L53-L61】. One potential trigger for this is if EEDD did not fully disclose aspects like the role of the US parent (beneficial ownership) in the original AR request. In that event, the FBR could take the position that the ruling was never valid due to non-disclosure of material facts, and **reassess prior years without the protection of the ruling**.

This creates a risk of **back taxes**: FBR could reopen the last 6 years of assessments and attempt to tax the income under a different characterization (e.g. as PE business profits or as a domestic-law royalty at 15%)【19†L163-L169】【4†L59-L67】. The AR had given EEDD comfort to operate under the 12% royalty regime; if that comfort is removed retroactively, EEDD/Engro might face tax demands for underpaid amounts (for example, the difference between 12% and 15% on past royalties, or additional tax if a PE net-basis tax would have yielded more).

**Implications:** The **invalidation of the Advance Ruling** introduces uncertainty and potential dispute for both past and future periods. EEDD would lose the assurance it had and could be forced into litigation to defend its prior tax treatment. It also means that going forward, **any tax position EEDD takes (no tax on charter, etc.) is subject to challenge**, to be resolved via normal audit and appellate processes rather than a binding ruling. This elevates the importance of having strong support for EEDD’s new tax positions (in absence of an AR). In summary, the contract split *nullifies the old ruling* and opens the door to FBR applying a less favorable interpretation both prospectively and (if void ab initio) retrospectively.

### GAAR and OECD Principal Purpose Test (PPT) – Anti-Avoidance Risk

**Risk:** The planned restructuring could be viewed by authorities as **tax-motivated avoidance**, inviting the application of **General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR)** under domestic law and the **Principal Purpose Test (PPT)** under tax treaties/MLI. Pakistan’s GAAR (Section 109 of the Income Tax Ordinance) empowers the Commissioner to **disregard or re-characterize transactions** that lack commercial substance or are entered into primarily to avoid tax【19†L177-L185】【11†L118-L123】. If splitting the contract is seen as a form-over-substance tactic (simply separating payments on paper to claim treaty exemptions), the FBR could use GAAR to **collapse the two contracts back into one “arrangement”** or otherwise deny the tax benefit of the new structure. For instance, they might say the charter and O&M agreements together still amount to a single integrated project (a wet lease of an FSRU with services) and thus should be taxed in the same manner as before.

Furthermore, under the OECD/Pakistan treaty anti-abuse provisions (PPT, as introduced via the Multilateral Instrument and mirrored in domestic law amendments), a **treaty benefit can be denied** if obtaining that benefit was **one of the principal purposes** of an arrangement, unless it is in line with the object and purpose of the treaty. In practice, if the FBR concludes that the **main purpose of splitting the contract was to secure a lower tax outcome** (e.g. no tax on charter fees under Article 7), they can invoke PPT to deny treaty privileges. Pakistan has explicitly legislated that **treaty provisions are subject to anti-avoidance rules** – tax authorities may **ignore any treaty benefit that results in a reduced tax liability** under GAAR principles【19†L186-L193】. 

The risk here is heightened because the timing and context make the tax motivation apparent: EEDD operated under one arrangement (taxable at 12%) and now seeks to restructure in a way that a major portion (charter hire) becomes untaxed. Without clear non-tax business justifications, this could be seen as **treaty shopping or abuse** of the treaty.

**Implications:** If GAAR or PPT is invoked, the FBR could **override the intended tax outcome** of the new contracts. For example, they might **deem the split contract to be a “tax avoidance scheme”** and tax EEDD’s income as if no split occurred (i.e. continue with withholding on the combined amount or simply assert PE taxation on all of it). They could also specifically refuse treaty benefits – meaning **denial of the UAE treaty exemption for charter fees**, or denial of any reduced rate, on the grounds that the restructuring’s principal purpose was to avoid Pakistani tax【19†L179-L187】【19†L186-L190】. The result would be that EEDD ends up in the same or worse tax position as before, potentially after protracted litigation. GAAR/PPT also carry reputational risk – they imply an accusation of tax avoidance which EEDD/Engro would want to dispel through demonstrating genuine commercial rationale.

---

**Summary of Risks:** In sum, the key tax risks of the contract split include the creation of a taxable PE, loss of treaty benefits (UAE treaty protection) due to reclassification or beneficial owner issues, increased or misapplied withholding obligations, the invalidation of the prior favorable Advance Ruling, and anti-avoidance actions by tax authorities (GAAR/PPT) that could nullify the intended benefits of the restructuring. These risks need to be carefully managed with proactive strategies, as discussed next.

## 2. Risk Mitigation Recommendations

For each of the above risk areas, we recommend the following measures to mitigate or manage the exposure:

**a. Managing Permanent Establishment Risk:**

- **Limit EEDD’s Physical Presence:** Structure the O&M operations to minimize the scope of EEDD’s physical presence in Pakistan. For example, consider using **local personnel or contractors** for routine operations. If a reputable local contractor (or Engro’s own staff) can handle certain O&M functions under Engro’s supervision, EEDD’s employees could limit their on-site involvement to short-term visits or remote support. Reducing continuous on-site presence helps argue that EEDD has no fixed place of business in Pakistan. (If the treaty had a service-PE time threshold, keeping aggregate days below that would be crucial, though many treaties with Pakistan don’t explicitly have one – so focus on avoiding a “fixed base”.)

- **Independent Contractor Model:** EEDD can subcontract O&M services to an **independent third-party company** in Pakistan. If truly independent (not an agent of EEDD), this may avoid creating a PE for EEDD. It’s important that the contractor not be effectively under EEDD’s control or exclusively working for EEDD (which could otherwise be seen as a dependent agent). A well-documented service agreement with a third party can help show EEDD itself is not carrying on business in Pakistan – the local contractor is. This mitigates PE risk, though EEDD would need to oversee quality via contract rather than on-site management.

- **Local Subsidiary for O&M:** A stronger (but more involved) mitigation is for Excelerate/EEDD to **set up a Pakistani subsidiary or branch** to handle O&M. A subsidiary would be a resident company – eliminating non-resident PE issues (it will pay local tax on its profits, but EEDD DMCC itself stays offshore with respect to charter income). If a branch is set up, the PE is then formalized and can be managed (see structuring options below for how to handle its taxation). In either case, having a local vehicle accept the O&M functions means EEDD DMCC itself could more credibly restrict its Pakistan activities to only leasing the FSRU (passive income). **Note:** A branch PE would incur full Pakistan taxation on O&M and could potentially taint the charter income as well (by attribution), so if the goal is to **completely avoid EEDD having a PE**, a **separate subsidiary** is preferable. The subsidiary approach shifts the tax burden to a controlled local entity (which can be optimized), protecting EEDD’s charter income from being pulled into a Pakistan tax net.

- **PE Declaration and Compliance (if unavoidable):** If despite best efforts EEDD is deemed to have a PE (for example, because maintaining operational control of the FSRU is essential), then mitigate by **managing the PE’s taxable profits**. Ensure that the internal transfer pricing between EEDD’s head-office and PE attributes only the necessary profit to the PE (e.g. O&M activities could be characterized as low-margin if justified by a cost-plus model). Also, maintain **proper documentation of expense allocations** to the PE to maximize deductions and keep the taxable base low. In parallel, **register the PE with tax authorities** and comply with filing requirements – a compliant stance may make authorities more amenable to any claims for deductions or treaty interpretations. In summary, if you must have a PE, treat it as a **disclosed, limited-function operation** in Pakistan to contain the tax exposure.

**b. Mitigating FSRU Classification (Royalty vs. Business Income):**

- **Obtain Expert Opinions/Precedents:** Compile supporting technical analysis to bolster the position that the FSRU charter is **not an “ICS equipment” royalty**. This may include opinions from industry experts that an FSRU is a **floating plant/facility** that actively regasifies LNG (more akin to a **mobile industrial plant** than mere equipment rental). Highlight that Engro is paying for a *service of regasification* and vessel availability, not just renting a static equipment to use independently. If any international tax commentaries or precedents (e.g. OECD commentary on royalties) distinguish between **active leasing operations** vs. passive equipment leasing, include those. For instance, cite that the inclusion of ICS equipment in royalty definitions was not intended to cover **full-service, operational leases** where the lessor operates the asset (supporting the view that such income is business profit)【4†L1-L9】.

- **Engage FBR Early (if possible):** To avoid a unilateral reclassification that FBR later disputes, consider proactively **seeking clarification or a ruling from the FBR on the charter hire characterization** under the new split. This could be done via a new **Advance Ruling application** focused solely on the lease contract, or via informal consultations with FBR’s International Tax/Policy unit. While there is a risk FBR will simply restate their prior position, an open dialogue allows EEDD to present the new arguments (machinery vs. equipment) and perhaps negotiate a consensus (for example, FBR might agree to treat charter as business income if certain conditions are met). Any written clarification obtained will protect Engro (withholding agent) and EEDD from future penalties on this issue.

- **Maintain Beneficial Ownership at EEDD Level:** A crucial element of keeping the UAE treaty applicable (and thus making the classification debate relevant) is demonstrating that EEDD **is the true beneficial owner** of the charter income. Actions to support this include: ensuring the **inter-company lease between EEDD and EELP** is on arm’s-length terms that leave EEDD with a reasonable profit, documenting that EEDD has full control over the FSRU’s use in the Engro contract, and perhaps **increasing the margin or risk borne by EEDD**. For example, if currently EEDD just passes a fixed amount to EELP, renegotiate that arrangement so EEDD’s payments to EELP are not automatically the residual – maybe a fixed lower lease fee so that EEDD retains more income (and risk of chartering). The more EEDD can show it isn’t a conduit (i.e., it has **independent rights and obligations**, and the profitability of the Engro deal affects EEDD), the stronger the case that the income truly “belongs” to EEDD for treaty purposes. This indirectly helps the classification issue: FBR will be more inclined to respect EEDD’s treaty position (and thus entertain the argument that Article 7 business profits applies) if EEDD is clearly the principal in the transaction.

- **Prepare for Alternative Outcome:** Despite best efforts, if it appears likely that FBR will insist on treating the FSRU hire as a royalty, plan to **mitigate the impact**. This could involve ensuring a **continued UAE treaty benefit (12% rate)** by defending EEDD’s treaty eligibility (beneficial ownership, as above). A 12% final tax is still better than a 15% or PE taxation scenario. Additionally, EEDD should be ready to **litigate the classification** if necessary – meaning, have a legal strategy and counsel in place to appeal a withholding or assessment that treats the charter as royalty. A court might be more persuaded by technical arguments and could overturn an FBR stance if strong evidence is presented that the payments are outside the intended scope of royalty in the treaty. Simply put, *plan for the worst-case (royalty taxation) while arguing for the best-case (exemption as business profits)*.

**c. Preserving Treaty Benefits (Pakistan-UAE vs. US Treaty):**

- **Demonstrate Substance in UAE:** To counter any challenge that EEDD is a shell, **build substance in the UAE operations of EEDD**. This could include having real offices, employees, and decision-making in the DMCC entity related to the FSRU project (if not already in place). If EEDD appears as a genuine operating company managing Excelerate’s regional projects (and not just a letterbox), FBR will have a harder time ignoring the UAE treaty. Obtain and provide a **Tax Residency Certificate (TRC)** for EEDD from UAE authorities for each tax year – this is a basic requirement to claim treaty benefits and shows EEDD is recognized as UAE-resident.

- **Address Beneficial Ownership Formally:** Consider drafting a **board resolution or intra-group agreement** affirming that EEDD is the beneficial owner of the income from Engro. While such internal declarations are not determinative, they signal intent. More tangibly, avoid any contractual obligation that EEDD must remit a fixed percentage of Engro revenues to EELP. Instead, any payments to the US parent should be framed as *commercial* (e.g. a lease of the vessel at a market rate, or a service fee) rather than an automatic pass-through of Engro’s payment. By decoupling the two contracts (Engro–EEDD and EEDD–EELP), EEDD can show it has **discretion over use of funds** (a hallmark of beneficial ownership). If needed, be prepared to disclose to FBR the terms of the EEDD–EELP arrangements to evidence that EEDD isn’t legally bound to send all funds onward (aside from a fair compensation for the asset use).

- **Evaluate Direct Contracting by EELP:** As a contingency, examine the scenario of **EELP (US) contracting directly with Engro** for the charter or services. This is not the preferred structure due to lack of UAE treaty and potential PE, but it may come into play if FBR effectively sees through EEDD. If that happens, ensure that EELP can claim **Foreign Tax Credits** in the US for any Pakistan tax paid (the US-Pak treaty won’t eliminate Pakistan tax, but the US would credit it). From a mitigation standpoint, if negotiations with FBR fail on the UAE front, one might negotiate under the US treaty context instead – for example, arguing that even under the US treaty, **no PE means no Pakistan tax on business profits** (since the US treaty doesn’t have an FTS article). However, this requires convincing FBR that no PE exists, which circles back to the PE mitigation above. In short, keep the **US treaty implications analyzed** and ensure compliance (TRC for EELP, etc.) if the income ends up being considered under that treaty.

- **Treaty Clearance Process:** Proactively use any available procedure to **get treaty relief at source**. In Pakistan, a taxpayer can sometimes apply to the tax authority for a **reduced withholding tax certificate** if treaty provisions warrant a lower rate or exemption. EEDD (or Engro) should consider applying for such certificate for the charter hire payments, claiming 0% under Article 7 (or 12% if that’s the fallback). If granted, this would legally permit Engro not to withhold (or to withhold at 0/12% as specified), eliminating uncertainty. If denied, it gives an early warning that FBR disputes the position, allowing EEDD to decide on next steps (e.g. continue with 12% withholding to be safe, or challenge the decision).

**d. Ensuring Correct Withholding Compliance:**

- **Coordination between Engro and EEDD:** The finance/tax teams of Engro and EEDD should align on how each payment will be handled before the split contracts go into effect. They should document the plan: e.g., “Engro will not deduct WHT on charter hire upon receiving XYZ documentation, but will deduct 9% on O&M fees (or 15% if instructed pursuant to gross election).” This mutual understanding prevents mistakes. EEDD should provide **supporting documents to Engro** such as: a copy of EEDD’s **UAE TRC**, a written **declaration of no PE** in Pakistan for the charter contract (if that is the position), and a **notice of exercise of the gross-tax option** for O&M (if EEDD decides to elect). Engro will need these on file to justify any reduced withholding to the FBR during audits.

- **Exercise Gross Tax Option Timely:** If EEDD chooses the **15% gross final tax** for O&M, it must file the election **within 15 days of the new O&M contract’s commencement**【5†L33-L41】【5†L43-L50】. Mark this deadline and draft the letter in advance. The letter should be submitted to the relevant Commissioner and an acknowledgment retained. This election locks in the tax treatment and avoids any ambiguity about whether 9% was minimum or final – it converts the O&M withholding into a **final discharge** at 15%【5†L47-L50】. Engro should then be notified to adjust the withholding to 15% from day one of the contract (or EEDD’s Pakistan PE should pay the difference later). By formally making this choice, EEDD **preempts any under-withholding risk** and simplifies compliance (no need for the PE to calculate net profit tax each year if this option is used).

- **Maintain Status Quo Withholding until Clarity (if needed):** As a conservative approach, Engro could initially **continue withholding 12% on charter hire** payments (i.e. treat them as royalties) until a clear directive or comfort is obtained that no withholding is required. This mitigates Engro’s risk of non-compliance. If EEDD is confident in the no-PE/not-royalty position, it can then file a return to claim a **refund** of any excess withholding on charter fees later, once the matter is resolved. While not ideal for cash flow, this approach “errs on the side of caution” and avoids potential penalties on Engro. This should be weighed against the likelihood of success in claiming that refund (which might involve litigation). Ideally, a better approach is obtaining FBR agreement to zero-rate the charter payments upfront, but absent that, continuing the old withholding temporarily is a safe harbor.

- **Split Invoices and Documentation:** Make sure Engro’s accounting and invoicing system clearly **segregates the two types of payments** post-split. Each invoice from EEDD should specify whether it’s “Charter Hire – FSRU Lease” or “O&M Service Fee” (with separate payment instructions if needed). This clarity will help both parties apply the correct withholding and will create a paper trail to support the tax positions (e.g. if charter hire is treated as exempt, having distinct invoices for it reinforces that it’s a separate stream potentially covered by Article 7). Documentation should also include any **withholding tax challans/receipts** for the O&M portion – these need to be properly credited to EEDD’s PE or final tax account.

- **Monitor Withholding Law Changes:** Stay alert to any Pakistan tax law changes in upcoming Finance Acts that could affect rates or definitions (for example, if the government changes the services WHT rate or redefines royalties). Being ahead of such changes allows recalibration of the strategy (e.g., if the services WHT rate is increased or if an exemption is introduced, etc.).

**e. Preserving Advance Ruling Reliance / Managing Retrospective Risk:**

- **Full Disclosure in New Filings:** If EEDD seeks a new ruling or faces audit, ensure **full and true disclosure** of all relevant facts this time. This includes the involvement of the US parent, the reasons for restructuring, and any changes from the scenario described in 2018. By being transparent now, EEDD can avoid accusations of misrepresentation. It can argue that the original AR was based on a good-faith interpretation of an ambiguous situation, not on any concealment. This may not stop FBR from voiding it, but it positions EEDD as a compliant taxpayer.

- **Statute of Limitations Strategy:** Understand that FBR can go back **6 tax years** for reassessment. Track the timeline – for example, if the first royalty payment was in 2015, those early years might already be time-barred (depending on Pakistan’s exact rules). If some early years are beyond 6 years, that limits the retroactive exposure. For the remaining open years (say 2019 onward), consider if there’s any benefit in delaying the split until certain key years fall out of range. However, given the 15-year contract span and the need to implement improvements, it may not be feasible to wait too long. At minimum, **budget for a potential back-tax claim**. EEDD should internally calculate what the worst-case liability could be if FBR recharacterizes past income (e.g., additional 3% of gross for past royalties to get to 15%, or tax on any profit differential under PE). Having a reserve or guarantee in place will reduce financial shock if FBR moves on this.

- **Legal Defense Preparedness:** In anticipation that FBR might declare the AR void and issue revised assessments, engage tax legal counsel early to **formulate a defense**. Possible defense arguments: the AR was valid for the facts given and those facts did not materially change until the contract split date (so it shouldn’t be void for earlier years); even if voided, the taxpayer relied on it so penalties should be waived under the circumstances; and substantively, the original position (royalty at 12%) was at least as much tax as was due (for instance, if EEDD’s actual PE profits would have yielded less tax than 12% of gross, argue no revenue loss to FBR). This line of defense could mitigate penalties and possibly negotiate a settlement for past years rather than protracted litigation.

- **Engage with FBR for Prospective Agreement:** It may be worth approaching the FBR to reach a **prospective understanding**: for example, EEDD could propose, “We will comply in manner X for future payments if FBR agrees not to disturb past arrangements under the Advance Ruling.” This kind of negotiation (possibly at the level of FBR’s Large Taxpayer Unit or Policy Wing) might result in a pragmatic solution. For instance, EEDD might agree to a particular withholding on charter hire (say 5% as a compromise) going forward, in exchange for FBR not reopening prior years. While not a formal process, such **alternative dispute resolution** or negotiated settlement can sometimes be achieved in complex cases to avoid litigation. If pursued, ensure any agreement is documented in writing with FBR’s sign-off.

**f. Guarding Against GAAR/PPT Challenges:**

- **Document Commercial Rationale:** To defend against the allegation of tax avoidance, EEDD and Engro should **clearly document non-tax reasons for splitting the contract**. For example, memos or board resolutions can state objectives like: “to improve transparency of costs for each component,” “to align the contracts with standard industry practice of separate charter and service agreements,” or “to facilitate compliance with accounting standards (IFRS 16) which require separate accounting of lease and service components.” If Engro’s LNG tariff or regulatory regime requires breakdown of capacity (lease) vs. operating costs, note that as a business driver. Emphasize improved risk allocation – e.g. the charter agreement deals with asset availability and is often financed separately, while the O&M agreement covers performance guarantees. By showing these legitimate reasons, the **“principal purpose” of the restructuring can be framed as commercial**, not merely obtaining a tax benefit. Keep emails or minutes that show these discussions occurred prior to implementation.

- **Align Pricing with Substance:** Ensure the pricing of the split is **arm’s-length and sensible**, not a token amount in one contract and most value in the other purely to save tax. The charter hire fee should be set in line with market lease rates for comparable FSRUs, and the O&M fee should reflect actual operating costs plus a normal margin for such services. If FBR sees that the charter fee is unreasonably high and O&M fee very low (or vice versa) solely to exploit a tax differential, they could invoke substance-over-form. A balanced allocation of revenue that can be justified with cost data and third-party benchmarks will lend credibility to the structure. It may be helpful to get a **transfer pricing analysis or valuation** to support the split of the original consolidated fee into two components.

- **Avoid Circular Arrangements:** Do not create any unnecessary interdependencies between the two contracts that could undermine their separate nature. For instance, avoid clauses like “if O&M contract is terminated, charter rate reduces/increases,” as that would signal they are effectively one arrangement. Each contract should be able to stand on its own terms as a commercially reasonable deal. By truly **decoupling the agreements**, you reduce the chance of the tax authority recombining them under GAAR. 

- **PPT Safeguard in Treaties:** Recognize that post-MLI, Pakistan’s treaties (including with UAE and US) now likely have PPT in force. The PPT standard is subjective (“one of the principal purposes”). To mitigate this, EEDD should be ready to argue that **tax was at most a secondary consideration**, and the restructuring is consistent with the intent of the treaties. For example, the object and purpose of the treaty is to prevent double taxation without creating opportunities for avoidance – here EEDD can argue it is **not seeking double non-taxation**, just a correct application of treaty definitions (business profits vs. royalties)【18†L19-L27】【18†L29-L37】. Also, emphasize that **Pakistan will still tax the O&M profits** fully; the change only affects the character of one income stream. Thus, the overall tax paid may not drastically fall (especially if EEDD’s profit on charter is largely passed to the US and presumably taxed there, meaning no treaty abuse of achieving zero tax). These arguments can be refined in professional opinions to counter any PPT accusation.

- **Seek Advance Tax Rulings/Certainty if Available:** While one AR is being effectively set aside, it might still be possible to seek a **new Advance Ruling on specific anti-abuse concerns**. Pakistan’s ruling process might not entertain a purely tax-motivated query, but EEDD could pose genuine uncertainty questions (e.g., “Will splitting the contract trigger any anti-avoidance provisions under Pakistani law?”). Even if a formal ruling isn’t given, having the query on record shows transparency. Alternatively, consult the **Appellate Tribunal’s guidance** or any available APA (Advance Pricing Agreement) mechanism if relevant for transfer pricing of the split. The more upfront EEDD/Engro are, the harder it is for FBR to later claim the arrangement was covertly designed for tax avoidance.

In summary, a combination of **substance, documentation, transparent engagement, and fallback planning** will mitigate the identified risks. Below, we further discuss broader structuring options to achieve tax efficiency and compliance.

## 3. Structuring Options for Tax Efficiency and Compliance

Beyond the risk-specific mitigations, EEDD and Engro should consider the following **structural approaches to optimize tax outcomes** while staying within the law:

### Separate Legal Entities for Separate Functions

One structural option is to mirror the contract split with a **structural split**: EEDD (UAE) handles the leasing function, and a **Pakistani entity handles the O&M function**. This could be a **wholly-owned subsidiary of EEDD** or Engro could even form a joint venture with Excelerate for O&M services. The benefits of this structure include:

- **Elimination of Cross-Border WHT on Services:** Payments for O&M would go to a resident entity, so Engro would not apply section 152 withholding. The local entity would pay corporate tax on its profits instead. If structured as a cost-plus service provider, its profit margin (and hence tax) can be kept modest. For example, if the local subsidiary earns a 5% margin on O&M costs, and corporate tax is 29%, the effective tax on the gross service fee might be ~1.45% of that fee – much lower than 9% WHT. This substantially **reduces withholding tax exposure** on the service component, aligning with the goal of tax efficiency.

- **Preservation of Treaty Exemption on Charter:** The local O&M company would have no claim on the charter hire fee; EEDD DMCC would continue to receive that. EEDD’s position for the charter fee (no PE, treaty protection) is strengthened because EEDD itself is not performing services in Pakistan – it’s only leasing the asset. The risk of EEDD having a PE via O&M is removed; EEDD’s activities in Pakistan would be limited to perhaps monitoring the contract, which should not constitute a PE if done remotely or via occasional visits. Thus the **business profits exemption on charter hire is more defensible**.

- **Commercial Focus and Compliance:** Separating entities allows each to focus on compliance with their respective jurisdictions – the Pakistani company deals with local tax filings, employment laws for crew, etc., while EEDD deals with UAE/US compliance. It provides clarity for FBR that the O&M profits are being taxed in Pakistan (through the local entity), potentially appeasing concerns of “too much income escaping tax.”

However, drawbacks include the administrative effort of setting up a new company, potential sales tax implications on inter-company service arrangements, and possibly higher operational costs. Also, care must be taken that the local subsidiary is **adequately capitalized and truly performing the functions** (to avoid GAAR claims that it’s a sham conduit just shifting income). Given that Engro and Excelerate have a long-term partnership, establishing a local vehicle might be feasible and could even be positioned as capacity-building for Pakistani operations.

### Gross Basis Taxation Election for O&M Services

If using a local entity is not desired, and EEDD must provide O&M via a PE, then taking advantage of the **gross basis taxation option** is a key structuring choice:

- **Elect final taxation under Rule 19**: As noted, Rule 19 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 allows a non-resident with a PE deriving fees for technical services (FTS) to irrevocably elect **15% of gross as final tax**【5†L27-L35】【5†L41-L49】. By structuring EEDD’s Pakistan presence as a **branch (PE)** and making this election at the contract’s start, EEDD caps its Pakistan tax exposure on O&M at 15% of the service fee. This simplifies tax calculation and avoids the scenario of minimum tax carry-forwards. It may result in a slightly higher tax than the 9% withholding if EEDD’s profit is low, but it **provides certainty** (tax will not exceed 15% even if profit margins grow). It also avoids complex profit attribution debates with tax auditors – which can often lead to protracted disputes – because the tax is simply on gross receipts.

- **Implement via Contract Terms:** To operationalize this, EEDD could structure the O&M contract such that Engro **withholds 15%** on payments (with EEDD’s agreement), treating it as final. Alternatively, maintain 9% withholding and EEDD remits the additional 6% upon assessment – but the cleaner approach is adjusting withholding to the final tax rate from the outset (Engro may require FBR confirmation for this). Either way, the election ensures compliance is straightforward: once the tax is paid, no further corporate tax or assessments on that income should arise. EEDD’s branch would file a return claiming the income was taxed under section 6 (final tax regime).

- **When to choose 15% final vs. normal 29% net:** This decision depends on expected profitability of O&M. If O&M is near break-even (low profit), **paying 15% on gross could be higher** than 29% on net (which might be small). In that case, EEDD might prefer to stick with the **normal regime (9% WHT as advance and file for net tax)**, accepting the complexity in hopes of a lower effective rate. But if O&M has healthy margins or if EEDD values certainty over a possibly lower tax, the gross election is safer. We recommend modeling both scenarios. Structurally, building in flexibility is tricky – the election must be made up front. However, one could negotiate with Engro to factor the tax cost into the O&M fee: e.g., if electing 15% final, perhaps the O&M fee could be set slightly higher to account for the higher tax, especially if Engro can pass that cost through in its tariff. This depends on contract dynamics, but it’s worth considering in the pricing strategy.

### Optimizing Contract Terms to Avoid PE and Withholding

Aside from entity structure and tax elections, the **contracts themselves can be structured** to mitigate PE and withholding issues:

- **Bareboat Charter + Local Crew Lease:** One idea is to convert the charter hire into a **“bareboat” lease (no crew)**, and have Engro lease the crew or services separately from either a local provider or EEDD’s affiliate. If Engro technically takes on the operation of the FSRU (even if via contract manpower supply), EEDD would only be leasing a vessel *without providing personnel*. In tax terms, a pure bareboat lease strengthens the argument that EEDD has **no fixed place of business** in Pakistan (the FSRU may be in Pakistan, but if no EEDD staff or agents are operating it, EEDD might be seen as simply earning rent offshore). Engro could contract with, say, a crewing company that seconded Excelerate’s crew. This arrangement is admittedly somewhat artificial because the same people might be doing the job, but legally it splits the functions. If executed carefully (with genuine contracts for crew services through an intermediary), it’s another layer of defense against an EEDD PE.

- **Service Duration and Rotation Clauses:** In the O&M contract, include clauses that **limit the duration of any single employee’s stay in Pakistan** and require periodic rotation outside the country. For example, if a service PE under a treaty might be argued only if personnel stay beyond X days, keeping each individual below that threshold could be useful. Even if the treaty doesn’t specify, it demonstrates an effort to avoid permanent presence. Additionally, include a clause that significant managerial decisions or maintenance overhauls will be handled from outside Pakistan (e.g., at EEDD’s UAE office or via remote monitoring). This can be used to argue that the **core business operations are conducted abroad**, and the in-country presence is auxiliary (though admittedly, running an FSRU is a core activity).

- **Payment Structuring:** Structure payments from Engro to minimize Pakistani tax leakage. For instance, if for some reason a **success fee or bonus** is payable on performance, consider attaching it to the charter agreement rather than O&M (if the charter payment is treaty-exempt). Conversely, any fixed fees that might fall under Pakistan tax regardless could be shifted to the O&M side which is capped at 15% final tax. Basically, allocate revenues in a way that **more of the taxable elements are subject to capped or reduced rates** while preserving treaty-protected elements in the charter hire. However, be cautious not to deviate from arm’s-length principles.

- **Gross-up Clauses:** Include a **tax gross-up clause** in both contracts. This isn’t a tax avoidance per se, but it ensures that if unforeseen Pakistani taxes are imposed on either payment, the responsible party (Engro) will gross-up the payment so that EEDD receives the agreed net amount. For instance, if it turns out charter hire is subject to 15% WHT, Engro would increase the payment such that after withholding EEDD still gets full charter fee. This protects EEDD’s economics. From a structuring perspective, it doesn’t reduce tax, but it allocates tax risk contractually. Engro may or may not agree to this (it increases their cost unless they can pass it through to their customers/regulator), but it’s worth discussing given the tax uncertainties.

- **Timeline of Commencement:** Structurally, choose the **start date of the new contracts carefully**. If possible, align the commencement with the tax year or quarter for cleaner break in tax reporting. Also, avoid starting the new structure while an old invoice period is mid-way – ideally, finish a tax period under the old contract and start fresh under the new. This prevents confusion over which regime applied to which portion of income and simplifies accounting.

By implementing the above structural choices, EEDD and Engro can significantly improve the tax profile: the goal being to **reduce or eliminate Pakistani withholding on the large charter fee**, and manage the service fee in a predictable, optimized manner (either through a local entity or final tax election). All of these must be weighed against operational practicality, but from a tax planning standpoint, they are viable tools.

## 4. Internal Planning and Next Steps for EEDD and Engro

Finally, we outline internal planning recommendations to ensure successful execution of the contract split from a tax standpoint, including documentation, communication with authorities, and timeline management:

**A. Robust Documentation:** Both parties should maintain comprehensive documentation to support the new structure and the reasoning behind it:

- **Revised Contracts:** Draft the **charter hire agreement and O&M services agreement** with clear terms. Define the scope of each to avoid overlap. Include pricing mechanisms, responsibilities, and termination provisions separately. This clarity will be a first line of defense in showing they are **independent agreements**. Attach schedules if necessary to show how fees were arrived at (e.g., a schedule showing the cost components of O&M fee).

- **Board Resolutions/Approvals:** Have each company’s board (or authorized committee) formally **approve the contract split**, citing expected benefits (operational clarity, risk management, compliance with policies, etc.). These resolutions can later be presented to show that the decision was made for sound business reasons with due governance, not in an ad hoc manner for tax only.

- **Memorandum of Rationale:** Internally, prepare a memo summarizing the **commercial rationale for restructuring** (as discussed in GAAR mitigation). Circulate this to relevant executives in tax, finance, and legal. This not only aligns the team on messaging but also timestamps your intent. If tax authorities question the purpose, you have a contemporaneous document to share (if strategic) or at least to draw from when responding.

- **Tax Advice and Opinions:** Keep copies of all **tax advice obtained** (for example, this report, opinions from EY or legal counsel). These will guide implementation and can also demonstrate to FBR that you sought professional guidance to **comply with the law (not evade it)**. If any positions are particularly aggressive (like treating charter as non-taxable), a formal legal opinion supporting the position (with references to law/treaty) can be invaluable. In a dispute, a tax opinion might protect against penalties by showing you had reasonable cause.

- **Beneficial Owner Affidavit:** If beneficial ownership is a concern, have EEDD sign an **affidavit or certification** that it meets the criteria of beneficial owner for the income, and have EELP (the US parent) corroborate that it has no direct claim over the payments from Engro. While not legally binding on FBR, such documentation adds to the factual matrix supporting treaty claims.

- **Transfer Pricing Documentation:** If there are intra-group transactions (e.g., EEDD leasing the FSRU from EELP, or charging a fee to a local subsidiary if one is created), prepare transfer pricing documentation. Pakistan has transfer pricing rules and even though EEDD is non-resident, any Pakistani entity (Engro or a new subsidiary) involved should show that related-party payments are at arm’s length. This defuses any argument that the structure is a profit-shifting scheme disadvantaging Pakistan. For example, if EEDD’s charter rate to Engro is X, document that EEDD’s lease cost from EELP is lower and comparable to market lease rates, justifying EEDD’s profit.

**B. Communication with Tax Authorities:**

- **Pre-split Consultation:** It can be beneficial to request a meeting with the **FBR’s International Tax or Large Taxpayer unit** (whichever oversees Engro/EEDD’s file) *before* implementing the change. In this meeting, outline the plan and ask for the FBR’s views or any procedural requirements. While FBR may not give a binding answer on the spot, this shows good faith. They might provide practical guidance (for instance, advising to apply for a new ruling or how to handle WHT interim). Make sure minutes of any such meeting are recorded and agreed upon.

- **Advance Ruling Application (if pursued):** If you decide to file for a new Advance Ruling on critical aspects (like “are charter payments taxable if contract separated?”), do so as early as possible. The ruling process can take time and you’d want a response ideally before or soon after the new contracts commence. Include all pertinent facts in the application to avoid any claim of misrepresentation. Even if the ruling outcome is uncertain, the act of applying shows transparency.

- **Notification of Change:** Once the contracts are signed and effective, **formally notify the FBR** that the prior Advance Ruling scenario has changed. This can be a letter referencing the AR number/date, stating that as of [effective date], the single contract has been bifurcated and that henceforth, the AR may no longer be applicable. This manages expectations – the local tax office won’t be caught off guard when Engro’s next withholding filings suddenly show a different pattern. It may also help assert later that you did not “hide” the change; you put FBR on notice. In the same letter (or a separate filing), EEDD’s position on how each stream will be treated can be outlined (e.g., “charter hire to be treated under Article 7 of treaty absent PE; O&M subject to sec.152(2A) with gross tax option elected”). Again, while FBR might not agree, you have documented your position officially.

- **Engro’s Involvement:** Engro, as a Pakistani company, will likely interact with FBR regularly (through tax returns, WHT statements, etc.). Ensure Engro’s tax team is prepared to **answer FBR queries** about the payments. For instance, if FBR asks “Why has the royalty withholding reduced drastically?”, Engro should be ready to explain that the contract nature changed and provide copies of the new agreements and EEDD’s treaty documents. Having a united front – Engro and EEDD telling the same story – is crucial. If needed, Engro can seek an FBR clarification itself on how to treat the payments (since it doesn’t want to violate withholding rules). Engro could request a written directive from its Commissioner under section 159 of the Ordinance for a lower or zero rate on charter payments, based on EEDD’s residency and no PE declaration. This is a local procedure Engro can use to protect itself.

**C. Timeline and Milestones:**

Develop a detailed **implementation timeline** that covers all steps with responsible persons and deadlines. Key milestones to include:

- **Contract Drafting and Signing:** Set a target date for finalizing the two new contracts (e.g. by end of QX 2025). Ensure that termination or amendment of the old contract coincides with the effective date of new ones to avoid overlap.

- **Internal Approvals:** Dates for board approvals from Excelerate/EEDD and Engro, as well as any lender or regulatory consents if required (for example, if the FSRU or terminal financing agreements require notification of material contract changes).

- **Tax Authority Filings:** Mark the date to submit any Advance Ruling application or withholding tax reduction request. Also mark the **15-day window** post-contract effective date for the Rule 19 gross tax election – e.g., if contracts start July 1, 2025, the election letter must be in by July 16, 2025【5†L33-L41】. Assign responsibility for drafting and sending that letter.

- **TRC and Documents:** If not already obtained, request the 2025 UAE **Tax Residence Certificate** for EEDD well in advance (sometimes it takes weeks). For 2026 and onward, note to obtain a fresh TRC each year. Likewise, if a US treaty might apply, ensure Excelerate LP’s US residency proof is available. Diary these annually.

- **Engro Withholding Adjustments:** Coordinate with Engro on **when they will implement the new WHT rates** in their payment system. Ideally, the first invoice under new contracts should reflect the new treatment (0% on charter, 9% or 15% on service). Engro might need to configure its accounting software or get internal approval to not deduct on charter – that might take time, so start that conversation early (possibly conditioned on receiving the TRC and a legal memo from EEDD).

- **Monitoring and Reaction:** Set checkpoints post-implementation: e.g., 3 months in, review that all filings were done (election, WHT payments correctly made). Also, anticipate that FBR could send a query or notice within a year – be prepared with draft responses. Mark the statutory timeframes: in Pakistan, WHT statements are filed monthly/quarterly and annual tax returns will need to reflect these transactions (Engro’s corporate tax return will show amounts paid to non-residents, etc., and EEDD’s branch if any will file returns). Ensure all forms capture the new reality (for instance, Engro might have to report royalty vs. service payments separately now).

- **Contingency Planning:** Decide ahead of time what to do if certain things don’t go as planned. For example, if the Advance Ruling request is denied or delayed beyond X date, will you proceed anyway or postpone? If FBR issues a show-cause notice for prior years’ tax, who will handle it (appoint a tax litigation team)? Having an action plan for these contingencies will allow quick responses rather than reactive scrambling.

**D. Ongoing Compliance and Review:**

- **PE Registration (if applicable):** If EEDD is maintaining a branch for O&M, register with the FBR (obtain National Tax Number for the branch) and obtain any necessary provincial registrations (for example, sales tax on services in Sindh, if the O&M is considered a service liable to provincial sales tax – worth checking with indirect tax advisors). Also open a Pakistan bank account for the PE if needed for tax payments.

- **Financial Reporting Impact:** The contract split may have accounting impacts (IFRS 16 lease accounting for Engro and Excelerate’s books). Inform your auditors of the change. Often, tax planning and accounting are linked; e.g., IFRS 16 requires separating lease and service components – your move actually aligns with that, so ensure the finance team leverages this as a supporting argument for why the split was done (audit trail).

- **Training and Internal Alignment:** Train the accounts payable and receivable teams of Engro and EEDD on the new process (so Engro’s team doesn’t accidentally keep withholding 12% on the whole or vice versa). Update any internal tax compliance checklists. Make sure the change is reflected in Engro’s **withholding tax returns** (so the payments are correctly categorized in the statements sent to FBR).

- **Monitor Tax Climate:** Keep an eye on any signs of how the FBR is viewing such arrangements. For instance, if any tax audit reports or court decisions come out regarding **FSRU leases or similar cases**, analyze those immediately for impact. The LNG sector and related tax issues (like the Tribune article highlighting FBR’s stance on Engro’s LNG terminal) indicate FBR’s awareness【28†L99-L107】. Being forewarned of FBR’s position via public sources or industry groups can help you adjust strategy (perhaps engaging lobby efforts if needed through industry associations to clarify tax rules for FSRUs).

- **Exit/Modification Strategy:** Although the focus is on implementing the split now, plan for how this arrangement might evolve. For example, if down the line Engro purchases the FSRU or the charter ends early, what are the tax consequences? Or if EEDD decides to transfer the FSRU to another affiliate – consider the tax impact (like any Pakistan source retirement of asset, etc.). Having a forward-looking view ensures no surprises. In immediate terms, also consider if any **project agreements or government consents** (like Port Qasim Authority, or the LNG supply chain agreements) require notice of this contract change.

By following the above steps, EEDD and Engro will create a solid audit trail and preparedness level that greatly reduces tax risk. The internal planning is just as important as the technical positions – successful tax planning often comes down to execution details and proving your case when asked. In conclusion, with meticulous planning, clear documentation, and strategic use of available tax provisions, the proposed contract split can be achieved in a **tax-efficient manner** while managing compliance in both Pakistan and the home jurisdictions. The aim should be to legitimately avail treaty and domestic law benefits (where applicable) **without crossing into “avoidance scheme” territory**, and to be ready to defend the structure as a sound business decision that also respects the tax laws.

**Subject: Technical Challenges in Filing Monthly Sales Tax Return – Request for Resolution and Guidance**

Respected Sir/Madam,

We write on behalf of our client, *United Energy Pakistan Limited* (“UEPL” or “the Company”), to highlight certain challenges encountered in the preparation and filing of monthly sales tax returns due to recent systemic changes in the return structure. The issues being faced are outlined below, along with a request for appropriate guidance and resolution from your good office.

---

**1. Nature of Operations and Reporting Obligations of the Operator**

UEPL is engaged in the exploration and production of oil and gas from multiple petroleum concessions across Pakistan. Being an upstream exploration and production (E&P) company, UEPL operates under a specialized accounting and reporting framework tailored to its sector-specific needs. Consequently, the classification and recording of assets, liabilities, income, and expenditures within its books of accounts substantially differ from standard commercial or industrial entities.

As the designated **operator** of various fields, UEPL bears exclusive responsibility for conducting operations, maintaining full and accurate accounts, incurring costs, processing payments, and fulfilling all tax-related obligations, including the reporting of relevant data in monthly sales tax returns. The operator’s reporting encompasses both its own share and, where applicable, the operational aspects of non-operators as well.

---

**2. Historical Filing Practice and Changes Introduced by FBR**

Historically, E&P companies, including UEPL, have followed the practice of:

- Declaring their respective share of monthly sales in **Annexure C** of the sales tax return; and  
- Reporting full production details relating to **natural gas and LPG** in **Annexure J**, including production attributable to non-operators.

This approach aligned with the regulatory requirement to discharge Federal Excise Duty (FED) on the entire volume of production prior to your good office becoming the manufacturer of the concession.

However, with the recent enhancements made to the FBR’s sales tax return filing system, **Annexure C is now auto-populated based on figures reported in Annexure J**. This system-driven link has created a mismatch between the actual revenue (based on the operator’s share) that UEPL intends to report in Annexure C, and the full production data disclosed in Annexure J. As a result, reconciliation between the two annexures has become problematic.

We respectfully request your good office to examine this matter and provide necessary guidance or system-level adjustments to enable proper reporting by E&P operators in line with their revenue-sharing model and legal obligations.

---

**3. Inconsistency in Unit of Measurement for Crude Oil**

It is also submitted that **Annexure J**, which was previously applicable only to natural gas and LPG, has now been extended to cover **crude oil** effective from **March 2025**. While the inclusion of crude oil in Annexure J is acknowledged, we wish to point out a critical inconsistency in the reporting mechanism—**the unit of measurement currently available for crude oil is restricted to kilograms (KG),** whereas the E&P sector universally adopts **metric tons** for reporting crude oil production and sales.

To ensure consistency with industry norms and to avoid reporting inaccuracies, we respectfully request that the return filing system be updated to incorporate **metric tons** as the standard unit of measurement for crude oil under Annexure J.

---

**4. Request for Resolution and Future Coordination**

In light of the above, we request your good office to kindly:

- Review and resolve the reconciliation issue between Annexure C and Annexure J for E&P operators;
- Enable appropriate reporting in line with actual revenue-sharing models and the operator’s obligations; and
- Update the unit of measurement for crude oil to “metric tons” in Annexure J.

We trust your office will appreciate the technical and sector-specific challenges faced by UEPL and other E&P operators, and will take necessary steps in coordination with relevant departments to facilitate accurate and compliant reporting.

Should any further clarification or meeting be required, we remain available to provide assistance and engage constructively on this matter.

With highest regards,  
Yours faithfully,  

**[Authorized Representative]**  
on behalf of  
**United Energy Pakistan Limited**

**Subject:** Clarification on Adjustability of Advance Tax under Section 236C and Related Matters

Dear [Client's Name],

Thank you for your follow-up email and for raising important questions regarding the treatment of advance tax collected under Section 236C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”), particularly in light of the recent amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2024.

Please find our detailed response below:

**1. Capital Gains on Immovable Property – Post Finance Act, 2024**

The Finance Act, 2024, effective from **July 1, 2024**, introduces a new regime for taxation of capital gains on disposal of immovable property. Under the revised framework, **any immovable property purchased on or after July 1, 2024**, and subsequently disposed of, will attract **capital gains tax at a flat rate of 15%**, **irrespective of the holding period**. This amendment removes the earlier tiered exemption structure based on duration of holding.

It is important to clarify, however, that **the tax deducted under Section 236C remains adjustable against the individual’s overall tax liability**, including salary income under Section 149, except in a specific circumstance discussed below. While the employee may now be liable to capital gains tax on account of an early disposal, the nature of the deduction under Section 236C does not automatically convert into final tax. It continues to retain its character as **advance tax**, unless rendered minimum under the special condition noted below.

**2. Minimum Tax under Section 236C – Exception**

As previously advised, **where the same property is both purchased and sold within the same tax year**, the advance tax collected under Section 236C is treated as **minimum tax** under the Ordinance and, consequently, is **not adjustable**. This specific provision overrides the general adjustability of the tax and must be carefully considered before any adjustment is allowed.

To ensure compliance, we recommend obtaining a **written declaration from the concerned employee** confirming that the property was **not acquired and sold within the same tax year**. In the absence of a same-year transaction, no further examination of the holding period or property documentation is necessary, and the advance tax may be safely adjusted against the salary tax liability.

**3. Historical Practice of Holding Period Verification**

We appreciate that prior to the Finance Act, 2024, your team exercised prudence by verifying whether the applicable holding period had elapsed before allowing adjustment of Section 236C tax. This approach aligned with the earlier regime under which capital gains were exempt after a prescribed holding period.

However, it is important to distinguish between **the existence of a capital gains liability** and **the nature of tax deducted under Section 236C**. Even where the gain is taxable—due to early disposal or, now, under the flat rate regime—the **advance tax collected remains adjustable** unless the transaction qualifies as a same-year purchase and sale. Therefore, holding period is not a relevant factor in determining the **adjustability** of Section 236C; rather, it influences the **amount of capital gains tax**, which will ultimately be assessed in the return.

**4. Adjustability of Other Withholding Taxes**

Your understanding is correct—**any tax withheld under provisions of the Ordinance that is designated as "adjustable"** (such as tax on sale of goods, rendering of services, imports, etc.) can be **credited against the individual’s final tax liability**, including tax withheld under Section 149. The Ordinance does not restrict the adjustment of such taxes to their respective income categories, unless they are expressly declared to be “minimum” or “final” in nature.

Accordingly, where withholding tax is advance in nature and the employee is not otherwise required to file a return, it is permissible to allow its adjustment through payroll, provided valid CPRs and declarations are available to substantiate the claim.

**5. Properties Acquired Before vs. After July 1, 2024**

We wish to emphasize that the flat 15% capital gains tax rate is applicable **only to properties purchased on or after July 1, 2024**. For immovable properties acquired **prior** to this date, the previous regime based on holding periods and corresponding exemptions continues to apply. Hence, when considering the capital gains implications for any employee, the **date of acquisition** remains a key factor in determining which regime governs the transaction.

---

**Conclusion**

In view of the above, we confirm the following:

- **Section 236C tax is adjustable** unless the property is purchased and sold within the same tax year.
- The **existence of a capital gains liability** (whether under the new flat rate or old regime) **does not preclude adjustment** of Section 236C, provided it is not minimum tax.
- Written declarations from employees should be obtained to confirm non-applicability of the same-year condition.
- **Other adjustable withholding taxes** may also be offset against salary tax where supported by valid documentation.
- Properties acquired before July 1, 2024, remain governed by the previous holding period regime for CGT purposes.

Should you require assistance in drafting an employee declaration template or need further support in evaluating the applicability of withholding adjustments, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Warm regards,  
**[Your Name]**  
Taxation Manager

**Subject:** Adjustability of Advance Taxes (Sections 236C & 236K) against Salary Tax Liability (Section 149)

Dear [Client Name],

Thank you for your query regarding whether the advance taxes deducted under Sections 236C and 236K of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the “Ordinance”) can be adjusted against the tax liability computed under Section 149 of the Ordinance. We are pleased to provide the following clarification in formal detail:

Sections **236C** and **236K** of the Ordinance deal with advance tax on property transactions (sale and purchase of immovable property, respectively). In general, both Section 236C (tax on sale/transfer of property) and Section 236K (tax on purchase/transfer of property) impose **withholding (advance) taxes** at the time of the transaction, which are **advance in nature and adjustable** against the taxpayer’s final income tax liability【10†L37-L45】. This means that the amounts collected under these sections are **not final taxes** (except as noted below) but prepayments of tax that can be credited against the taxpayer’s ultimate tax due (such as the tax liability on salary income computed under Section 149 of the Ordinance). In other words, a taxpayer can normally subtract the tax paid under Sections 236C/236K from their overall tax liability for the year when determining the net tax payable or refundable【10†L37-L45】.

However, it is important to highlight a specific **exception** regarding **Section 236C** (advance tax on sale of property). **If the same property was both purchased and sold within the same tax year, then the advance tax collected on its sale under Section 236C is treated as a *minimum tax*** for that transaction【6†L73-L76】. In such a scenario, the Ordinance deems the Section 236C tax as the minimum (or final) tax liability on the property income, **meaning it is **not adjustable**** against other tax liabilities. This rule is essentially an anti-avoidance measure to discourage quick buy-and-sell turnover of properties within one fiscal year. **Put simply, if a property is acquired and disposed of in the same tax year, the tax under Section 236C becomes non-adjustable (final) for that sale【6†L73-L76】.** 

In **all other circumstances**, both **Section 236C and Section 236K taxes remain fully adjustable**. If the property was **not** both bought and sold in the same year (which is the typical case), the advance taxes under **236C** and **236K** continue to function as **advance tax credits**. They can thus be **adjusted against the individual’s tax liability** under Section 149 (salary withholding) or any other taxable income when computing the annual tax. Aside from the special same-year disposition case under 236C, there is no provision in the law that renders these taxes as final; by default they are meant to be **credited in the taxpayer’s tax return or payroll tax calculation**【10†L37-L45】. Consequently, an employee who has paid advance tax on a property purchase or sale can have that amount offset against his/her tax-on-salary liability, reducing the amount of tax to pay under Section 149, **provided that the Section 236C tax is not subject to the above exception**.

**Procedural Compliance:** To ensure proper application of these rules, we recommend obtaining a **written confirmation from each relevant employee** (whose salary tax is being computed under Section 149 and who seeks to adjust 236C/236K taxes) **affirming that the property in question was not both purchased and sold within the same tax year**. This confirmation will serve as evidence that the advance tax under Section 236C does **not** fall under the “same-year sale” minimum tax category, and therefore remains adjustable for that employee’s tax computation. This step is crucial for compliance: it protects against inappropriately crediting an amount that should have been treated as a final/minimum tax in the rare case of a same-year purchase-and-sale transaction【6†L73-L76】.

If an employee **confirms that no such same-year property transaction occurred**, then **no further review of their property documents or holding period is required** from our end. In the absence of a same-year flip, the advance taxes under Sections 236C and 236K can be safely treated as **adjustable tax credits**, and we can proceed to adjust these amounts against their Section 149 tax liability without additional verification. Simply put, if there was no purchase and resale in the same tax year, the law treats the 236C/236K deductions as normal advance taxes that reduce the person’s overall tax liability, and we do not need to scrutinize the property details beyond the employee’s written declaration. This approach balances compliance with efficiency, ensuring that we give due credit for advance taxes paid while adhering to the conditions set out in the Ordinance.

**Conclusion:** In summary, **advance tax withheld under Sections 236C and 236K is generally adjustable against the final tax liability (including salary income tax under Section 149)**, consistent with the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001【10†L37-L45】. The **only caveat** is that under Section 236C, if the property was **acquired and sold within the same tax year, the tax on its sale becomes a minimum (non-adjustable) tax** and cannot be credited against other income taxes【6†L73-L76】. In all other cases, both 236C and 236K taxes are treated as **advance payments of tax** and **should be credited** accordingly in the annual tax computation. We therefore advise adjusting these taxes against the employees’ tax liabilities under Section 149, **after obtaining the aforementioned confirmation** that no same-year purchase-and-sale occurred for the properties in question. By doing so, we ensure compliance with the Ordinance while giving the employees the benefit of the tax credits to which they are entitled.

We trust that this addresses your query comprehensively. Our team remains available if you have any further questions or require additional assistance regarding the tax treatment of such transactions. Please feel free to contact us for any clarification.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Sincerely,  
**[Your Name]**  
Taxation Manager  
[Your Company Name]

**References:** Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Sections 236C, 236K, 149 (as amended); relevant tax guidelines and Finance Act provisions【10†L37-L45】【6†L73-L76】.

**Subject:** Follow-up on Adjustability of Advance Tax under Section 236C and Related Queries

Dear [Client's Name],

Thank you for your follow-up email and the pertinent questions regarding the treatment of advance tax under Section 236C in light of the recent amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2024.

We address each of your points as follows:

1. **Capital Gains Tax on Immovable Property – Post Finance Act 2024**

You are correct in noting that the Finance Act, 2024, has introduced a significant amendment to the taxation of capital gains on the disposal of immovable property. Effective **July 1, 2024**, any **disposal of immovable property purchased on or after this date** will be subject to **capital gains tax at a flat rate of 15%**, **regardless of the holding period**. This effectively eliminates the previously applicable exemption based on the length of holding.

However, please note that **this 15% tax is on capital gains**, not on gross consideration. The advance tax collected under **Section 236C** continues to be treated as **adjustable** under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, unless it falls under the same-year purchase and sale exception, in which case it becomes **minimum tax**. In all other cases, **Section 236C remains an advance tax**, and is **not a final discharge of tax liability**. Therefore, even if the employee is subject to capital gains tax due to early disposal of property, the tax collected under Section 236C can still be adjusted against any other tax liability, including tax on salary under Section 149, provided the same-year exception does not apply.

2. **Historical Practice Based on Holding Period**

Your earlier practice of requiring confirmation that the prescribed holding period had been met before allowing adjustment against salary withholding was based on the premise that capital gains were **exempt** after a certain period. However, that approach was more cautious than strictly required under the law. As per the scheme of the Ordinance, **advance tax deducted under Section 236C is adjustable unless the specific minimum tax condition applies** (i.e., the same property was bought and sold in the same tax year). The exemption or non-exemption of capital gain does not affect the *adjustability* of Section 236C tax; rather, it determines whether there is any **underlying tax liability**. The tax deducted under 236C does not lose its nature as an **advance tax** simply because the disposal triggers a taxable capital gain due to the holding period not being met.

Therefore, even if the employee is liable to pay capital gains tax due to non-fulfilment of the prior holding period condition, **Section 236C tax remains adjustable** unless the disposal falls under the same-year transaction condition.

3. **General Principle of Adjustability for Other WHT**

Yes, your understanding is correct. **Any advance tax deducted under the Ordinance that is categorized as “adjustable” in nature** (such as tax withheld on sale of goods, contracts, or services under Sections 153 or 148, etc.) can be **adjusted against any other tax liability of the taxpayer**, including salary tax under Section 149, subject to proper declaration and documentation.

The Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, permits the **set-off of adjustable advance tax across various heads of income**, unless a specific provision declares such tax to be “minimum” or “final” tax in nature. Thus, any employee who has suffered adjustable withholding tax, and who is not otherwise filing a return due to being solely salary-based, may claim adjustment against the salary tax withheld during the year, provided the relevant CPRs and declarations are made available.

4. **Additional Clarification – Properties Purchased After July 1, 2024**

We would also like to emphasize that **the flat 15% capital gains tax rate only applies to properties purchased on or after July 1, 2024**. For immovable properties acquired **before** this date, the **old regime based on holding periods** and **partial or full exemption** of capital gains continues to apply. Hence, when assessing whether an employee is liable to capital gains tax and whether any Section 236C adjustment is appropriate, it is important to consider the **date of acquisition of the immovable property**.

---

**Conclusion:**

In summary:

- Advance tax under **Section 236C remains adjustable**, except in the case of same-year purchase and sale.
- The imposition of capital gains tax due to shorter holding period **does not impact the adjustability** of Section 236C.
- Properties purchased after July 1, 2024, attract **flat 15% CGT** regardless of holding period.
- **Any other withholding tax categorized as adjustable** may also be offset against salary tax under Section 149, in accordance with the law.

Should you require, we would be happy to assist in preparing a standard declaration format for employees confirming that no same-year property transaction occurred, to support appropriate adjustments during payroll processing.

Please let us know if we can be of further assistance.

Warm regards,  
**[Your Name]**  
Taxation Manager  
[Your Company Name]

**BEFORE THE COMMISSIONER (APPEALS)**  
**SINDH REVENUE BOARD**  
**KARACHI**

---

### **IN THE MATTER OF APPEAL UNDER SECTION 57 OF THE SINDH SALES TAX ON SERVICES ACT, 2011**

**Appellant:** M/s Shell Pakistan Limited  
**SNTN:** S0804143-1  
**Subject:** Appeal against Order-in-Original No. 2686 of 2025 dated April 18, 2025  
**Adjudicating Authority:** Mr. Muhammad Yousuf Bukhari, Deputy Commissioner (Unit-21), SRB

---

### **GROUNDS OF APPEAL**

1. **Erroneous Demand on License Fee Charged to Dealers – Rs. 71,244,855**  
The learned Adjudicating Officer has grossly erred in raising a sales tax demand of Rs. 71,244,855 on account of license fees charged to dealers, allegedly under the scope of franchise services, without duly appreciating that the appellant had already discharged the tax liability attributable to the Province of Sindh. The appellant apportioned the license fee geographically, and the portion pertaining to Sindh was duly declared in its monthly sales tax returns and paid accordingly. The impugned order fails to acknowledge these payments and instead assesses the full amount without lawful basis, resulting in an unlawful duplication of tax liability.

2. **Non-Recognition of Prorated Tax Payments on Royalty and Trademark License Fees – Rs. 29,816,365**  
The impugned demand of Rs. 29,816,365 on royalty and license fees paid to Shell Brands International AG is likewise untenable. The appellant had meticulously apportioned the payments based on revenues generated from each province and Islamabad Capital Territory and deposited sales tax with the respective provincial authorities. The Sindh component was correctly reported and paid to SRB. Moreover, during constitutional proceedings before the Honourable Sindh High Court, SRB categorically submitted that it allows credit of sales tax paid to other jurisdictions, subject to production of valid documentary evidence. The impugned order, however, fails to consider this submission and disallows legitimate cross-jurisdictional credits without assigning cogent reasons, thereby violating the principles of legitimate expectation and administrative consistency.

3. **Misclassification of Technical Services as Franchise Services – Rs. 180,613,100**  
The learned Officer has further misapplied the law by treating technical services availed from Shell International Petroleum Company Ltd. (SIPC) for the period July 2011 to December 2012 as franchise services and raising a tax demand of Rs. 180,613,100. These services pertain to business support functions, and SRB has itself consistently classified them as *Business Support Services* from July 1, 2013 onward. The appellant has duly discharged tax on such services under the appropriate tariff heading from that date. Furthermore, the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue, in the appellant’s own case, has conclusively held that such services are not classifiable as franchise services. The retrospective reclassification now sought by SRB is not only inconsistent with SRB’s past administrative practice and settled legal position but is also contrary to judicial precedent, and therefore unsustainable in law.

4. **Disregard of Established Legal and Factual Positions**

**Subject: Clarification on Interpretation of Section 59AA(4) in Relation to Business Loss and Unabsorbed Depreciation**

Dear [Client's Name],

Thank you for your acknowledgment and for raising a pertinent follow-up query regarding the interpretation of Section 59AA(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

To address your query directly: the restriction imposed by Section 59AA(4)—which provides that "no relief under this section shall be available in respect of any loss which occurred prior to the formation of the group"—applies only in the context of losses claimed under the **group taxation regime** introduced by Section 59AA. This restriction pertains specifically to the consolidation of taxable income and losses at the group level for the purposes of computing group tax liability.

In our earlier opinion, we delineated the treatment of business losses and unabsorbed depreciation **in the context of unbundling** and not group taxation per se. For tax purposes, losses—particularly **business losses incurred prior to the effective date of the scheme of arrangement—remain with the transferor entity (KE in this case)** and are not transferred or allocated to the demerged entities, except for **unabsorbed depreciation** which, by established legal and administrative interpretation, can be apportioned to the transferee companies along with the relevant assets.

Therefore, **Section 59AA(4) does not override or restrict the treatment of unabsorbed depreciation allocated to transferee entities as part of a court-sanctioned demerger**. The clause is meant to prevent pre-group formation business losses (including both business loss and unabsorbed depreciation) from being claimed under the *group taxation regime* and does not impact the general treatment of unabsorbed depreciation under sections 22, 56, and 57 of the Ordinance in a demerger context. This position is supported by past interpretations and administrative practices which recognize the transfer of unabsorbed depreciation with assets, while retaining business losses with the original entity.

In summary, **Section 59AA(4) applies only to limit the availability of group taxation relief for pre-group losses**, but does not preclude the allocation of unabsorbed depreciation to transferee entities in a demerger. As such, your understanding is correct: **business losses remain with KE**, while **unabsorbed depreciation can be attributed to the respective recipient companies, subject to tax treatment consistency and audit trail of the transferred assets**.
