**Subject:** Response to Notice under Sections 111 & 122(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (dated May 6, 2025) – Tax Year 2019 – *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Limited*  

**Dear Sir,**

We write on behalf of *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Limited* (“the Company”) in response to your above-mentioned notice alleging suppression of sales amounting to Rs. 75,739,593 for Tax Year 2019. At the outset, we respectfully submit that the proceedings initiated are unfounded in fact and law. The Company has **fully declared and duly taxed** the aforesaid sales, and the manner in which the notice and prior proceedings were handled is procedurally irregular. We request that the notice under Section 122(9) be withdrawn and the Section 111 proceedings be annulled, on the following grounds:

## 1. Denial of Reasonable Opportunity (Procedural Impropriety)

The chronology of events shows a clear breach of fair procedure and FBR’s own instructions: 

- **Section 111 Notice and Hasty Order:** A show-cause notice under Section 111 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 was issued to the Company on April 22, 2025, requiring compliance by May 5, 2025 – a window of **only 9 working days** (excluding weekends) which is unreasonably short. On May 5, 2025 (the deadline), the Company submitted a written request for extension, citing genuine reasons to need additional time to gather and present records. **This extension request was summarily rejected on the same day, and an ex parte order under Section 111 was passed immediately on May 5, 2025**, without affording the Company a fair opportunity to be heard.

- **Violation of FBR’s Directions – 15 Working Days:** This abrupt conclusion of proceedings contravenes the principles of natural justice and the Federal Board of Revenue’s **own internal directions** which **require a reasonable opportunity of at least fifteen working days** for concluding such proceedings. FBR’s instructions dated December 13, 2024 (issued in light of the Supreme Court’s judgment on Section 111/122) mandate a careful sequence: issue a specific notice under Section 111, **wait for and consider the taxpayer’s reply**, pass a speaking order under Section 111, *then* proceed with a Section 122(9) notice if warranted【18†L47-L55】. In the present case, by refusing to grant any extension and finalizing the order on the very day of the reply deadline, the department failed to adhere to these binding instructions and denied the taxpayer a meaningful chance to explain its position.

In summary, the **haste in concluding the Section 111 proceedings (within the bare minimum time and on the same day as the extension request)** is arbitrary and unlawful. It offends due process and fairness. We respectfully submit that any order so passed in breach of FBR’s guidelines and without proper hearing cannot be sustained. 

## 2. No Concealment – Sales Already Declared and Taxed under Final Tax Regime

**There is no “suppression” or concealment of the Rs. 75,739,593 in sales.** The entire amount in question was **fully disclosed in the Company’s tax filings (under the Final Tax Regime) and in its sales tax returns** for the relevant periods. The allegation that this represents untaxed or hidden income is therefore incorrect. We outline the disclosures below:

- **Declaration in Sales Tax Returns:** *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.* filed monthly sales tax returns during Tax Year 2019 (covering the period July 2018 – June 2019), wherein the sales revenue of Rs. 75.74 million was duly reported. These official sales tax declarations evidence that the Company did not “suppress” its sales; on the contrary, the turnover was documented with the tax authorities contemporaneously. The record of sales tax returns (copies of which can be produced) confirms the sales figures now under scrutiny. It is illogical to assume the Company would disclose these sales for indirect tax purposes but intend to conceal them for income tax purposes.

- **Income Offered to Tax under Final Tax Regime (FTR):** Crucially, the **Company’s income from these sales was subject to the Final Tax Regime (FTR)**, as the receipts were from **export of services** on which a **presumptive tax of 1%** had already been paid/deducted as final discharge. In accordance with Section 115(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.* filed a **Statement of Final Taxation** for Tax Year 2019, declaring its relevant receipts and the tax thereon. The Company **declared taxable income of Rs. 59,212,100** in this statement (representing its export sales for the period it operated during the year) and paid 1% final tax on these receipts, as required by law. By doing so, the Company fulfilled its income tax liability on that income, since under the law the tax so withheld/paid is a **“full and final discharge” of tax liability for those receipts【23†L82-L90】**. 

    - Under Section 169 of the Ordinance (Final Tax Regime provisions), income on which final tax has been paid **“shall not be chargeable to tax under any head of income”** nor subject to further tax/adjustment【30†L94-L102】【30†L107-L115】. In other words, once the 1% final tax on export proceeds was paid, that income was **not required to be declared in a normal return nor could it be added again to taxable income**. The law **prohibits any additional assessment on such final-taxed amounts【30†L107-L115】**, barring exceptional circumstances which do not apply here. Therefore, the Department’s attempt to treat the declared export receipts as “concealed income” for normal tax purposes is fundamentally misconceived and contrary to the Final Tax Regime framework. 

- **No Unexplained Amount:** The invocation of Section 111 presumes an **unexplained or concealed income**. Here, the source and nature of the Rs. 75.74 million are entirely explained – these were proceeds of the Company’s business, already reported and taxed. The Department had **“definite information”** of these sales from the sales tax filings, and the Company’s own final taxation statement acknowledged them. Thus, there is no item of income that was hidden from the tax authorities. On facts, **Section 111 is not applicable**: you cannot allege “suppression of sales” when those very sales were transparently declared and taxed. Any addition made under Section 111 on this premise would be unwarranted and unlawful.

In light of the above, the Section 111 proceedings – which form the basis of the subsequent Section 122(9) notice – are **without merit**. The amount in question was already subjected to tax and disclosed; there is *no* revenue loss or evasion to address. Proceeding with an amendment of assessment under Section 122 based on a non-existent concealment not only violates the Final Tax Regime protections but also amounts to double taxation of the same income, which is impermissible.

## 3. Merger of Work Clothing into Industrial Clothing – Legal Effect

It is imperative to highlight that *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Limited* **no longer existed as a separate entity in 2019** due to a merger. The Company was amalgamated with *Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Limited* pursuant to a Scheme of Amalgamation that was duly **sanctioned by the Hon’ble High Court** via Order in J.C.M. No. 25 of 2018, dated March __, 2019. The merger took effect **from January 1, 2019** (the “Effective Date”). As a result of this court-sanctioned merger:

- **Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. stood dissolved** (without winding-up) as of the Effective Date, and **all its assets, liabilities, rights, and obligations vested by operation of law in Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.** (the surviving entity). In other words, from January 2019 onward, Work Clothing ceased to exist for legal and tax purposes, and Industrial Clothing assumed its business activities. 

- **Legal Proceedings Implication:** Any tax proceedings relating to Work Clothing after the Effective Date must legally be addressed in the name of the successor, Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. Initiating or continuing proceedings against a defunct entity is a nullity; it has been held as a settled principle that **actions against a non-existent company are invalid ab initio【24†L1-L4】**. The Department was duly notified of this merger (the fact of amalgamation is a matter of public record and was communicated through the merger scheme and regulatory filings). Therefore, the **notice dated May 6, 2025 issued to “Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.” is itself questionable and irregular**, since by that name the entity does not legally exist post-merger. Any assessment amendment should have been directed, if at all, to the successor company and cognizant of the merged status.

- We are providing, for your ready reference, a **copy of the High Court’s Merger Order (JCM 25/2018)** and the merger scheme documents. These establish the merger’s effective date and the dissolution of Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. as of that date. The law gives full force to such court orders; consequently, the tax machinery must give effect to the merger in its proceedings as well.

## 4. All Sales Accounted for in Successor Company’s Tax Returns

The merger during Tax Year 2019 means that the **sales spanning that year were split between the two companies’ respective tax filings**, and *collectively cover the entire Rs. 75.74 million*. Specifically:

- **July–December 2018 (Pre-Merger):** For the first half of the tax year (prior to merger), *Work Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.* itself carried out business. The Company **declared sales of Rs. 59,212,100 for the period July–Dec 2018**. These sales were reported in the monthly sales tax returns for those months, and the income therefrom was **offered to tax under the FTR** via the Section 115(4) statement for Tax Year 2019 (as noted above). The 1% final tax on this amount (approximately Rs. 592,121) was duly paid. Thus, the tax obligations on the **pre-merger period sales were completely discharged by Work Clothing** in its own capacity【30†L107-L115】.

- **January–June 2019 (Post-Merger):** Following the merger effective January 1, 2019, any sales made in the remaining half of the fiscal year were made by the amalgamated enterprise (under the name of Industrial Clothing). **These sales (approximately Rs. 16,527,493, being the balance of the Rs. 75.74 million)** were **declared in the sales tax returns for Jan–June 2019** by Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. Furthermore, Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. **included the revenue from Jan–June 2019 in its Income Tax Return for Tax Year 2020** (since Industrial Clothing’s tax year 2020 covered the financial year ending June 30, 2019, or alternatively the year ending December 31, 2019, depending on its accounting period). In that return, the income from the acquired Work Clothing business was reported and the applicable tax was paid. In short, the **successor company took up and duly reported the post-merger income** of Work Clothing as part of its own taxable income in the appropriate tax year, in accordance with law and the merger arrangement.

- We can confirm that **Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.’s tax filings evidence the inclusion of Work Clothing’s remaining sales**. The relevant excerpts from Industrial Clothing’s Tax Year 2020 return and financial statements (showing the combined revenue) are available for verification. This ensures that no part of Work Clothing’s 2019 sales went unreported. The **entire Rs. 75,739,593** was either reported by Work Clothing for the first half or by Industrial Clothing for the second half of the year – there is **no leakage or omission**.

Given the above, the Department’s basis for alleging suppressed sales appears to be a misunderstanding. It seems the sales for the full year 2019 were compared against only the amount declared by Work Clothing in its final tax statement (Jul–Dec 2018), without recognizing that the remainder was filed by the successor company. Once the merger and consequent split in reporting are understood, it becomes clear that the **full amount was taxed and declared between the two entities’ filings**. Therefore, **no income escaped assessment**: it was **assessed under the final tax regime for one part and under the successor’s return for the other**. The law does not permit taxing it yet again by treating it as “undeclared”.

## **Conclusion and Prayer**

In view of the facts and legal position explained above, the **initiation of proceedings under Sections 111/122(9) is unjustified** and the impugned actions are **without lawful authority**. The Company has complied with its tax obligations in good faith, and the merger has been carried out with due regulatory and legal sanction. There is simply no concealment of income nor any tax loss that would warrant the harsh invocation of Section 111 or an amendment under Section 122.

**We therefore respectfully request as follows:** 

- **Withdrawal of Section 122(9) Notice:** Kindly withdraw the show-cause notice dated May 6, 2025 issued under Section 122(9) (read with Sections 111 and 122) for Tax Year 2019, as the very foundation for this notice (the allegation of suppressed income) is negated by the facts on record. Any continuation of this proceeding would amount to taxing the same income twice and penalizing the taxpayer without cause.

- **Annulment of Section 111 Proceedings:** We further request that the order purporting to add Rs. 75,739,593 as concealed income under Section 111 be set aside/annulled. The proceedings were conducted in breach of due process (rendering the order voidable, if not void), and substantively, the addition is unsustainable given that the amount was already taxed and explained. We urge you to recognize that the Section 111 order is unlawful and should be revoked in the interest of justice and in line with the FBR’s own directives and the law.

Lastly, we draw your attention to the **documentary evidence** accompanying this letter, including: **(a)** Copy of the High Court’s Merger Order (JCM No. 25 of 2018) and Scheme of Amalgamation, **(b)** Copy of the Company’s Statement under Section 115(4) for Tax Year 2019, and **(c)** Relevant extracts of Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd.’s Tax Year 2020 income tax return and the Company’s sales tax filing summaries. These corroborate every factual assertion made herein. We trust that after reviewing these documents and our submissions, you will kindly **reconsider the stance** and resolve the matter in accordance with law by dropping the proceedings.

We appreciate your time and urge a swift resolution. **Thank you** for your fair consideration of this reply. If any further information or clarification is required, please do let us know; the Company remains available to cooperate fully. 

Yours sincerely,  

*(Authorized Representative for Work Clothing (Pvt.) Limited – now merged into Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Limited)*  

cc: **Commissioner Inland Revenue, Zone–Corporate, RTO Faisalabad** (for information)

Here is a more refined and polished version of the reply, with enhanced emphasis on the absence of concealment and the transition due to the High Court-sanctioned merger:

---

**WORK CLOTHING (PRIVATE) LIMITED**  
**Tax Year 2019**  
**Response to Notice under Section 122(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**

Dear Madam,

We refer to your notice bearing Barcode No. 100000239744602 dated May 6, 2025, issued under Section 122(9) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 ("Ordinance"), alleging suppression of sales amounting to Rs. 75,739,593 for tax year 2019.

At the outset, we wish to respectfully submit that the alleged suppression of sales is entirely misconceived and factually incorrect. There has been no concealment of income whatsoever. The entirety of the Rs. 75.74 million in sales was duly declared and offered to tax—partly by our client in its own filings up to December 31, 2018, and subsequently by Industrial Clothing (Private) Limited, the successor entity following a High Court-sanctioned merger effective January 1, 2019.

**Lack of Reasonable Opportunity and Premature Finalization under Section 111**

Your good office initiated proceedings under Section 111 of the Ordinance through a notice dated April 22, 2025, requiring compliance by May 5, 2025. Our client filed an extension application on the compliance date, which was rejected without justification, and an order under Section 111 was passed the very next working day. This summary disposal is in direct conflict with FBR’s own directive dated December 13, 2024—requiring at least fifteen working days for proper conclusion of proceedings and prescribing a sequenced approach beginning with a specific notice, followed by a considered response, and a speaking order before any further action. The undue haste with which the order was passed deprived our client of a fair opportunity and is inconsistent with the settled principles of natural justice.

**No Concealment – Sales Were Duly Declared and Taxed**

There is no basis for the allegation of concealment. The entire Rs. 75.74 million in sales was transparently reported to the tax authorities:

- For the period July to December 2018, our client declared sales of Rs. 59,212,100 in its monthly sales tax returns and filed a Statement under Section 115(4) of the Ordinance, offering this income under the Final Tax Regime (FTR). The 1% tax, being final discharge under Section 169, was duly paid.

- The balance sales of Rs. 16,527,493, pertaining to January to June 2019, though still appearing under our client’s name in the sales tax returns due to administrative delays, were in fact declared in the income tax return of Industrial Clothing (Private) Limited for tax year 2020, as per the merger arrangement and accounting year followed.

It is important to reiterate that the alleged "undeclared income" was not only reported but also taxed—part under the FTR and part under the normal regime by the successor entity. The claim of suppression is thus founded on a misapprehension of the correct legal and factual position.

**Merger into Industrial Clothing (Pvt.) Ltd. – Legal Effect and Tax Consequences**

Our client ceased to exist as a separate legal entity upon its amalgamation with Industrial Clothing (Private) Limited, effective January 1, 2019, through a scheme of amalgamation sanctioned by the Hon’ble High Court in JCM No. 25 of 2018. From that date, all assets, liabilities, and tax obligations vested in Industrial Clothing. Therefore, any proceedings beyond this date ought to have been initiated in the name of the successor company. Initiating proceedings against a non-existent entity is a nullity in law. For ease of reference, a copy of the High Court's merger order is enclosed as Annexure ‘A.’

**Conclusion**

In view of the above, the alleged concealment lacks both legal and factual merit. The income in question was:

- Declared by our client for the pre-merger period under the final tax regime;
- Appropriately reported by the successor entity for the post-merger period;
- Fully taxed in accordance with the law, with no element of evasion or suppression.

Accordingly, we respectfully urge your good office to withdraw the notice under Section 122(9), as it is predicated on a fundamental misreading of the facts and an unlawful order under Section 111. Continuation of these proceedings would unjustifiably result in double taxation and cause undue hardship to the taxpayer despite full compliance.

Yours sincerely,  
**[Authorized Representative's Name]**  
On behalf of Work Clothing (Private) Limited (now merged with Industrial Clothing (Private) Limited)

---

# Response to Notice under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (Tax Year 2018)

**Date:** June 5, 2025  

**To:**  
Mr. Umair Malik  
Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue  
Zone-VI, Range-B, Large Taxpayers Office (LTO) Karachi  

**Subject:** Reply to Notice under Section 221(2) – Tax Year 2018 (Rectification of Alleged Mistake in Assessment Order)

**Dear Sir,**

We refer to your notice dated May 29, 2025 issued under Section 221 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“ITO 2001”) for Tax Year 2018, regarding the proposed rectification of our assessment order. The notice suggests that a **minimum tax under Section 113** should be levied on the amount of **tariff differential subsidy** received by K-Electric Limited (“the Company”) during the year, treating the omission of such tax as a “mistake apparent from the record.” We hereby submit this formal response on behalf of K-Electric Limited, outlining our objections and legal position. We respectfully urge that the notice be withdrawn for the reasons detailed below.

## 1. Section 221 is Limited to Correcting Apparent Mistakes, Not Creating New Tax Liabilities

Section 221 of the ITO 2001 empowers the tax authority to rectify **“mistakes apparent from the record”** in an order. This provision is **strictly circumscribed** to correcting obvious errors (such as clerical slips or arithmetic miscalculations) that are **patent on the face of the record【23†L334-L341】【23†L341-L349】**. It **cannot be invoked to impose a new tax liability or re-open debatable issues**, as that would go beyond the scope of a mere rectification. The Hon’ble Superior Courts have consistently held that a rectification under Section 221 **is not a mechanism for revising or reassessing a matter of contention**, but only for correcting *obvious errors* that do not require elaborate reasoning or investigation【23†L334-L341】【23†L341-L349】. In **National Foods Ltd. (1992 PTD 570)**, the August Supreme Court interpreted the rectification power (under an analogous provision) and underscored that any mistake to be rectified must be one that **“floats on the surface of the record”**, obvious enough that it **“immediately strikes”** the reader as an error, and **does not require inquiry or deliberation**【23†L339-L345】【23†L345-L349】. Where resolving an issue would necessitate a **“long drawn process of reasoning”** or involves **two conceivable views**, it **falls outside the ambit of rectification**【23†L334-L341】【23†L341-L349】. 

In the present case, the applicability of minimum tax to the tariff differential subsidy is a substantive **legal and factual issue**, not a clerical or arithmetical mistake. It was **never an “obvious error” on the face of the assessment order**, but rather a conscious treatment of income based on the law and facts as understood during the assessment. The attempt to introduce a new tax charge now, under cover of “rectifying a mistake,” is **misplaced and unlawful**. Our assessment order as originally passed contained no inadvertent slip in computation; instead, it reflected the assessing officer’s deliberate position (with which your office now apparently disagrees). Such a **change of opinion** cannot be achieved through Section 221. Doing so **exceeds the statutory authority** conferred by Section 221 and contradicts the intent and language of that provision【35†L163-L170】【35†L165-L170】. Indeed, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has cautioned that where no *patent error* exists on the record, any attempt to **“rectify”** the order in effect amounts to an **impermissible review or revision** of the order【35†L163-L170】【35†L165-L170】. In **CIT Karachi v. Abdul Ghani (PLD 2007 SC 308)**, it was emphatically held that an authority cannot “sit on its own judgment” under the guise of rectification unless a clear and self-evident error is present on the record【35†L163-L170】. Charging a fresh tax where none was originally assessed is **far beyond the pale of Section 221**, and any such order would be ultra vires (without lawful authority)【35†L163-L170】【35†L165-L170】.

## 2. Rectification Power Cannot be Used to Levy or Enhance Tax

It is our firm position that **Section 221 cannot be used as a back-door to levy additional tax**. The rectification jurisdiction is **remedial** and *limited to corrections*; it **cannot create a new tax demand** that was not part of the original order. In other words, an omission to tax an item (especially when that omission was a result of an interpretative decision by the assessing officer) is not the kind of “mistake” that Section 221 can lawfully address. Using Section 221 in this manner would effectively convert it into a **reassessment or appeal**, which it is not. Courts have consistently clarified that **rectification is not a substitute for appeal** or reassessment【23†L334-L341】【23†L341-L349】. If an issue is **debatable or requires examination of evidence or law**, the proper course is to use the normal appellate or revisionary remedies – **not** the rectification provision【23†L339-L345】【23†L345-L349】. 

In the instant case, the question of **minimum tax on subsidy** involves interpretation of Section 113 of ITO 2001, factual characterization of the subsidy, and interaction with tax exemptions – all of which are complex matters of law and fact. Rectification cannot extend to such matters without overstepping legal boundaries. The **Hon’ble Lahore High Court** has noted in analogous circumstances that an order which effectively **reappraises facts or re-interprets law** to impose a liability, rather than correcting an obvious clerical mistake, is **“out of the contours of section 221”**【35†L153-L161】【35†L155-L163】. Charging a new tax through rectification would **defeat the purpose** of the rectification provision and render the statutory scheme of assessments and appeals nugatory. We submit that Section 221 **must not be stretched beyond its limited mandate**, and doing so in our case would be unjust and unlawful.

## 3. Issue Already Raised and Contested in Audit Proceedings

The subject matter of the notice – **the applicability of minimum tax under Section 113 on the tariff differential subsidy** – is **not a new issue** that arose after the assessment; it was in fact **explicitly raised and examined during the audit/amendment proceedings** for Tax Year 2018. During the course of an audit (under Section 177) and subsequent amended assessment proceedings under **Section 122(5A)** of ITO 2001, your department scrutinized the Company’s treatment of the tariff differential subsidy. The very question of whether that subsidy should be included in turnover for the purposes of minimum tax under Section 113 was **identified, debated, and addressed** by the assessing officer at that time. In other words, the tax authority had its opportunity during the audit to assess the subsidy receipt under the minimum tax provisions – and indeed it **took a position and made an adjustment** in the amended order (as detailed in point 4 below). 

Given this history, it is **factually incorrect** to characterize the non-levy of Section 113 on the subsidy as a “mistake” or oversight in the original assessment order. It was a *conscious issue under audit*. Once an issue has been examined in an audit and an order under Section 122(5A) has been passed, any further attempt to revisit the same issue via Section 221 is improper. **Rectification is not meant to cover issues that were already the subject of inquiry and determination** – especially not issues that remain **unresolved pending final outcome of those proceedings**. The notice under reply effectively seeks to re-open the concluded (or at least actively litigated) audit issue through a parallel path, which is neither legally tenable nor procedurally fair.

## 4. Minimum Tax on Tariff Subsidy Was Already Assessed – and Decided in Taxpayer’s Favor

As noted above, during the assessment proceedings (post-audit) under Section 122(5A), the department **did assess minimum tax on the tariff differential subsidy**. Specifically, an amount of **Rs. 32,970,950,000** (the tariff differential subsidy received from the Government) was treated by the assessing officer as part of the Company’s turnover and subjected to minimum tax under Section 113. This resulted in an additional tax demand of **Rs. 412,136,875** on that subsidy. However, this matter **did not end there** – the Company exercised its legal remedies against that amended assessment. Ultimately, the dispute over the minimum tax on the subsidy was **decided in the Company’s favor** under Section 124A of ITO 2001. We understand that the **order under Section 124A** gave effect to a higher authority’s ruling on the treatment of the subsidy (effectively recognizing that the tariff differential subsidy is **not subject to minimum tax**, in line with the Company’s stance). Thus, the impugned tax of Rs. 412.137 million was deleted and is **no longer part of the assessed tax liability**, as per the order under Section 124A.

In light of the above, there is **no “omission” or mistake** in the record – the record clearly shows that the issue was raised by the department and *resolved in the taxpayer’s favor*. The attempt now to levy the same tax again via rectification is **tantamount to undoing the effect of the Section 124A order**. It is respectfully submitted that your office **cannot ignore or override** the outcome of that duly concluded proceeding. Using Section 221 in this manner would violate the finality of the order passed under Section 124A, which holds the field unless overturned by a competent appellate forum. Put simply, the department **already had its chance to impose the tax and that attempt was adjudicated against the department’s position**. There is no apparent error here—only a disagreement with the outcome, which is not grounds for rectification.

## 5. Department’s Appeal on the Same Issue is Pending Before the ATIR

After the issue was decided in the Company’s favor (as mentioned above), the tax department **availed its appellate remedy** by filing an appeal before the **Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR)**. We are given to understand that the department’s appeal, challenging the relief granted to the Company regarding the minimum tax on the tariff subsidy, is **currently pending** adjudication before the ATIR. This means that the **identical issue** – whether the tariff differential subsidy is subject to minimum tax – is *sub judice* before the highest fact-finding appellate forum in the tax hierarchy. All arguments from both sides will be heard and a judicial decision will be made by the Tribunal in due course. 

In this scenario, the issuance of a rectification notice on the very same point effectively **parallels the appellate proceedings**. It creates a situation where two different wings of the tax administration are pursuing the same matter along two separate tracks: one before the appellate forum and another through an ostensible “mistake correction.” This duplicative approach is contrary to principles of judicial propriety and tax administration. Once an appeal has been filed on a matter, the original assessing authority **should not interfere with the subject of that appeal** except to implement the final appellate order. Notably, the law (and fairness) dictate that the outcome of the appellate process should not be preempted or circumvented.

## 6. **Notice under Section 221 Constitutes Parallel Proceedings, Rendering the Appeal Infructuous**

By initiating rectification proceedings under Section 221 while the department’s own appeal is awaiting decision, the department is, in effect, **mounting a collateral attack** on the favorable order that is under challenge. If the rectification were to be carried out (i.e. the minimum tax imposed through Section 221), it would **moot the pending appeal** or at least undermine it severely – because the department would achieve through rectification what it seeks through the appeal, i.e. the revival of the tax on the subsidy. This is an unacceptable *end-run* around the appellate process. It is well-settled that **parallel proceedings on the same issue should be avoided** to prevent conflicting outcomes and to uphold the integrity of the adjudicative process. The Hon’ble Lahore High Court has condemned such tactics, observing that where a taxpayer’s appeal was already filed, a rectification by the lower authority on the same matter was improper and beyond jurisdiction【35†L185-L193】. In essence, **once an issue is seized by an appellate forum, the proper course is to await that forum’s verdict**, rather than trying to proactively “fix” the original order. Continuing with the Section 221 notice not only violates the limited scope of that provision, as explained, but also **renders the appellate proceedings illusory** – a scenario that our courts and tribunals frown upon as a misuse of process.

We submit that allowing the Section 221 notice to proceed would amount to **parallel litigation** and would prejudice the Company’s legitimate expectation of having the matter decided once, on its merits, by the appellate forum. It would also be a **miscarriage of justice** to burden the taxpayer with a duplicate proceeding and potentially a duplicate demand on an issue already won at one forum. The taxpayer should not be vexed twice for the same matter. For these reasons, fundamental fairness and the orderly administration of justice demand that the rectification notice be withdrawn.

**Conclusion and Prayer:** In light of the above facts and legal authorities, it is abundantly clear that the impugned notice under Section 221 is **misconceived in law and fact**. The so-called “mistake” identified by your office is not a mistake at all, but a contested issue that lies outside the narrow ambit of Section 221. Rectification cannot be used to **impose a new tax** or to **re-agitate matters** already settled (or awaiting settlement) in audit and appeal. To proceed with such a rectification would be to **exceed your lawful jurisdiction** and nullify the ongoing appellate process【35†L185-L193】. We respectfully request that the notice dated May 29, 2025 be **withdrawn/cancelled** forthwith. The tax authorities are instead invited to await the outcome of the appellate proceedings before the ATIR, which is the proper forum for this dispute.

We trust that you will give due consideration to the legal points raised herein. The Company remains available to provide any further information or clarification your office may require. Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Yours faithfully,  

**For K-Electric Limited**  

*Authorized Representative*  

---

**References:**  

1. Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Section 221 (Rectification of mistakes).  
2. *National Foods Ltd. vs. CIT* – Supreme Court’s interpretation of rectification scope (1992 PTD 570)【23†L339-L345】【23†L345-L349】.  
3. *CIT Karachi vs. Abdul Ghani* – PLD 2007 SC 308: rectification jurisdiction is limited to errors apparent on record; no re-appraisal absent patent mistake【35†L163-L170】.  
4. High Court judgment in *Paracha Textile Mills Ltd.* (2010 PTD 1016) – rectification can correct only patent errors and not serve as review; two opinions on an issue means not an “apparent” mistake【23†L334-L341】【23†L341-L349】.  
5. Lahore High Court I.T.R. No.274/2024 – principle that if an issue was contested and decided, attempting rectification is outside the scope of Section 221 and improper, especially when appeal is pending【35†L185-L193】. (Referenced in **Business Recorder**, August 11 2022, and KTBA letter)【11†L174-L182】【35†L153-L161】.

**Subject: Objection to Enforcement of Section 138(3A) – Constitutional and Procedural Concerns**

Dear [Tax Authority's Name],

On behalf of our client, we respectfully submit the following objections regarding the enforcement of Section 138(3A) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as amended by the Tax Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025:

1. **Violation of Constitutional Rights**: The immediate recovery of tax liabilities under Section 138(3A), irrespective of pending appeals or existing stay orders, infringes upon the fundamental right to a fair trial and due process as guaranteed by Article 10A of the Constitution. This provision effectively nullifies the taxpayer's ability to seek appellate relief before enforcement actions commence citeturn0search1.

2. **Undermining Judicial Authority**: By mandating immediate tax recovery following a decision by the High Court or Supreme Court, the provision disregards the appellate process, including the right to seek a review under Article 188 of the Constitution. This approach undermines the authority of the judiciary and the sanctity of its decisions citeturn0search1.

3. **Bypassing Parliamentary Procedure**: The promulgation of this amendment through a Presidential Ordinance, without parliamentary debate or approval, contravenes Article 77 of the Constitution, which stipulates that taxation measures require legislative endorsement. This bypasses the democratic process and the principle of "no taxation without representation" citeturn0search1.

4. **Potential for Arbitrary Enforcement**: Granting the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) the power to recover taxes immediately, without affording taxpayers the opportunity to exhaust legal remedies, opens the door to arbitrary enforcement. This could lead to harassment and erode public trust in the tax system citeturn0search1.

5. **Negative Impact on Business Confidence**: The business community has expressed grave concerns over this amendment, warning that such coercive measures could deter investment and disrupt economic activity. The Karachi Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCCI) and other trade bodies have called for the immediate withdrawal of the ordinance to restore confidence among taxpayers citeturn0search4.

In light of the above, we urge the tax authorities to reconsider the enforcement of Section 138(3A) and to initiate a comprehensive review of its constitutional and legal implications. We advocate for a balanced approach that ensures tax compliance while upholding the rights of taxpayers and the principles of justice.

Sincerely,

[Your Name]

Please only only read the below response:

Mr. Umair Malik										May 27, 2025
Deputy Commissioner Inland Revenue
Zone-VI, Range-B, Large Taxpayers Office (LTO) 					       DT 000
Karachi


Dear Sir


K-ELECTRIC LIMITED
TAX YEAR 2016
NOTICE UNDER SECTION 221 OF THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001 [ORDINANCE] 
  READ WITH SECTION 138(3A) OF THE ORDINANCE FOR RECTIFICATION AND 
  RECOVERY OF TAX PAYABLE IN THE LIGHT OF DECISION OF HON’BLE 
  SINDH HIGH COURT DECISION DATED SEPTEMBER 30, 2024 


We refer to your notice No. 100000242266968 dated May 26, 2025, issued under section 221 of the Ordinance for tax year 2021 for rectification of the assessment order dated January 29, 2021 under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance. As per your notice, a minimum tax under section 113 of the Ordinance should be levied on the amount of tariff differential subsidy received by our client during the year, treating the non-levy of the same as omission apparent from the record warranting rectification under section 221 of the Ordinance. 

2.	In this context, our legal objection and position concerning your proposed action under section 221 of the Ordinance is given in the ensuing paragraph, for which reasons we respectfully request to withdraw your notice under an intimation to our client. Outlining our objections and legal position. We respectfully urge that the notice be withdrawn for the reasons detailed below.

3.	CONSTITUTIONAL OBJECTION TO SECTION 138(3A) OF THE ORDINANCE

3.1	At the outset, we submit that the insertion of section 138(3A) into the Ordinance, via the Tax Laws (Amendment) Ordinance, 2025, is unconstitutional. This provision mandates the immediate recovery of tax liabilities once a High Court or the Supreme Court has ruled on a pertinent issue, regardless of any ongoing appeals, statutory timelines, or existing stay orders. Such enforcement disregards the taxpayer's right to due process and a fair trial as guaranteed under Article 10A of the Constitution. Moreover, the promulgation of this amendment through presidential ordinance, bypassing parliamentary debate, contravenes Article 77 of the Constitution, which stipulates that taxation measures require legislative approval. The business community has expressed grave concerns over this amendment, warning that such coercive measures could deter investment and disrupt economic activity.

3.2	In light of the above, we urge your good office to reconsider the enforcement of section 138(3A) and to initiate a comprehensive review of its constitutional and legal implications. We advocate for a balanced approach that ensures tax compliance while upholding the rights of taxpayers and the principles of justice.


4.	SECTION 221 IS LIMITED TO CORRECTING APPARENT MISTAKES, NOT CREATING NEW TAX LIABILITIES

4.1	Section 221 of the Ordinance empowers the tax authority to rectify “mistakes apparent from the record” in an order. This provision is strictly circumscribed to correcting obvious errors (such as clerical slips or arithmetic miscalculations) that are patent on the face of the record. It cannot be invoked to impose a new tax liability or re-open debatable issues, as that would go beyond the scope of a mere rectification. 

4.2	In this respect, the Hon’ble Superior Courts have consistently held that a rectification under section 221 is not a mechanism for revising or reassessing a matter of contention, but only for correcting obvious errors that do not require elaborate reasoning or investigation. In National Foods Limited, reported as 1992 PTD 570, the August Supreme Court interpreted the rectification power (under an analogous provision) and underscored that any mistake to be rectified must be one that “floats on the surface of the record”, obvious enough that it “immediately strikes” the reader as an error, and does not require inquiry or deliberation. Where resolving an issue would necessitate a “long drawn process of reasoning” or involves two conceivable views, it falls outside the ambit of rectification.

4.3	In the present case, the applicability of minimum tax to the tariff differential subsidy is a substantive legal and factual issue, not a clerical or arithmetical mistake. It was never an “obvious error” on the face of the assessment order, but rather a conscious treatment of income based on the law and facts as understood during the assessment. The attempt to introduce a new tax charge now, under the guise of “rectifying a mistake,” is misplaced and unlawful. In the instant case, assessment order as originally passed contained no inadvertent slip in computation; instead, it reflected the assessing officer’s deliberate position (with which your office now apparently disagrees). Such a change of opinion cannot be achieved through section 221 of the Ordinance. Doing so exceeds the statutory authority conferred by section 221 of the Ordinance and contradicts the intent and language of that provision. 

4.4	Indeed, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has cautioned that where no patent error exists on the record, any attempt to “rectify” the order in effect amounts to an impermissible review or revision of the order. In CIT Karachi v. Abdul Ghani, reported as PLD 2007 SC 308, it was emphatically held that an authority cannot “sit on its own judgment” under the guise of rectification unless a clear and self-evident error is present on the record. Charging a fresh tax where none was originally assessed is far beyond the pale of section 221, and any such order would be ultra vires (without lawful authority).


5.	RECTIFICATION POWER CANNOT BE USED TO LEVY OR ENHANCE TAX

5.1	It is settled position that section 221 cannot be used as a back-door to levy additional tax. The rectification jurisdiction is remedial and limited to corrections; it cannot create a new tax demand that was not part of the original order. In other words, an omission to tax an item (especially when that omission was a result of an interpretative decision by the assessing officer) is not the kind of “mistake” that section 221 can lawfully address. Using section 221 in this manner would effectively convert it into a reassessment or appeal, which it is not. Courts have consistently clarified that rectification is not a substitute for appeal or reassessment. If an issue is debatable or requires examination of evidence or law, the proper course is to use the normal appellate or revisionary remedies not the rectification provision.

5.2	In the instant case, the question of minimum tax on subsidy involves interpretation of section 113 of the Ordinance, factual characterization of the subsidy, and interaction with tax exemptions all of which are complex matters of law and fact. Rectification cannot extend to such matters without overstepping legal boundaries. The Hon’ble Lahore High Court has noted in analogous circumstances that an order which effectively reappraises facts or re-interprets law to impose a liability, rather than correcting an obvious clerical mistake, is “out of the contours of section 221”. Charging a new tax through rectification would defeat the purpose of the rectification provision and render the statutory scheme of assessments and appeals nugatory. We submit that section 221 of the Ordinance must not be stretched beyond its limited mandate, and doing so in our client’s case would be unjust and unlawful.


6.	ISSUE ALREADY RAISED AND CONTESTED

6.1	The subject matter of the notice i.e. the applicability of minimum tax under section 113 on the tariff differential subsidy is not a new issue that arose after the assessment. The very question of whether that subsidy should be included in turnover for the purposes of minimum tax under section 113 was identified, debated, and addressed by the assessing officer at that time. In other words, the tax authority had its opportunity during the audit to assess the subsidy receipt under the minimum tax provisions and indeed it took a position and made an adjustment in the amended order. 

6.2	Given this history, it is factually incorrect to characterize the non-levy of section 113 on the subsidy as a “mistake” or oversight in the original assessment order. It was a conscious issue under audit. Once an issue has been examined in an audit and an order as a result thereof has been passed, any further attempt to revisit the same issue through section 221 is improper. Rectification is not meant to cover issues that were already the subject of inquiry and determination especially not issues that remain unresolved pending final outcome of those proceedings. The notice under reply effectively seeks to re-open the concluded (or at least actively litigated) audit issue through a parallel path, which is neither legally tenable nor procedurally fair.


7.	MINIMUM TAX ON TARIFF SUBSIDY WAS ALREADY ASSESSED – AND DECIDED IN TAXPAYER’S FAVOR

7.1	As noted above, during the assessment proceedings under section 122(5A) of the Ordinance, the department assessed minimum tax on the tariff differential subsidy. Specifically, an amount of Rs 22,880,854,000 (the tariff differential subsidy received from the Government) was treated by the assessing officer as part of our client’s turnover and subjected to minimum tax under section 113. This resulted in an additional tax demand of Rs 228,808,540 on that subsidy. 

7.2	Nevertheless, this matter did not end there, our client exercised legal remedies against that amended assessment. Ultimately, the dispute over the minimum tax on the subsidy was decided in our client’s favor under section 124A of the Ordinance by the Commissioner (Appeals). Thus, the impugned tax of Rs 228,808,540 was deleted and was no longer part of the assessed tax liability, as per the order under section 124A.

7.3	There is no “omission” or mistake in the records clearly show that the issue was raised by the department and decided in our client’s favor. The attempt now to levy the same tax again through rectification is tantamount to undoing the effect of section 124A order. It is respectfully submitted that your office cannot ignore or override the outcome of that duly concluded proceeding. There is no apparent error here, only disagreement with the outcome, which is not a ground for rectification.


8.	DEPARTMENT’S APPEAL ON THE SAME ISSUE PENDING BEFORE THE ATIR

8.1	After the issue was decided in our client’s favor (as mentioned above), the tax department availed its appellate remedy by filing an appeal before the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR). We are given to understand that the department’s appeal, challenging the relief granted to our client regarding the minimum tax on the tariff subsidy, is currently pending adjudication before the ATIR. This means that the identical issue whether the tariff differential subsidy is subject to minimum tax – is sub judice before the highest fact-finding appellate forum in the tax hierarchy. All arguments from both sides will be heard and a judicial decision will be made by the Tribunal in due course.

8.2	In this scenario, the issuance of a rectification notice on the very same point effectively parallels the appellate proceedings. It creates a situation where two different wings of the tax administration are pursuing the same matter along two separate tracks: one before the appellate forum and another through an ostensible “mistake correction.” This duplicative approach is contrary to principles of judicial propriety and tax administration. Once an appeal has been filed on a matter, the original assessing authority should not interfere with the subject of that appeal except to implement the final appellate order. Notably, the law (and fairness) dictate that the outcome of the appellate process should not be preempted or circumvented.


9.	NOTICE UNDER SECTION 221 CONSTITUTES PARALLEL PROCEEDINGS, RENDERING THE APPEAL 	INFRUCTUOUS

9.1	By initiating rectification proceedings under section 221 of the Ordinance while the department’s own appeal is awaiting decision, the department is, in effect, mounting a collateral attack on the favorable order that is under challenge. If the rectification were to be carried out (i.e. the minimum tax imposed through section 221), it would moot the pending appeal or at least undermine it severely because the department would achieve through rectification what it seeks through the appeal, i.e. the revival of the tax on the subsidy. This is an unacceptable end-run around the appellate process. 

9.2	It is well-settled that parallel proceedings on the same issue should be avoided to prevent conflicting outcomes and to uphold the integrity of the adjudicative process. The Hon’ble Lahore High Court has condemned such tactics, observing that where a taxpayer’s appeal was already filed, a rectification by the lower authority on the same matter was improper and beyond jurisdiction. In essence, once an issue is seized by an appellate forum, the proper course is to await that forum’s verdict, rather than trying to proactively “fix” the original order. Continuing with the section 221 notice not only violates the limited scope of that provision, as explained, but also renders the appellate proceedings illusory, a scenario that our courts and tribunals frown upon as a misuse of process.

9.3	We submit that allowing the section 221 notice to proceed would amount to parallel litigation and would prejudice to our client’s legitimate expectation of having the matter decided once, on its merits, by the appellate forum. It would also be a miscarriage of justice to burden the taxpayer with a duplicate proceeding and potentially a duplicate demand on an issue already won at one forum. The taxpayer should not be vexed twice for the same matter. For these reasons, fundamental fairness and the orderly administration of justice demand that the rectification notice be withdrawn.


10.	In light of the above, it is abundantly clear that the impugned notice under section 221 is misconceived in law and fact. The so-called “mistake” identified by your office is not a mistake at all, but a contested issue that lies outside the narrow ambit of section 221. Rectification cannot be used to impose a new tax or to re-agitate matters already settled (or awaiting settlement) in audit and/or appeal. To proceed with such a rectification would be to exceed your lawful jurisdiction and nullify the ongoing appellate process. We respectfully request that the notice dated May 26, 2025, be withdrawn/cancelled forthwith. The tax department is instead invited to await the outcome of the appellate proceedings before the ATIR, which is the proper forum for this dispute.


11.	We trust that you will give due consideration to the legal points raised herein. Our client remains available to provide any further information or clarification your office may require. Thank you for your attention to this matter.


Yours truly




cc	Mr. Pervez Musani
Director Taxation 
K-Electric Limited
Second Floor BOC Building
KE House, 39-B, Sunset Boulevard
Phase II, DHA
Karachi

To ensure accuracy and transparency, the Company has prepared the reconciled production statements for March and April 2025, reflecting the correct details of opening stock, actual production (based on cost of sales), and closing stock. These are enclosed herewith as *Annexure A*, and are being submitted for the record and for any future reference, including audit proceedings.

We also wish to highlight that the Company has engaged with the Oil Companies Advisory Council (OCAC) and other industry participants regarding this issue. It is understood that similar challenges have been faced across the sector. Some entities have either refrained from submitting Annexure J or have submitted declarations based on actual production while formally communicating the position to the tax authorities.

To provide accurate tax advice, could you please clarify the following:

1. What is the jurisdiction or country in which the SPV will be registered and operate?
2. Will the SPV be structured as a private limited company or some other entity?
3. Is there any specific incentive or exemption policy from the tax authority (e.g., Nepra or relevant energy regulators) that Prime Green Energy has previously availed?
4. Do you want us to reference the most recent tax laws or a specific tax year?

This will help ensure that we consider the correct laws and tax treatment in our research.

Dear Sir/Madam,

I hope this message finds you well. I am writing in response to your inquiry regarding the tax implications for the proposed Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) – a private limited company to be formed (in collaboration with Prime Green Energy Pvt. Ltd) for building, owning, and operating a solar power plant that will supply 100% of its electricity to a single industrial consumer. Below is a summary of the relevant Pakistani income tax provisions and our interpretations, addressing your specific questions:

## **1. Corporate Income Tax Exemption for the Solar Power SPV**  
Under Pakistan’s Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, **profits and gains derived from an electric power generation project are **_**generally exempt from corporate income tax**_**, subject to certain conditions【42†L179-L187】. In particular, **Clause 132 of Part I of the Second Schedule** provides a tax exemption for income of companies formed solely to carry out power generation projects (which includes solar power projects)【30†L60-L67】. However, recent amendments have imposed **time-bound eligibility criteria** for new projects. According to the law as updated: 

- **Government Approval Deadline:** The exemption applies only if the company/project entered into an agreement with, or was issued a Letter of Intent (LOI) by, a Federal or Provincial Government entity on or before **30 June 2021**, **and** obtained a corresponding Letter of Support (LOS) on or before **30 June 2023**【42†L179-L187】【1†L383-L389】. This effectively means that **new power projects initiated after these cutoff dates do not automatically qualify for the tax holiday**. Projects that met these deadlines are “grandfathered” and continue to enjoy the exemption for their operational life (now capped at the project’s life or 25 years from commissioning, whichever is earlier, per Finance Act 2022)【16†L179-L187】. 

- **Sole Purpose Entity:** The SPV must be **organized as a company dedicated exclusively to operating the power plant**. The tax ordinance historically required that the project be “owned and managed by a company” formed for that purpose and registered in Pakistan【11†L279-L288】. In practice, this means the SPV’s memorandum of association should restrict its business to electricity generation/supply from the solar project. Having the sole objective of power generation is a key condition for the income to be treated as exempt. 

- **No Prior Business Reconstruction:** The project/company **should not be formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business**【11†L283-L288】. In other words, the tax exemption is intended for **new, greenfield projects** rather than a reorganization of an already operational taxable entity. If the SPV is a completely new company for a new solar plant (not just a continuation of an older business), this condition is satisfied by design.

- **Private Ownership:** Another condition in the law is that the company not be owned 50% or more by the government or a local authority【11†L290-L293】 (this is usually not an issue for privately-sponsored projects, but it’s worth noting that the classic IPP tax exemption was meant for independent power producers, not government-run projects).

If **your SPV meets the above criteria**, then **its income from the solar plant would be **_**exempt from corporate income tax**_** under the Ordinance**【30†L60-L67】. Notably, the exemption covers income generated from the sale of electricity (and has even been interpreted by courts to cover incidental income related to the project’s operations)【11†L299-L307】. This means the SPV would not pay the standard corporate tax (currently around 29% for companies) on its profits from the project.  

However, **if the project does _not_ meet the government approval timeline** – for example, if this SPV is being set up now without having obtained an LOI by the June 2021 deadline – then **the SPV would **_**not**_**** be entitled to the above tax exemption under current law**. In that case, its income would be taxable at the normal corporate rate and it would be subject to the usual tax regime (depreciation, tax credits, etc., but no blanket exemption). Given that your scenario involves a dedicated supply to a private industrial customer (as opposed to selling to the national grid under a government power purchase agreement), it’s important to confirm whether any LOI or implementation agreement with a government body was in place by the required date. If not, the SPV will likely fall outside the scope of Clause 132’s exemption as it stands【42†L179-L187】. (There have been industry appeals on this point, because the 2021 proviso unintentionally excluded some private power arrangements from the exemption【42†L185-L193】, but unless the law is amended, one should assume no exemption for post-2021 projects without government LOI.)

## **2. Withholding Tax on Electricity Payments by the Industrial Off-taker**  
In Pakistan’s tax framework, businesses making certain payments are required to withhold income tax at source under Section 153 of the Income Tax Ordinance (commonly on payments for goods, services, contracts, etc.). **Electricity payments, however, are a special case.** **The law **_**exempts payments for electricity supplied by a power company from the scope of withholding tax**_**.** Specifically, **Clause 46AA of Part IV of the Second Schedule** stipulates that **Section 153’s withholding requirements do **_**not**_** apply to payments made to companies for the supply of electricity (or gas)**【25†L2000-L2008】. In practical terms, this means when the industrial establishment pays the SPV for the electricity each month, it is **not required to deduct any income tax from the payment**. The full amount can be paid to the SPV without withholding. 

To clarify, this exemption from withholding is **irrespective of whether the SPV’s income is tax-exempt or taxable**. It’s a blanket rule aimed at utility payments. For example, just as distribution companies (e.g. WAPDA, KE) receive power payments gross, a private power producer supplying a single client is accorded the same treatment. Thus, your industrial customer should **not withhold tax on the electricity bill payments** to the SPV【25†L2000-L2008】. We do recommend informing the customer of this provision, and the SPV should keep a copy of the relevant law handy, to avoid any confusion with their accounts department. If necessary, a specific exemption certificate can be obtained from FBR, but generally the law itself (Second Schedule clause 46AA) is sufficient authority for no tax deduction. 

## **3. Conditions and Procedures to Avail the Tax Exemption**  
To ensure the SPV qualifies for the corporate tax exemption (if it is eligible under the timing rules discussed above), you should be mindful of a few **important conditions and procedural steps**:

- **Formation of the SPV:** Incorporate the company with the **correct object clause** (power generation). The SPV’s constitutional documents should reflect that its *sole purpose is to build/own/operate the solar power plant and supply electricity*. This satisfies the “owned and managed by a company formed for operating the project” requirement【11†L279-L288】. Since you’ve indicated it will be a private limited company, ensure it is duly registered under the Companies Act and has its **registered office in Pakistan** (standard practice, which aligns with the condition in the law【11†L279-L288】).

- **Government LOI/LOS (If applicable):** If not already obtained, determine whether the project can secure an official **Letter of Intent and Letter of Support from a relevant government agency**. For renewable energy projects, typically the Alternative Energy Development Board (AEDB) or Provincial Energy Department issues LOIs, and entities like the Private Power Infrastructure Board (PPIB) issue LOS for projects under the power policy. These letters would need to have been in place by the cutoff dates (June 2021 for LOI, June 2023 for LOS) to **claim the Clause 132 exemption**【42†L179-L187】. Make sure you have copies of these letters and any project agreements with government, as **evidence to support the tax-exempt status** of the SPV’s income.

- **Power Generation License:** Separately from tax, ensure the SPV obtains a **generation license from NEPRA** (or the relevant authority) to operate the solar plant and deliver power to the industrial client. While this is a regulatory requirement (not a tax requirement), having the proper license and approvals will reinforce that the SPV is a bona fide power producer under Pakistan’s power policies – which ties into qualifying under the “electric power generation project set up in Pakistan” language of the tax exemption【1†L383-L389】. Compliance with sector regulations can thus be indirectly relevant for tax purposes.

- **Tax Filings and Compliance:** To avail the exemption, the SPV will still need to **file corporate income tax returns** annually, even if its taxable income is zero due to the exemption. In the return, the **income from the sale of electricity would be declared but shown as exempt** under the relevant clause of the Second Schedule. It’s prudent to **cite “Clause 132, Part I, Second Schedule, Income Tax Ordinance, 2001” in the return** and attach supporting documents (e.g. the LOI/LOS, power purchase agreement or energy supply contract, and the generation license) to substantiate the claim. Typically, no special approval from FBR is required to claim an exemption that is clearly granted by law, but maintaining a robust record is important in case of any query or audit.

- **Withholding Tax Exemption Certificate:** As noted above, receipts from electricity sales are not subject to withholding under Section 153【25†L2000-L2008】. To reinforce this, the SPV **may apply for an exemption certificate from the tax authorities under Section 159** of the Ordinance, confirming that no tax is to be withheld on its electricity receipts (given the statutory exemption). This is not strictly mandatory, but can be useful for the SPV’s customer (the industrial buyer) for their internal compliance peace of mind. Similarly, if the SPV expects to earn any ancillary income (for example, interest on bank deposits of project funds), and if that income would have otherwise had tax withheld (e.g. banks withholding on interest under Section 151), the SPV can present its **exempt status certificate** to avoid upfront deductions. (Courts have held that interest earned on funds related to an exempt power project is also exempt as part of the project’s “profits and gains”【11†L299-L307】, but obtaining a ruling or certificate in advance can prevent cash flow issues.)

- **Other Taxes:** The SPV should also confirm if any other taxes or duties apply. For instance, **minimum tax on turnover** has been an issue for power companies in the past. Currently, **power distribution companies** have sought clarity that the minimum tax under Section 113 does not unfairly apply when their income is regulated【42†L147-L155】【42†L165-L173】. In the case of an IPP/solar project company enjoying a profits exemption, the minimum tax is generally not applicable (since the exemption overrides it), but it’s wise to monitor Finance Act changes on this front. Additionally, **sales tax** on the sale of electricity should not be applicable when the seller is an IPP selling to an end consumer; electricity is typically taxed as a supply by distribution companies under a separate regime, so in your one-customer scenario this may not arise (the arrangement may be considered a supply of power which could be outside the scope of sales tax, or subject to specialized treatment). You may want to seek a specific ruling on the sales tax aspect from a sales tax expert or **consult NEPRA’s guidelines** if any, to ensure the billing is structured correctly.

In summary, **if the SPV’s solar power project falls under the qualifying criteria (established under the pre-2021 power policy framework with the necessary government approvals), it can avail a full corporate income tax exemption on its operating profits**【1†L383-L389】. This is a significant incentive provided to encourage investment in renewable energy. On the other hand, if those criteria are not met, the SPV would be treated like a normal company for tax purposes (no special exemption). Regardless of exemption status, **the industrial buyer is **_**not**_** obliged to withhold tax on the electricity payments** to the SPV, due to the specific exclusion for electricity supply payments in the tax law【25†L2000-L2008】. 

**Recommended Action:** Review any existing LOI, LOS, or energy purchase agreements to ascertain the SPV’s eligibility for the tax holiday. If eligible, prepare the documentation to support the exemption. If not eligible, factor the standard corporate tax into the project’s financial model (though note that even without an exemption, the SPV would still benefit from accelerated depreciation and other normal tax allowances for renewable energy assets, which can reduce taxable income significantly in initial years). It would also be prudent to engage with the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) or a tax advisor to obtain any available clarification or certification in advance, ensuring smooth compliance. Recent industry commentary (e.g. by K-Electric and others) suggests there have been requests to extend or reinstate tax breaks for private power producers【42†L185-L193】, but until any new legislation is passed, we must adhere to the current law as explained above.

Please let us know if you need further details on any of the above points or assistance with the procedural steps. We will be happy to help facilitate the compliance process for your SPV. 

Sincerely,  
[Your Name]  
Tax Advisor / Consultant  

**References:**  

- Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Second Schedule, Part I, Clause 132 (exemption for profits of power generation projects)【42†L179-L187】【1†L383-L389】; Part IV, Clause 46AA (exclusion of electricity payments from withholding tax)【25†L2000-L2008】.  
- Federal Board of Revenue / Government of Pakistan – Finance Act 2021 & 2022 amendments to tax exemptions for IPPs【42†L173-L184】【16†L179-L187】.  
- National Electric Power Regulatory Authority (NEPRA) / Power Policy 2015 – Incentives for private power projects including income tax exemptions【19†L142-L150】.  
- Business Recorder news report, *“Finance Bill 2022: Fundamental policy for IPPs changed,”* highlighting the continuation and duration of tax exemptions for power plants under the pre-2021 regime【16†L179-L187】.  
- Supreme Court of Pakistan rulings (e.g. *Uch Power Pvt. Ltd. case*) interpreting the scope of “profits and gains” from power generation projects and confirming conditions for tax exemption【11†L279-L288】【11†L299-L307】.  
- PwC Pakistan Tax Summaries (2024) – confirming tax exemption for electric power generation profits (with applicable cut-off dates)【1†L383-L389】.  
- Clause 46AA, Part IV Second Schedule (via Finance Act 2020) – list of recipients excluded from withholding tax (includes companies paid for supply of electricity)【25†L1998-L2006】.

Please read the below email and prepare a response on email format: 

Prime green energy Private Ltd is considering to collaborate with another company and form an SPV. This SPV will sign a contract with an industrial establishment to build, own and operate a solar plant. The electricity produced from this solar plant will be 100% supplied to the industrial establishment for its energy needs. The solar plant will seek necessary approvals from Nepra.

We wish to understand the corporate income tax implications of the SPV on supply of electricity to the industrial establishment. We have been given to understand by the company we are collaborating to form an SPV, that we will be subject to 29% corporate income tax. Our understanding from Prime Green energy’s experience is that solar entities that have the sole objective of generating and supplying electricity are exempt from income tax implications. Can you please advise on this and whether the industrial establishment while making payment for its monthly electricity bills is going to deduct any withholding tax?

Thank you for the clarification. I’ll look into the corporate income tax implications for an SPV registered in Pakistan that will build, own, and operate a solar power plant dedicated to supplying electricity to an industrial establishment. I’ll also examine the relevant provisions under the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, particularly those concerning exemptions for solar energy entities, and clarify whether withholding tax would apply on electricity payments from the industrial client.

I’ll get back to you shortly with a detailed response.
The jurisdiction of the SPV is Pakistan; might be a private limited company, and an exemption is available in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

**Subject:** Taxability of Receipts under FTR/NTR Regimes and Applicability of Super Tax

Hi Anwar,

Thank you for your email.

As per our understanding, FOTCO received amounts of Rs. 694 million and Rs. 1,399 million during the tax period July 2024 to June 2025, which relate to outstanding balances from prior years. Of these, Rs. 694 million pertains to the Final Tax Regime (FTR), while Rs. 1,399 million falls under the Normal Tax Regime (NTR).

The key questions are:
1. Whether income tax should be discharged on the Rs. 694 million under the FTR regime.
2. Whether the Rs. 1,399 million, relating to NTR, should be subject to Super Tax under section 4B, considering it pertains to tax years 2020 and 2021—periods during which the Super Tax rate under section 4B was zero.

**1. Income Tax on Rs. 694 Million under FTR Regime:**  
Under the FTR regime, income is generally taxed on a **receipt basis**, and the applicable withholding tax is treated as final.
