We need your guidance regarding the correct tax treatment for capital gains on an investment in a mutual fund (money market) where more than 50% of the portfolio is debt-based.
Specifically, we would appreciate your advice on the following:
The tax chargeability on capital gains from this investment, considering it qualifies as a separate block of income.
The applicable withholding tax rate on redemption.
Whether, given the separate block of income treatment, the tax should be considered within the normal tax regime (NTR), or if it would be NTR/MTR plus tax on the separate block of income.
Your input on this matter will be highly appreciated. Please let us know if any additional information is required.
Pakistan.
Could you please confirm which jurisdiction this tax query relates to (e.g., Pakistan, UAE, etc.)? Tax treatment varies by country, and this will help ensure accurate guidance.

Thanks for confirming the jurisdiction is Pakistan. I’ll look into the correct tax treatment of capital gains on debt-based mutual fund investments in Pakistan, including chargeability, applicable withholding tax on redemption, and how these gains fit within the normal tax regime or separate block of income. I’ll get back to you shortly with a detailed response.

# Tax Treatment of Capital Gains from Debt-Based Mutual Funds in Pakistan

Investments in money market or income mutual funds (where more than 50% of the portfolio income is derived from debt instruments) have a distinct tax treatment in Pakistan. In particular, **capital gains** from selling (redeeming) your mutual fund units are handled as a **separate block of income** and not mixed with your normal taxable income. Below is a detailed breakdown addressing each concern:

## Capital Gains as a Separate Block of Income

**Chargeability:** Capital gains realized on the sale/redemption of mutual fund units are taxed under a separate regime, rather than under the normal tax slab rates. Section 37A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 specifically deals with capital gains on **securities**, which include units of mutual funds and collective investment schemes. For **individual investors (filers)**, the tax on these capital gains is a **flat percentage of the gain**, **independent of your other income**【1†L463-L470】【12†L177-L185】. This means such gains are not added to your salary/business income for rate determination; instead, they are taxed in isolation at prescribed rates (often referred to as **“separate block” or final tax**).

- **Tax Rate on Capital Gains:** For **individuals/AOPs** who are on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL), the **capital gains tax (CGT)** on mutual fund units (whether equity or debt-based funds) is **15% of the gain**【11†L134-L144】. This 15% is the applicable **separate block tax rate** (also often the final tax) on the gain. It applies irrespective of your income bracket since it’s outside the Normal Tax Regime.

- **Special Treatment for Filers vs Non-Filers:** Being a filer (ATL) is important. If you are a **non-filer (inactive taxpayer)**, the benefit of the fixed 15% rate is not fully available. Under recent changes, **non-filers** must pay tax on such capital gains at **normal slab rates** (with a minimum of 15% and up to 45%)【9†L88-L94】【12†L177-L185】. In other words, non-filers are effectively pushed into the Normal Tax Regime for these gains (with at least 15% tax), whereas **filers are charged a flat 15%**. This creates an incentive to file taxes to avail the concessional flat rate on capital gains.

- **Holding Period Consideration:** Previously, Pakistan’s tax law provided an exemption on capital gains from listed securities (including mutual fund units) if the holding period exceeded 6 years. **No capital gains tax was charged on securities held for more than 6 years**. This rule still applies to assets **acquired on or before June 30, 2024** – for those, if you hold your mutual fund units for over six years, no CGT is due on redemption【3†L551-L554】【11†L146-L148】. However, **for units acquired after July 1, 2024, the flat 15% tax applies regardless of holding period** (the Finance Act, 2024 removed the unlimited holding period exemption for new acquisitions)【6†L1392-L1400】【12†L177-L185】. In short, long-term holdings bought after mid-2024 no longer enjoy a full exemption; they will be taxed at 15% whenever sold (for filers).

**Key Point:** Treat these capital gains as a separate block of income (often part of the Final Tax Regime). You **cannot offset** this gain with losses from other heads of income, nor can you reduce it by deductions/allowances applicable to normal income. Likewise, the tax paid on this gain is typically **final** – it satisfies your tax liability on that gain without further recalculation under the normal regime【1†L463-L470】【9†L88-L94】. You will report the capital gain in the “capital gains” section of your tax return (separately from salary, business income, etc.), and tax is computed at the fixed rate.

## Withholding Tax on Redemption of Units

When you redeem (sell) units of a mutual fund, the fund manager (Asset Management Company or the trustee of the fund) is **required to withhold applicable capital gains tax at source** and deposit it to the FBR. The withholding acts as an advance/final tax on your capital gain.

- **Rate of Withholding on Redemption:** For **individual investors**, the withholding tax on capital gain at the time of redemption is **15% of the gain**【11†L134-L144】. This applies to gains from **money market or debt-based funds** just as it does for equity funds – currently there is no higher rate for individuals on debt-fund gains; it’s a flat 15% for filers in either case. (Before Finance Act 2024, this withholding was 10%, but it has since been increased to 15%【6†L1376-L1384】【12†L183-L190】.)

- **If Investor is a Company:** The regime distinguishes between “stock funds” and “other funds” for **corporate investors**. A “stock fund” typically means a mutual fund with a high equity exposure (often defined by tax law as a fund with a certain minimum percentage invested in stocks). A “money market fund” with >50% in debt would be classified as **“other fund” (non-stock fund)**. In the case of a **company** redeeming units: 
  - If it’s an equity **stock fund**, CGT is withheld at **15%**.
  - If it’s a **debt/money-market fund**, CGT is withheld at **25%** for the company【11†L128-L136】【11†L134-L144】.
  
  These rates for companies reflect that corporate investors in debt-heavy funds pay a higher flat CGT (25%) on redemption. (Note: 25% aligns roughly with corporate tax rates and was intended to prevent companies from getting a lower rate via mutual fund investments.)

- **No Tax Withheld for Long Holding (Legacy Investments):** As noted, if your units were acquired on or before June 30, 2024 and you have held them for over **6 years**, **no capital gains tax will be withheld on redemption**【11†L146-L148】. The mutual fund will not deduct CGT in such cases, as the gain is exempt by law. This is more relevant for long-term investments made prior to the recent law change. For units bought after July 1, 2024, however, the fund will always deduct 15% (for individuals) whenever you redeem, regardless of holding period.

- **Final Discharge:** The amount withheld by the mutual fund at redemption is typically considered **full and final discharge of tax liability on that capital gain** (for filers). In practice, this means if you’re a filer, the 15% WHT on your gain is your final tax on that income – you generally won’t owe additional tax on it when filing your return, nor can you claim a refund if your personal tax rate is lower【3†L548-L554】【10†L118-L125】. (Do ensure to report the gain and tax withheld in your return under “Separately Taxed / Final Tax Income” sections.)

**Applicable Law:** The above withholding mechanism and rates are outlined in the **First Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** – specifically **Division VII, Part I** (which deals with tax on **capital gains from securities**) and the related provisions. The Finance Act, 2024 amended these rates (as noted below). Section 37A of the Ordinance is the governing section for taxation of securities (including mutual fund units), and Section 100B along with the **Eighth Schedule** (for stock exchange transactions) provides the framework for how such gains are computed and taxed. Mutual funds, via their trustees, act as withholding agents for this purpose.

## Normal Tax Regime (NTR) vs Final Tax Regime for This Income

Given that capital gains from mutual fund investments are a separate block of income, **they are not part of the Normal Tax Regime (NTR)** calculation of your total income. Instead, they fall under what is often called the **Final Tax Regime (FTR)** or a *separately taxed income* category. Here’s how it works in practice:

- **Exclusion from NTR:** You do **not** include these capital gains in your taxable income when computing tax under the normal slabs/rates. For example, if you have a salary or business income, you will calculate tax on those under the normal progressive rates (for individuals) or corporate rate (for companies) **separately**. The capital gain from the mutual fund is taxed **in addition** at the fixed rate (15% or 25% as applicable) on its own【1†L463-L470】. Essentially, the CGT on mutual fund units is **ring-fenced** – taxed on its own and kept apart from the NTR calculation of other income.

- **Return Filing:** In your income tax return, Pakistan’s FBR forms have separate sections for “Capital Gains” and “Final / Separate Income.” You would declare the gain from the mutual fund under that section, and the tax withheld (15%) is usually treated as the final tax paid on that gain. It does not get recomputed based on your tax slabs. So, whether your regular income falls in a 0%, 10%, or 35% tax bracket, it doesn’t affect the tax on the mutual fund gain – that remains at 15% final (assuming filer status).

- **Minimum Tax Regime (MTR) Consideration:** If you (or your company) are under a **Minimum Tax Regime** for other income (for instance, certain businesses have to pay a minimum tax on turnover under section 113 of the Ordinance), the capital gain from mutual funds is **outside that regime**. Incomes that are subject to final/separate tax are typically *excluded* from the computation of minimum tax and normal tax, since they are not part of taxable income. For example, a company might be paying minimum tax on its business turnover due to low profits, but any gain from a mutual fund investment would still be taxed separately at 25% (if it’s a debt fund) and would **not be added to the turnover or profit for minimum tax calculations**. In other words, you pay the 25% on that gain and still separately compute minimum tax on your other business revenues (the two do not offset each other). The same logic applies to individuals – if some other income was under a minimum or fixed tax scheme, this capital gain remains independently taxed.

- **Summary:** **Treat this mutual fund capital gain as NTR + Separate Block.** This means you calculate your normal tax (NTR or even MTR) on your regular income **as usual**, **plus** you account for the tax on the capital gain **separately**. The phrase **“NTR/MTR plus tax on the separate block”** is apt – your normal income goes through NTR or MTR, and *in addition* you pay the tax on this separate block of income at the prescribed rate. This income is neither aggregated with your other income for rate purposes nor is its tax adjustable against other tax liabilities (except that the withheld amount itself is the tax for that income). Essentially, it falls under the Final Tax Regime – a tax that is *separately charged and not blended into the normal regime*【9†L88-L94】.

## Recent Changes and Finance Act Updates

Pakistan’s tax laws for mutual fund income have seen a few important changes in recent Finance Acts (especially the Finance Act, 2023 and 2024):

- **Increase in Capital Gains Tax Rate:** The **Finance Act, 2024** (applicable from Tax Year 2025 onward) increased the tax rate on capital gains from mutual funds. Previously, the effective CGT (withholding) on mutual fund redemptions for individuals was **10%**. This has been **raised to 15%** to bring it in line with the flat rate on stock securities【6†L1376-L1384】【12†L183-L190】. Mutual funds, collective investment schemes (CIS), and REITs must now withhold 15% for individuals/AOPs at redemption (up from 10%). For companies, the rate became 15% for stock funds (up from 10%), while remaining 25% for other funds【6†L1376-L1384】. This change ensures uniformity and increased revenue collection from these gains.

- **Removal of 6-Year Exemption (Prospective):** As discussed, the longstanding rule of “no tax on securities held > 6 years” was narrowed. The Finance Act, 2024 clarified that this exemption only applies to assets acquired on or before 30 June 2024. Any mutual fund units (or other listed securities) bought on or after July 1, 2024 will **always incur the 15% tax on gains** no matter how long they are held【6†L1392-L1400】. This was a significant change to discourage long-term holdings purely for tax avoidance and to simplify the regime.

- **Higher Tax on Mutual Fund Dividends (Profit on Debt funds):** Although your question is about capital gains, it’s worth noting a related change for completeness. The **Finance Act, 2023** had already differentiated dividend taxation for mutual funds, and **Finance Act, 2024** further reinforced it. If a mutual fund derives **more than 50% of its income from profit on debt** (i.e. it’s essentially a money market or income fund), then any **dividends** you receive from that fund are taxed at **25% (final)**, instead of the standard 15% on dividends【3†L589-L594】【12†L187-L192】. Both the tax rate and the withholding rate on such dividends is 25%. This change was made to eliminate the arbitrage where investors could previously get only 15% tax on what is effectively interest income by investing through a mutual fund. Now, the law aligns the tax on those mutual fund dividends with the tax on interest income. (For reference, **Section 150** of the Ordinance and Division I, Part III of First Schedule cover dividend taxation; a proviso was added for mutual funds >50% debt income). **Important:** This 25% applies to **dividend distributions** from the fund. **Capital gains** on redemption, however, follow the CGT regime discussed (15% for individuals), regardless of the fund’s portfolio mix【10†L112-L120】【10†L118-L125】.

- **Mutual Funds’ Own Tax Exemption:** Mutual funds themselves remain **exempt from corporate income tax** as long as they distribute at least 90% of their income (excluding capital gains) to unit holders【10†L84-L92】. This rule (Clause 99, Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance) is unchanged. It means the fund does not pay tax on its profit; the tax incidence is passed to investors via withholding on dividends and capital gains. Recent finance acts did not remove this incentive, so most mutual funds ensure they qualify by distributing income. This context explains why investors face withholding on gains/dividends – because the fund is not taxed at the fund level if it passes income out.

In summary, **capital gains from a debt-based (≥50% debt) mutual fund are taxed as a separate block at a flat rate (15% for individuals on ATL)**. The mutual fund will deduct this tax upon redemption of units, and that deduction is typically final. The income is **not integrated into the normal tax regime** (so it won’t affect or be affected by your other taxable income or tax brackets). You should report it separately in your return and the tax withheld suffices for that income. Any **withholding on redemption is at 15%** for individual investors (25% if the investor is a company, since your fund is not equity-based)【11†L134-L144】. Finally, ensure you stay on the Active Taxpayers List to benefit from the favorable flat rate; otherwise, the gain could be subjected to higher slab rates (as a non-filer)【9†L88-L94】.

**References:**

- PwC Tax Summaries – **Pakistan (Individual) – Income Determination**【1†L463-L470】【3†L548-L554】  
- Atlas Asset Management – *Taxation of Mutual Funds* (updated May 30, 2025)【11†L134-L144】【11†L146-L148】

Tax Treatment of Capital Gains from Debt-Based Mutual Funds in Pakistan
Investments in money market or income mutual funds (where more than 50% of the portfolio income is derived from debt instruments) have a distinct tax treatment in Pakistan. In particular, capital gains from selling (redeeming) your mutual fund units are handled as a separate block of income and not mixed with your normal taxable income. Below is a detailed breakdown addressing each concern:
Capital Gains as a Separate Block of Income
Chargeability: Capital gains realized on the sale/redemption of mutual fund units are taxed under a separate regime, rather than under the normal tax slab rates. Section 37A of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 specifically deals with capital gains on securities, which include units of mutual funds and collective investment schemes. For individual investors (filers), the tax on these capital gains is a flat percentage of the gain, independent of your other income. This means such gains are not added to your salary/business income for rate determination; instead, they are taxed in isolation at prescribed rates (often referred to as “separate block” or final tax).
•	Tax Rate on Capital Gains: For individuals/AOPs who are on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL), the capital gains tax (CGT) on mutual fund units (whether equity or debt-based funds) is 15% of the gain. This 15% is the applicable separate block tax rate (also often the final tax) on the gain. It applies irrespective of your income bracket since it’s outside the Normal Tax Regime.
•	Special Treatment for Filers vs Non-Filers: Being a filer (ATL) is important. If you are a non-filer (inactive taxpayer), the benefit of the fixed 15% rate is not fully available. Under recent changes, non-filers must pay tax on such capital gains at normal slab rates (with a minimum of 15% and up to 45%). In other words, non-filers are effectively pushed into the Normal Tax Regime for these gains (with at least 15% tax), whereas filers are charged a flat 15%. This creates an incentive to file taxes to avail the concessional flat rate on capital gains.
•	Holding Period Consideration: Previously, Pakistan’s tax law provided an exemption on capital gains from listed securities (including mutual fund units) if the holding period exceeded 6 years. No capital gains tax was charged on securities held for more than 6 years. This rule still applies to assets acquired on or before June 30, 2024 – for those, if you hold your mutual fund units for over six years, no CGT is due on redemption. However, for units acquired after July 1, 2024, the flat 15% tax applies regardless of holding period (the Finance Act, 2024 removed the unlimited holding period exemption for new acquisitions). In short, long-term holdings bought after mid-2024 no longer enjoy a full exemption; they will be taxed at 15% whenever sold (for filers).
Key Point: Treat these capital gains as a separate block of income (often part of the Final Tax Regime). You cannot offset this gain with losses from other heads of income, nor can you reduce it by deductions/allowances applicable to normal income. Likewise, the tax paid on this gain is typically final – it satisfies your tax liability on that gain without further recalculation under the normal regime. You will report the capital gain in the “capital gains” section of your tax return (separately from salary, business income, etc.), and tax is computed at the fixed rate.
Withholding Tax on Redemption of Units
When you redeem (sell) units of a mutual fund, the fund manager (Asset Management Company or the trustee of the fund) is required to withhold applicable capital gains tax at source and deposit it to the FBR. The withholding acts as an advance/final tax on your capital gain.
•	Rate of Withholding on Redemption: For individual investors, the withholding tax on capital gain at the time of redemption is 15% of the gain. This applies to gains from money market or debt-based funds just as it does for equity funds – currently there is no higher rate for individuals on debt-fund gains; it’s a flat 15% for filers in either case. (Before Finance Act 2024, this withholding was 10%, but it has since been increased to 15%.)
•	If Investor is a Company: The regime distinguishes between “stock funds” and “other funds” for corporate investors. A “stock fund” typically means a mutual fund with a high equity exposure (often defined by tax law as a fund with a certain minimum percentage invested in stocks). A “money market fund” with >50% in debt would be classified as “other fund” (non-stock fund). In the case of a company redeeming units:
o	If it’s an equity stock fund, CGT is withheld at 15%.
o	If it’s a debt/money-market fund, CGT is withheld at 25% for the company.
These rates for companies reflect that corporate investors in debt-heavy funds pay a higher flat CGT (25%) on redemption. (Note: 25% aligns roughly with corporate tax rates and was intended to prevent companies from getting a lower rate via mutual fund investments.)
•	No Tax Withheld for Long Holding (Legacy Investments): As noted, if your units were acquired on or before June 30, 2024 and you have held them for over 6 years, no capital gains tax will be withheld on redemption. The mutual fund will not deduct CGT in such cases, as the gain is exempt by law. This is more relevant for long-term investments made prior to the recent law change. For units bought after July 1, 2024, however, the fund will always deduct 15% (for individuals) whenever you redeem, regardless of holding period.
•	Final Discharge: The amount withheld by the mutual fund at redemption is typically considered full and final discharge of tax liability on that capital gain (for filers). In practice, this means if you’re a filer, the 15% WHT on your gain is your final tax on that income – you generally won’t owe additional tax on it when filing your return, nor can you claim a refund if your personal tax rate is lower. (Do ensure to report the gain and tax withheld in your return under “Separately Taxed / Final Tax Income” sections.)
Applicable Law: The above withholding mechanism and rates are outlined in the First Schedule to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – specifically Division VII, Part I (which deals with tax on capital gains from securities) and the related provisions. The Finance Act, 2024 amended these rates (as noted below). Section 37A of the Ordinance is the governing section for taxation of securities (including mutual fund units), and Section 100B along with the Eighth Schedule (for stock exchange transactions) provides the framework for how such gains are computed and taxed. Mutual funds, via their trustees, act as withholding agents for this purpose.
Normal Tax Regime (NTR) vs Final Tax Regime for This Income
Given that capital gains from mutual fund investments are a separate block of income, they are not part of the Normal Tax Regime (NTR) calculation of your total income. Instead, they fall under what is often called the Final Tax Regime (FTR) or a separately taxed income category. Here’s how it works in practice:
•	Exclusion from NTR: You do not include these capital gains in your taxable income when computing tax under the normal slabs/rates. For example, if you have a salary or business income, you will calculate tax on those under the normal progressive rates (for individuals) or corporate rate (for companies) separately. The capital gain from the mutual fund is taxed in addition at the fixed rate (15% or 25% as applicable) on its own. Essentially, the CGT on mutual fund units is ring-fenced – taxed on its own and kept apart from the NTR calculation of other income.
•	Return Filing: In your income tax return, Pakistan’s FBR forms have separate sections for “Capital Gains” and “Final / Separate Income.” You would declare the gain from the mutual fund under that section, and the tax withheld (15%) is usually treated as the final tax paid on that gain. It does not get recomputed based on your tax slabs. So, whether your regular income falls in a 0%, 10%, or 35% tax bracket, it doesn’t affect the tax on the mutual fund gain – that remains at 15% final (assuming filer status).
•	Minimum Tax Regime (MTR) Consideration: If you (or your company) are under a Minimum Tax Regime for other income (for instance, certain businesses have to pay a minimum tax on turnover under section 113 of the Ordinance), the capital gain from mutual funds is outside that regime. Incomes that are subject to final/separate tax are typically excluded from the computation of minimum tax and normal tax, since they are not part of taxable income. For example, a company might be paying minimum tax on its business turnover due to low profits, but any gain from a mutual fund investment would still be taxed separately at 25% (if it’s a debt fund) and would not be added to the turnover or profit for minimum tax calculations. In other words, you pay the 25% on that gain and still separately compute minimum tax on your other business revenues (the two do not offset each other). The same logic applies to individuals – if some other income was under a minimum or fixed tax scheme, this capital gain remains independently taxed.
•	Summary: Treat this mutual fund capital gain as NTR + Separate Block. This means you calculate your normal tax (NTR or even MTR) on your regular income as usual, plus you account for the tax on the capital gain separately. The phrase “NTR/MTR plus tax on the separate block” is apt – your normal income goes through NTR or MTR, and in addition you pay the tax on this separate block of income at the prescribed rate. This income is neither aggregated with your other income for rate purposes nor is its tax adjustable against other tax liabilities (except that the withheld amount itself is the tax for that income). Essentially, it falls under the Final Tax Regime – a tax that is separately charged and not blended into the normal regime.
Recent Changes and Finance Act Updates
Pakistan’s tax laws for mutual fund income have seen a few important changes in recent Finance Acts (especially the Finance Act, 2023 and 2024):
•	Increase in Capital Gains Tax Rate: The Finance Act, 2024 (applicable from Tax Year 2025 onward) increased the tax rate on capital gains from mutual funds. Previously, the effective CGT (withholding) on mutual fund redemptions for individuals was 10%. This has been raised to 15% to bring it in line with the flat rate on stock securities. Mutual funds, collective investment schemes (CIS), and REITs must now withhold 15% for individuals/AOPs at redemption (up from 10%). For companies, the rate became 15% for stock funds (up from 10%), while remaining 25% for other funds. This change ensures uniformity and increased revenue collection from these gains.
•	Removal of 6-Year Exemption (Prospective): As discussed, the longstanding rule of “no tax on securities held > 6 years” was narrowed. The Finance Act, 2024 clarified that this exemption only applies to assets acquired on or before 30 June 2024. Any mutual fund units (or other listed securities) bought on or after July 1, 2024 will always incur the 15% tax on gains no matter how long they are held. This was a significant change to discourage long-term holdings purely for tax avoidance and to simplify the regime.
•	Higher Tax on Mutual Fund Dividends (Profit on Debt funds): Although your question is about capital gains, it’s worth noting a related change for completeness. The Finance Act, 2023 had already differentiated dividend taxation for mutual funds, and Finance Act, 2024 further reinforced it. If a mutual fund derives more than 50% of its income from profit on debt (i.e. it’s essentially a money market or income fund), then any dividends you receive from that fund are taxed at 25% (final), instead of the standard 15% on dividends. Both the tax rate and the withholding rate on such dividends is 25%. This change was made to eliminate the arbitrage where investors could previously get only 15% tax on what is effectively interest income by investing through a mutual fund. Now, the law aligns the tax on those mutual fund dividends with the tax on interest income. (For reference, Section 150 of the Ordinance and Division I, Part III of First Schedule cover dividend taxation; a proviso was added for mutual funds >50% debt income). Important: This 25% applies to dividend distributions from the fund. Capital gains on redemption, however, follow the CGT regime discussed (15% for individuals), regardless of the fund’s portfolio mix.
•	Mutual Funds’ Own Tax Exemption: Mutual funds themselves remain exempt from corporate income tax as long as they distribute at least 90% of their income (excluding capital gains) to unit holders. This rule (Clause 99, Part I of Second Schedule to the Ordinance) is unchanged. It means the fund does not pay tax on its profit; the tax incidence is passed to investors via withholding on dividends and capital gains. Recent finance acts did not remove this incentive, so most mutual funds ensure they qualify by distributing income. This context explains why investors face withholding on gains/dividends – because the fund is not taxed at the fund level if it passes income out.
In summary, capital gains from a debt-based (≥50% debt) mutual fund are taxed as a separate block at a flat rate (15% for individuals on ATL). The mutual fund will deduct this tax upon redemption of units, and that deduction is typically final. The income is not integrated into the normal tax regime (so it won’t affect or be affected by your other taxable income or tax brackets). You should report it separately in your return and the tax withheld suffices for that income. Any withholding on redemption is at 15% for individual investors (25% if the investor is a company, since your fund is not equity-based). Finally, ensure you stay on the Active Taxpayers List to benefit from the favorable flat rate; otherwise, the gain could be subjected to higher slab rates (as a non-filer).

**Subject:** Tax Treatment of Capital Gains on Redemption of Units in Debt-Based Mutual Funds

Dear [Client Name],

Thank you for your email.

We appreciate your detailed query regarding the tax implications on capital gains arising from investments in a mutual fund (money market) where more than 50% of the portfolio consists of debt-based instruments. Please find below our guidance on the matter, structured to address each of your specific concerns:

---

### 1. **Capital Gains as a Separate Block of Income**

Capital gains from the redemption of mutual fund units—whether equity-based or debt-based—are treated under a **separate block of income**, as governed by **Section 37A** of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001.

- **Tax Chargeability**: For individual investors appearing on the Active Taxpayers List (ATL), capital gains from mutual fund units are taxed at a **flat rate of 15%**. This treatment is separate from your normal taxable income and is not aggregated with salary or business income for tax rate determination.

- **Final Tax Treatment**: This gain is not adjustable against any other income or losses, and the tax paid thereon is generally considered **final**—meaning no further tax liability arises on such gain, nor can it be adjusted or refunded based on your overall tax profile.

- **Holding Period**: For units acquired **on or before June 30, 2024**, a six-year holding exemption still applies—i.e., no capital gains tax is levied if the units are held for more than six years. However, for units acquired **on or after July 1, 2024**, this exemption has been withdrawn, and a 15% CGT applies regardless of the holding period.

---

### 2. **Withholding Tax on Redemption**

Under the Finance Act, 2024, the **withholding tax (WHT)** mechanism was aligned with the revised capital gains regime:

- **Individuals / AOPs (Filers)**: The Asset Management Company (AMC) or fund trustee is required to withhold **15% of the capital gain** at the time of redemption. This WHT is treated as **final tax** for individuals on ATL.

- **Corporate Investors (Filers)**: For companies investing in **non-stock funds** (i.e., funds where more than 50% of income is derived from debt instruments), the WHT on capital gains is **25%**. This ensures that corporate investors do not obtain a lower effective tax rate via mutual fund investments.

- **Non-Filers**: For both individuals and companies not appearing on the ATL, the gain may be subject to **higher slab-based rates** under the Normal Tax Regime, starting from 15% and going up to 45%. The flat rate benefit is therefore reserved for compliant taxpayers.

---

### 3. **Interaction with NTR/MTR – Final Tax vs Normal Regime**

Given the separate treatment of capital gains from mutual funds:

- These gains are **not part of the Normal Tax Regime (NTR)** and are excluded from the computation of tax liability on salary, business, or other income.

- Likewise, they are **excluded from the Minimum Tax Regime (MTR)** under Section 113, which typically applies to turnover or gross receipts. Since capital gains fall under the **Final Tax Regime (FTR)**, they are not subject to minimum tax thresholds.

- In practical terms, your normal income is taxed under NTR/MTR (as applicable), while **capital gains from mutual funds are taxed separately and additionally**, with no intermixing or offsetting allowed.

---

### 4. **Other Relevant Considerations**

- **Reporting in Tax Return**: These gains should be reported in the “**Capital Gains / Separately Taxed Income**” section of the return. The WHT deducted by the mutual fund is disclosed against that income and is typically treated as final discharge.

- **Dividends from Debt-Based Mutual Funds**: For completeness, please note that **dividends** received from mutual funds deriving more than 50% of their income from **profit on debt** are now taxed at a **flat 25%** for individuals as per the proviso to **Section 150**, introduced through Finance Act, 2023 and reinforced by Finance Act, 2024.

- **Mutual Fund Exemption**: Mutual funds themselves are exempt from tax under **Clause 99, Part I, Second Schedule**, provided they distribute at least 90% of their accounting income (excluding capital gains) to unit holders.

---

### 5. **Summary**

Based on a review of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), including the amendments introduced through the Finance Act, 2024 (“FA 2024”), and recent jurisprudence, we set out our comments below for your consideration.  

---

### **Capital Gains — Separate Block of Income**

Capital gains on the redemption of mutual fund units are governed by Section 37A of the Ordinance and are treated as a separate block of income. This means such gains are ring-fenced from other sources of income and are not aggregated for the purpose of determining tax liability under the normal tax regime (NTR). Moreover, as these gains are taxed under a standalone regime, they are also excluded from the scope of minimum tax under Section 113 of the Ordinance.  

Accordingly, capital gains realized by Shell Pakistan Limited on the redemption of units in a debt-based mutual fund are not subject to tax under either the NTR or MTR and instead attract a flat rate of tax applicable specifically to such gains.

---

### **Withholding Tax at Redemption — Applicable Rate and Nature**

At the time of redemption, mutual funds are required to withhold tax at source on the capital gains realized by the unitholder. Following the amendments introduced through FA 2024, the withholding tax rate applicable to **corporate investors** redeeming units in **debt-based mutual funds** has been prescribed at **25%**, regardless of the holding period or ATL (Active Taxpayers’ List) status of the unitholder.  

This tax is typically treated as a **final discharge of tax liability**, unless the taxpayer chooses to take a position under the charging provisions which yields a lower effective tax burden. This gives rise to the issue discussed below.

---

### **Charging vs. Withholding Rate — Taxpayer’s Right to Elect Beneficial Treatment**

A key interpretive issue arises from the apparent inconsistency between the **charging rates** under the main table of Division VII of Part I of the First Schedule and the **withholding rates** prescribed under the third proviso to the same Division.  

Under the charging provisions, where a corporate taxpayer is on the ATL both at the time of acquisition and disposal of the mutual fund units, the applicable tax rate is **15%**. However, mutual funds are required to deduct tax at a higher flat rate of **25%**, creating a potential tax over-deduction.  

In this context, it is important to note that under **Rule 1(5) of the Eighth Schedule**, the tax deducted at source may be treated as the final tax liability. Conversely, where the charging rate is more favorable, a taxpayer is entitled to apply the **15% rate in its return** and seek an **adjustment of the excess tax withheld**.  

This position is reinforced by established legal principles confirmed by the Sindh High Court in the case of *Indus Motors* (2021 PTD 460), wherein it was held that in the interpretation of fiscal statutes, any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of the taxpayer. Where two reasonable interpretations are available, the one that benefits the taxpayer should prevail. Accordingly, Shell Pakistan Limited may adopt the position that capital gains are taxable at 15% and the excess WHT (10%) is adjustable.

---

### **Filing Strategy and Procedural Considerations**

Where Shell Pakistan Limited opts to apply the 15% rate in its tax return, despite 25% WHT being deducted at source, it is advisable to take the following actions:  

- **Manually override** the system’s default treatment in the IRIS return by applying the 15% rate on capital gains and showing the 25% WHT as tax already deducted;
- **Claim the excess 10% as an adjustment** against other tax liabilities, ensuring alignment with the computation uploaded to the FBR portal;
- **Submit a formal explanation letter** to the Commissioner Inland Revenue having jurisdiction over the case, outlining the legal basis for applying the lower rate and adjusting the excess tax deducted;
- **Retain all relevant documentation**, including WHT certificates and evidence of ATL status on both acquisition and disposal dates, to substantiate the position adopted.

If any system-level issues in IRIS prevent correct declaration or adjustment, it may be appropriate to escalate the matter through relevant forums such as MUFAP or tax advisory associations, and, if required, explore legal recourse as a last resort.

---

### **Impact of Finance Act, 2024 — Broader Considerations**

The Finance Act, 2024 has introduced notable amendments that have direct implications for mutual fund investors:  

- The **six-year holding period exemption** on capital gains has been **withdrawn** for units acquired on or after **July 1, 2024**. Accordingly, all redemptions—irrespective of the holding duration—will attract capital gains tax at the applicable flat rate.

Importantly, capital gains from mutual fund redemptions are also **excluded from the scope of the Minimum Tax Regime (MTR)** under Section 113 of the Ordinance.

In the case of corporate investors such as Shell Pakistan Limited, the gain realized on redemption of units in a money market fund (debt-based fund) will be taxed at a **flat rate of 25%**, as prescribed by the **third proviso under Division VII, Part I, First Schedule**.

---

### 2. **Withholding Tax at Redemption**

Asset Management Companies (AMCs) are required to deduct **withholding tax on capital gains** at the time of redemption of mutual fund units. As per the Finance Act, 2024, the **withholding tax rate for corporate investors** in debt-based mutual funds is **25%**, regardless of whether the units were held for more than six years or the investor appears on the Active Taxpayers' List (ATL).

This **25% withholding tax is considered final** for corporate investors, and no further tax liability arises on such gains, provided the taxpayer does not seek to apply a more beneficial tax treatment under the charging provisions.

---

### 3. **Interaction with ATL Status and Tax Rate Election**

Post FA 2024, there exists an inconsistency between **withholding tax rates** and the **charging rates** under the First Schedule:

- For **companies appearing on ATL** at the time of both acquisition and disposal, the **charging rate under the main table** of Division VII is **15%**.
- For **non-ATL companies**, the rate is **29%**.
- However, in either case, the **withholding tax rate remains fixed at 25%** under the proviso.

This disparity provides scope for a taxpayer to adopt the **more beneficial rate** based on Rule 1(5) of the Eighth Schedule, which allows tax deducted to be treated as a discharge of tax liability. Relying on the interpretation principles laid down in the Sindh High Court judgment in *Indus Motors* (2021 PTD 460), a taxpayer may elect to:

- **Claim finality of 25% WHT**, if appearing off-ATL or if no further liability is desirable; or
- **Claim adjustment/refund** by applying the **15% charging rate** in the return and treating excess WHT as adjustable against other liabilities (particularly relevant for ATL-status companies).

To operationalize this, the taxpayer may need to manually override the default tax treatment in the IRIS return and file a letter with the relevant Commissioner explaining the position taken.

---

### 4. **Recent Legislative Developments – Finance Act, 2024**

The following changes introduced through FA 2024 are noteworthy:

- The **holding period-based exemption** on capital gains has been abolished for units acquired on or after July 1, 2024. Thus, all redemptions will now attract capital gains tax at the flat rates, regardless of how long the units were held.
- **Capital gains on disposal of debt-based mutual fund units** (including those derived from Sukuks and T-bills) continue to be taxed under Section 37A, unless the security is held to maturity, in which case the income may fall under “profit on debt” under Section 39.
- **Dividends** paid by mutual funds earning 50% or more income from profit on debt (e.g., sukuks, T-bills) are now subject to **enhanced withholding tax of 25%**, under the amended Division III, Part I of the First Schedule.

---

### 5. **Summary and Recommendations**

| Particulars                              | Position for Shell Pakistan Ltd. (Corporate Investor) |
|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------|
| Capital gains on redemption              | Taxed under Section 37A as a separate block of income  |
| Withholding tax at source                | 25% (final, unless beneficial position elected)         |
| Final tax or adjustable?                 | Taxpayer may elect to treat as final or adjust based on ATL status and favorable interpretation |
| Inclusion in NTR/MTR                     | **Excluded** from both regimes                         |
| Recent law amendments                    | No exemption for holding over 6 years; 25% applies on post-July 1, 2024 acquisitions |

In view of the above, Shell Pakistan Limited may consider treating the 25% withholding as final where advantageous. Alternatively, if appearing on ATL on both acquisition and disposal dates, the Company may revise the return to reflect tax liability at 15% and claim an adjustment for the excess withheld.

Should you require assistance in revising the tax return or drafting the accompanying communication to the Commissioner, we remain at your disposal.

Warm regards,  
**[Your Name]**  
Tax Consultant

**Subject:** Advisory on Tax Treatment of Capital Gains on Redemption of Units in Debt-Based Mutual Funds  
**Client:** Shell Pakistan Limited  

Dear [Client Name],

We refer to your query regarding the correct tax treatment of capital gains arising on redemption of units in a money market mutual fund, wherein more than 50% of the portfolio comprises debt instruments. You have sought guidance on the tax chargeability, applicable withholding tax (WHT) rate, and whether the gain is subject to the Normal Tax Regime (NTR) or Minimum Tax Regime (MTR).

Based on our detailed analysis of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance”), as amended by the Finance Act, 2024 (“FA 2024”), and in light of recent jurisprudence and interpretative commentary, our views are outlined below.

---

### 1. **Capital Gains as a Separate Block of Income**

Capital gains derived on redemption of mutual fund units—particularly in the case of open-end funds where more than 50% of the income is derived from debt instruments—are taxed under **Section 37A of the Ordinance** and are treated as a **separate block of income**. This implies that such gains are:

- **Excluded from the NTR computation** (i.e., not aggregated with income under salary, business, or other sources);
- **Not subject to Minimum Tax under Section 113** of the Ordinance;
- Taxed at a **flat rate**, which depends on the unitholder’s ATL status and holding period.

For corporate unitholders like Shell Pakistan Limited, **capital gains tax is applicable at a flat rate of 25%** in case of debt-based mutual funds, as per the **third proviso of Division VII, Part I of the First Schedule**.

---

### 2. **Applicable Withholding Tax and Discharge of Liability**

Mutual funds are required to withhold tax at source on capital gains at the time of redemption. The Finance Act, 2024 has introduced key amendments resulting in the following:

- A **uniform withholding tax rate of 25%** is applicable to **corporate investors**, regardless of ATL status or holding period;
- This WHT is considered **final discharge** of tax liability, unless a more beneficial position is adopted in the return.

This has led to an apparent conflict between the **charging rates under the main table of Division VII** and the **withholding rates under the proviso**.

---

### 3. **Reconciling Charging vs. Withholding Rates — Legal Interpretative Position**

Post FA 2024, corporate unitholders may face a situation where the **withholding tax rate (25%)** is **higher than the charging rate (15%)**, particularly when the company appears on ATL at both acquisition and disposal dates.

In such cases, a **beneficial interpretative position** may be adopted based on the combined reading of **Section 100B**, **Eighth Schedule**, and the principles laid down by the **Sindh High Court in Indus Motors (2021 PTD 460)**. The key takeaways are:

- Where there is ambiguity between rates under charging provisions and withholding provisions, the taxpayer may apply **the more beneficial rate**;
- Rule 1(5) of the Eighth Schedule allows the taxpayer to treat **withholding tax as full and final**, where beneficial;
- Alternatively, where the 15% rate under the main table is favorable (for ATL companies), the taxpayer may **manually compute capital gains at 15%** in the return and **claim adjustment of excess WHT** (i.e., the 10% overpaid).

For Shell Pakistan Limited, which qualifies under the ATL criterion, this may result in an effective tax rate of 15% rather than the default 25% withheld by the AMC.

---

### 4. **Operational Guidance and Filing Strategy**

Where Shell Pakistan Limited opts to apply the charging rate of 15% in the return, despite 25% WHT deduction, the following steps are advised:

- Reflect 15% capital gains tax in the **manually adjusted return** computation;
- Treat the **excess 10% WHT as adjustable tax** against any other head of income;
- File a **supporting letter with the concerned Commissioner Inland Revenue**, explaining the position and basis of manual override in the IRIS return;
- Maintain **relevant records and NCCPL/AMC certificates** evidencing tax deduction and ATL status at the time of acquisition and disposal.

This approach is supported by the legal doctrine that in tax matters, **ambiguities must be interpreted in favor of the taxpayer** (as reaffirmed in the *Indus Motors* case and long-standing fiscal jurisprudence).

---

### 5. **Impact of Recent Legislative Changes (Finance Act, 2024)**

A few critical amendments relevant to your investment strategy include:

- The **exemption on capital gains** previously available for securities held for more than six years has been withdrawn effective **July 1, 2024**;
- Gains on redemption of units acquired on or after this date are now **taxable at flat rates**, irrespective of holding period;
- Where mutual funds derive **50% or more of their income from profit on debt**, **dividends distributed** by such funds attract **enhanced dividend tax of 25%**, instead of the standard 15%.

Accordingly, even dividend income may warrant reassessment if your mutual fund portfolio leans heavily toward debt instruments (e.g., Sukuks, T-bills, PIBs).

---

### 6. **Summary of Recommended Position for Shell Pakistan Limited**

| Aspect                         | Tax Position                                                                 |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Nature of capital gains        | Separate block of income under Section 37A                                   |
| Applicability of NTR/MTR       | Excluded from both                                                            |
| Default WHT on redemption      | 25% deducted by AMC                                                          |
| Charging rate (ATL status)     | 15% (for ATL companies under main table, Division VII)                       |
| Recommended action             | Declare at 15% in return; claim excess 10% WHT as adjustable; notify FBR     |
| Recent FA 2024 impact          | Withdrawal of 6-year exemption; 25% WHT on high debt-based dividends         |

---

### 7. **Conclusion**

In light of the above, Shell Pakistan Limited may prudently elect to **apply the 15% charging rate** under Division VII of the First Schedule and **claim credit for the excess WHT** deducted by the mutual fund. This approach is supported both by fiscal interpretation principles and the statutory construction of the Ordinance post-FA 2024.

Should you require assistance with implementing the above position, revising your return, or preparing correspondence to the tax authorities, our team remains available to support you.

Warm regards,  
**[Your Name]**  
Tax Consultant

That the amended order seeks to revise an already concluded assessment by introducing unexplained income and increasing tax demand **without following proper procedures**, and in effect, attempts to achieve what would only be permissible through proceedings under section **122(5A)** or fresh audit, which were neither initiated nor concluded in this case.

That the impugned order has been passed **without issuance of a show-cause notice or opportunity of being heard**, thus violating the principles of **natural justice** and the appellant’s right to a fair hearing. The proceedings suffer from procedural impropriety and are thus void ab initio.

6. **Failure to Pass a Speaking Order – Violation of Settled Jurisprudence**  
That the order is **non-speaking**, devoid of reasoning, and does not disclose the basis for the tax adjustments made therein. It lacks findings of fact and legal analysis and is thus violative of the principles laid down by superior courts requiring a **reasoned and speaking assessment order**.

That the computation of tax liability in the order reflects a **mechanical and excessive assessment**, failing to account for approved deductions, tax credits, and refund adjustments. The artificial inflation of income has led to an **unjust and disproportionate tax burden** on the appellant.

# Grounds of Appeal (Tax Year 2020) – United Energy Pakistan Ltd.

**I. Section 65B Credit Is a Separate Incentive, Not Limited by Depreciation.**  Section 65B(1) grants a 10% *tax credit* on qualifying investment in plant and machinery in an industrial undertaking【41†L6201-L6208】.  This credit is an independent statutory incentive, distinct from depreciation allowances.  In contrast, the Third Schedule merely governs *depreciation* (capital allowances) on assets.  In fact, Third Schedule Part IV expressly gives **100% depreciation** for below‐ground installations (wells, drilling, etc.)【52†L34704-L34709】.  But nothing in Section 65B or elsewhere conditions the 65B credit on the rate of depreciation or limits it when full depreciation is allowed.  To the contrary, Section 65B(4) explicitly provides that if “no tax is payable” (for example, because depreciation has wiped out taxable income) the unused credit carries forward to future years【54†L6295-L6303】.  This shows Parliament envisioned scenarios of zero‐tax years yet preserved the credit.  

Moreover, courts have repeatedly treated tax credits as separate from income‐based deductions.  The Supreme Court explained in H.M. Extraction Ghee & Oil Industries v. FBR (2019 SCMR 1081) – cited with approval in CPLA-824-K/2023 – that “an exemption forms part of the assessment process, whereas a tax credit does not”【27†L2115-L2123】.  In other words, depreciation (an “exemption” from income) and a tax credit operate in different spheres of taxation.  Accordingly, allowing full 100% depreciation under the Third Schedule does *not* abrogate or reduce the entitlement to the separate 65B credit.  Had the legislature intended to deny the credit on fully depreciated assets, it would have said so explicitly.  In fact, by providing carryforward (65B(4)), the law anticipates that even when depreciation renders current tax zero, the credit benefit will materialize in later years.  Denying the credit here would defeat the legislative purpose of encouraging new investment.

**II. The Assets Are “Plant & Machinery” Installed in Time.**  UEPL’s below-ground installations (wells, pipelines, etc.) plainly qualify as “plant and machinery, already installed in an industrial undertaking” under Section 65B(1)【41†L6201-L6208】.  The Ordinance defines an “industrial undertaking” broadly to include any enterprise set up in Pakistan that “involves the use of … electrical energy or any other form of energy” and employs ten or more persons【40†L13-L17】.  UEPL’s E&P operations meet this definition: extracting gas is a capital-intensive industrial process, and the drilling/production facilities use energy and manpower well above the threshold.  There is no statutory carve-out excluding subsurface or offshore drilling equipment.  Indeed, the tax authority itself treated these installations as qualifying assets by granting 100% depreciation under the Third Schedule【52†L34704-L34709】.  It is illogical and arbitrary now to claim they are not plant and machinery simply because they enjoy full depreciation.

UEPL’s project timeline also satisfies the statutory cutoff.  Section 65B(2) provides that the credit applies only if the plant and machinery are “purchased and installed at any time between 1 July 2010 and the 30th day of June, 2021”【20†L1877-L1885】【44†L6254-L6262】.  The undisputed evidence shows UEPL *purchased and commissioned* the relevant installations before 30 June 2019 (well in advance of the June 2021 deadline).  This is confirmed by UEPL’s fixed-asset ledger and engineering records (capitalization dates) filed in the record.  The Supreme Court recently emphasized that **both** purchase and installation must occur within the window【20†L1877-L1885】【25†L1981-L1989】.  Here both elements are satisfied: ownership transferred (purchase) and operations commenced (installation) by June 2019.  Thus, UEPL falls within the first category of Section 65B taxpayers.  Any contrary finding is factually unsupportable.  (It bears noting that UEPL’s installation dates are well before even the 2019 amendments, so the assets indisputably meet any transitional test.  Even if installation had occurred later in 2020, it would still be by June 2021, preserving eligibility for credit under Section 65B.)

**III. Supreme Court (CPLA-824-K/2023) Does Not Abolish Section 65B Credit for Eligible Investments.**  The recent SC decision clarified, but did not nullify, Section 65B.  The Court held that the 2019 Finance Act amendments reducing the credit rate for Tax Year 2019 from 10% to 5% could be given effect, since Parliament clearly intended that change【28†L2167-L2174】.  However, the Court confined this change to tax year 2019 only: it struck down the proviso’s retrospective effect beyond that year.  In particular, the Court confirmed that **Section 65B remains in force**, with its original 10% rate applying to tax years after 2019 (subject, of course, to any future legislation).  The Court stated that “to preserve the vested rights… [of prior claimants] is impossible to do so without distorting the language of the proviso. The proviso… clearly expresses the legislative intent to reduce the rate of tax credit for the tax year 2019 from 10% to 5%”【28†L2167-L2174】.  No similar proviso applies to tax years 2020 and onwards; thus for TY 2020 (the year in issue) the credit remains 10%. 

Moreover, CPLA-824-K/2023 underscores that any person satisfying the purchase+installation condition still qualifies for the credit.  The Supreme Court explicitly held that where a taxpayer met both conditions before 1 July 2019 (as UEPL did), it had acquired a vested right to the credit【25†L1981-L1989】【26†L2048-L2057】.  That right did **not** automatically mature into a past-and-closed transaction until a claim was filed【27†L2147-L2155】. UEPL duly filed its claim (with its returns), so its vested right to the credit is established.  Crucially, the Court made clear that *only the 2019 rate was affected by the amendment*, not the underlying right to the credit itself.  The judgment thus leaves full room for Section 65B credit on all timely installations: UEPL’s installations being within the statutory window, the Section 65B credit must still be allowed (at the statutory rate for TY 2020).  

In short, the Supreme Court’s ruling means that for investments installed by June 2019, the credit rate for 2019 became 5%; but it **did not wipe out the Section 65B credit**. Subsequent installations (up to June 2021) remain entitled to credit at 10%.  UEPL’s installations pre-date the amendment and its claim was timely, so the credit is fully available.  

**IV. Applicable Law and Authorities.**  The ordinary rules of statutory interpretation reinforce our position.  Section 65B must be read literally and beneficially.  It contains no clause denying credit where depreciation was granted.  By contrast, in some contexts (e.g. the Finance Act 2021 amendments), the legislature explicitly *removed* depreciation benefits – yet even then it did not disturb Section 65B【59†L554-L562】.  In fact, the 2021 amendment omitted the Third Schedule entry for below-ground installations【59†L554-L562】, but left no entry abrogating Section 65B.  This shows that depreciation relief and investment credit are treated independently.

Binding case law also supports UEPL.  In *H.M. Extraction v. FBR* (SC, 2019) the Court distinguished tax credits from deductions, observing that credits “do not form part of the assessment process”【27†L2115-L2123】.  Likewise, *Molasses Trading v. Federation* (1993 SCMR 1905) and *Shahnawaz (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Pakistan* (Karachi DB 2011) recognize that a tax credit must be separately claimed and only crystallizes upon filing that claim【27†L2115-L2123】【27†L2129-L2134】.  UEPL complied with that procedure.  Earlier Karachi cases (e.g. *Gulshan Spinning Mills v. Govt. of Pakistan*, 2005 PTD 259) had held incorrectly that a credit matures at purchase, but the Supreme Court in CPLA-824-K/2023 expressly rejected that view【27†L2129-L2134】 and reaffirmed that both purchase and installation are required before a right vests【20†L1867-L1875】【25†L1981-L1989】.

Finally, fundamental constitutional law confirms that vested rights cannot be overridden except by clear statutory language【17†L1775-L1780】.  Here, the only “vesting” concern was the 2019 proviso, which Parliament explicitly enacted.  The Court affirmed Parliament’s power to enact such clauses but also held any ambiguity must be resolved in favor of the statutory text.  The proviso’s text is unambiguous in its narrow scope【28†L2167-L2174】.  No broader “taking away” of credit was mandated.  

**Conclusion:** UEPL respectfully submits that the tax authority erred on both law and fact.  Section 65B’s tax credit is a separate incentive from depreciation and remains available on UEPL’s below-ground plant and machinery.  UEPL satisfied all conditions (purchase and installation by the deadline, timely claim), entitling it to the full credit.  The recent Supreme Court decision does not extinguish UEPL’s credit; it only upheld a narrower statutory revision for TY 2019, leaving UEPL’s claim for TY 2020 unaffected.  On these grounds and the authorities cited, the disallowance of UEPL’s Section 65B credit should be reversed.

**Sources Cited:** Section 65B of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001【41†L6201-L6208】【44†L6254-L6262】【54†L6295-L6303】; Third Schedule (Depreciation: below-ground installations)【52†L34704-L34709】; *CPLA-824-K/2023* (SC, 18 Sept. 2024)【20†L1877-L1885】【25†L1981-L1989】【27†L2115-L2123】【27†L2129-L2134】【28†L2167-L2174】; *H.M. Extraction Ghee & Oil Ind. v. FBR* (2019 SCMR 1081)【27†L2115-L2123】; *Molasses Trading v. Federation* (1993 SCMR 1905)【27†L2115-L2123】; *Shahnawaz (Pvt.) Ltd. v. Pakistan* (2011 PTD 1558)【27†L2129-L2134】; relevant amendments and case law as discussed.

Below is the **revised and expanded set of appeal grounds**, now integrating references to the **Exploration & Production (E&P) sector** and emphasizing the **below-ground nature of the investments**—including **ancillary service costs** that form part of the capitalized cost of plant and machinery for E&P taxpayers.

---

### **Grounds of Appeal**  
Filed on behalf of **United Energy Pakistan Limited** against the amended assessment order dated May 8, 2025, passed under section 122(4) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 for Tax Year 2020:

---

1. **Misapplication of Section 65B to the E&P Sector**  
   The learned Officer failed to appreciate the distinct operational realities of the **Exploration and Production (E&P) sector**, where capital expenditure inherently includes substantial below-ground installations—such as wellheads, pipelines, and production facilities—classified as “plant and machinery.” In this industry, the process of installation necessarily involves drilling, civil works, and service-related components that are integral to the functioning of the asset and are **capitalized under IFRS and Pakistani tax law**. Disallowing tax credit based on the form of invoicing (e.g., drilling services) rather than on their **capital nature and function within an installed asset** reflects a narrow and erroneous interpretation inconsistent with industry practice.

2. **Improper Substitution of Depreciation with Tax Credit Entitlement**  
   The Officer’s finding that no credit is available under section 65B due to availability of **100% depreciation under the Third Schedule (for below-ground installations)** disregards the well-established principle that **tax credits and depreciation are distinct** incentives. The tax credit under section 65B is **not a deduction from income**, but a **direct reduction in tax liability**, aimed to stimulate capital investment. For E&P companies, which frequently engage in high-cost well development, such credit serves as an essential relief to offset substantial up-front capital risk—whether or not full depreciation is allowed.

3. **Disregard of Capitalization of Service-Related Costs**  
   The Officer’s conclusion that invoices relate only to services (e.g., drilling, rig operations) and hence do not qualify under section 65B ignores that for E&P entities, such expenditures are **capitalized as part of the asset cost** when they directly contribute to the installation and operation of a producing asset. Under IAS 16 and prevailing oil & gas industry accounting practices, **“services” such as drilling, cementing, logging, and well completion are recognized as part of the cost of plant and machinery.** The Department’s failure to examine the **function and capitalization treatment** of these costs reflects a superficial and flawed assessment.

4. **Contradictory Treatment of Assets Already Recognized for Depreciation**  
   The impugned order inconsistently holds that certain below-ground assets are not “plant and machinery” under section 65B, despite allowing **100% depreciation** under the Third Schedule. If the nature of the assets was accepted as qualifying for depreciation (i.e., as depreciable plant and machinery), denying credit under section 65B on the same assets is **legally untenable and internally inconsistent.**

5. **Failure to Consider Installation Dynamics Unique to E&P Operations**  
   The Officer overlooked that **installation in E&P operations involves a progressive transfer from Capital Work-in-Progress (CWIP) to operating assets**, triggered only when a well or facility becomes operational and meets technical commissioning criteria. UEPL demonstrated with supporting schedules that the relevant assets were both **acquired and installed before June 30, 2019**, and thus fall squarely within the time frame prescribed under section 65B(2), even as amended.

6. **Erroneous Interpretation of Supreme Court Judgment (CPLA-824-K/2023)**  
   The Officer misapplied the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment dated September 18, 2024, which merely upheld the **validity of the amended subsection (2)** of section 65B but did not eliminate credit where both **purchase and installation occurred before June 30, 2019.** UEPL’s investments fall within this category and therefore retain their eligibility under the statute. The judgment did not hold that full depreciation or sector-specific expenditure could override eligibility under section 65B.

7. **Failure to Acknowledge E&P Sector’s Statutory Status as an Industrial Undertaking**  
   UEPL qualifies as an “industrial undertaking” within the meaning of section 65B(1), being engaged in the **energy sector with significant physical infrastructure, mechanization, and industrial processes** in Pakistan. The Officer’s analysis lacks any consideration of this statutory qualification and improperly questions the applicability of section 65B without foundation.

8. **Disregard of Vested Right to Tax Credit Based on Pre-Amendment Eligibility**  
   The Officer failed to consider that the credit claimed under section 65B had become a **vested right** under the law as it stood at the time of investment and installation. UEPL acted in accordance with the then-prevailing statute and under interim relief granted by the Hon’ble Sindh High Court. The final decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court does not operate retrospectively to extinguish claims validly made and perfected under law.

9. **Violation of Principles of Evidence and Natural Justice**  
   The Officer failed to refute the detailed asset schedules and documentary evidence submitted, including breakdowns of capitalization, installation dates, and sample invoices. The summary rejection of these documents, without detailed examination or confronting the taxpayer’s specific evidence, constitutes a **violation of natural justice and fair hearing** under Article 10A of the Constitution of Pakistan.

10. **Non-Consideration of the Statutory Carry Forward Mechanism under Section 65B(4)**  
    Even if the credit could not be fully adjusted against the tax liability due to full depreciation, **section 65B(4)** allows carry forward of unutilized credit for up to two tax years. This provision was entirely ignored in the order, resulting in an incomplete and defective adjudication.

11. **Lack of Jurisdiction under Section 122(4) in the Absence of Fresh Information or Error**  
    The Officer exceeded jurisdiction under section 122(4), which allows revision only in the case of a **definite error or new information**. The issue of section 65B had already been addressed in previous amended orders and appellate proceedings. The current order merely re-evaluates a previously concluded issue without any fresh material or mistake on record, which is beyond the permissible scope of section 122(4).

---

**Subject:** Tax Treatment of Conveyance Benefits – Valuation of Perquisite and Recommended Course of Action

Dear [Client's Name],  

I hope this message finds you well.

We are writing to share our analysis and recommendations regarding the tax treatment of conveyance benefits provided to employees, particularly in cases where vehicles are leased and partially financed by the employee.

Under the general framework of the **Income Tax Ordinance, 2001**, all benefits or perquisites extended by an employer are treated as part of the employee’s salary income and are subject to tax in accordance with **Section 12**, specifically **Section 12(1)(b)**. For valuation purposes, the **Income Tax Rules** prescribe a formula for computing the value of conveyance perquisites, which, in the case of leased vehicles, is based on the **fair market value (FMV)** of the vehicle at the commencement of the lease.

In the present scenario, we understand that a portion of the vehicle cost is borne directly by the employee. Consequently, application of the standard valuation formula, without factoring in the employee’s contribution, results in a higher taxable benefit than what is actually enjoyed by the employee. This creates a disconnect between the notional perquisite value and the economic substance of the arrangement.

While the Rules do not currently provide for an adjustment to account for employee contributions, it is important to note that the **underlying intent of the law** is to tax the **actual benefit** provided by the employer. In light of this, it would be reasonable to adopt a **net-of-contribution approach**, whereby the perquisite value is determined by subtracting the employee’s contribution from the FMV of the vehicle. However, it is important to highlight that this position—though commercially sound—may be challenged by tax authorities, as it does not align strictly with the prescribed methodology.

As a more defensible alternative, we recommend that the **HR policy be revised** to reflect a lower entitlement in cases where employees contribute towards the vehicle cost. In practice, this would mean assigning a vehicle with an FMV equal to the net amount (i.e., FMV less the employee’s contribution), thereby ensuring that the perquisite value computed for tax purposes aligns with the revised policy and the actual benefit extended.

We would be pleased to assist in drafting the revised policy language and supporting documentation, should you decide to proceed with this approach.

Based on a complete review of the **Finance Bill 2025**, here are **social media-ready posts** prepared for **each key amendment**, following your structure:

---

### 📌 **Post #1 – Super Tax (Section 4C) – Broadened Scope & Harsh Minimum Limits**

**Main Heading**  
Section 4C has been overhauled! Now, even if a company reports a loss or low taxable income, **minimum super tax will still apply**—based on turnover thresholds. This targets low-profit or loss-making companies with large revenues.

**Sub Heading**  
Finance Bill 2025 introduces a **minimum super tax liability** under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Now, where a person has no taxable income or lesser taxable income than the minimum threshold, the super tax will still be imposed on turnover exceeding Rs. 300 million. Additionally, **progressive slab rates up to 10%** will continue to apply to high-income sectors such as banking, telecom, and others. This will significantly increase the tax burden for loss-making but high-revenue companies in FY2025–26.

**Pro Tip**  
Ensure your tax planning for FY2025–26 considers both **profit-based and turnover-based super tax triggers**—even loss-making entities are no longer exempt if turnover exceeds Rs. 300 million!

---

### 📌 **Post #2 – Withholding Tax Revamp – Section 148 Imports**

**Main Heading**  
A major shift in section 148: Importers under **FTR regime now reclassified under NTR** in many cases, while rates on commercial importers **are revised upward**. Stay alert to avoid costly compliance errors.

**Sub Heading**  
The Finance Bill 2025 proposes that **certain importers previously taxed under Final Tax Regime (FTR)**—especially commercial importers and industrial undertakings importing non-raw materials—will now fall under the **Normal Tax Regime (NTR)**. Moreover, withholding tax rates under section 148 have been revised across categories, including commercial and industrial importers, service providers, and exporters-cum-importers. This change aligns import tax treatment with sectoral profitability and discourages abuse of low-FTR treatment.

**Pro Tip**  
Check your business classification carefully. You may now be liable to pay higher tax **and file a return under normal regime**—even if you were previously under FTR.

---

### 📌 **Post #3 – Harsh Recovery Powers: Sections 138(3A) & 140**

**Main Heading**  
Recovery before appeal? Yes—**even if your appeal is pending**, tax authorities can now initiate bank attachment or asset seizure if High Court upholds the demand. A controversial override provision.

**Sub Heading**  
Sections 138 and 140 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, are proposed to be amended to allow **immediate recovery** of any tax demand that has been upheld by the High Court or Supreme Court—even if a review or appeal is pending. Notably, the new **section 138(3A) overrides all judgments to the contrary**. Similarly, section 140 now permits attachment of bank accounts **without prior notice** where recovery is linked to such court-upheld demands. This significantly compromises the principle of due process.

**Pro Tip**  
If your case is under litigation but a judgment exists on a similar issue, **stay applications must be filed immediately** to avoid aggressive recovery actions.

---

### 📌 **Post #4 – Sales Tax on Solar Panels – Exemption Scaled Back**

**Main Heading**  
Solar panels are no longer fully exempt! Sales tax reintroduced on import of solar panels under **Eighth Schedule at 18%**, though relief is still possible through EPC route.

**Sub Heading**  
The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to **shift solar panels from Sixth Schedule (exemptions)** to the **Eighth Schedule**, making them **subject to 18% sales tax**. However, relief may still be available if panels are imported as part of EPC (Engineering, Procurement & Construction) contracts for large-scale solar power generation projects, depending on future SROs or sector-specific policies. This move is expected to impact both domestic sales and renewable energy adoption unless mitigated by sectoral relief measures.

**Pro Tip**  
If you're planning solar imports, consult your tax advisor—**timing and route of import (standalone vs EPC)** now determines tax liability.

---

### 📌 **Post #5 – Federal Excise Duty: Barcoding, Track-and-Trace & Confiscation**

**Main Heading**  
Barcoding gets real teeth! FED Act, 2005, amended to allow **confiscation and seizure** of excisable goods **without barcodes**—especially for beverages, cigarettes, and other tracked sectors.

**Sub Heading**  
Amendments to the Federal Excise Act, 2005 empower tax officers to **seize or confiscate excisable goods** that are required to bear tax stamps, barcodes, or Unique Identification Marks (UIMs) but fail to do so. This is especially applicable to tobacco, sugar-sweetened beverages, and cement, where track-and-trace rules are being enforced. Failure to comply may result not only in fines but also loss of goods and cancellation of production licenses.

**Pro Tip**  
If you operate in the excisable sector, ensure **compliance with the latest barcoding and track-and-trace regulations**—non-compliance now carries severe consequences.

**🏠 New Stamp Duty Rates for Property Transfers in Islamabad!**  
The Finance Bill 2025 proposes a revised stamp duty on the transfer of immovable property within the Islamabad Capital Territory. Individuals who are on the Active Taxpayer List (ATL) will be subject to a reduced stamp duty of 1%, while non-filers will pay a higher rate of 2%. This amendment is designed to incentivize tax compliance and make real estate transactions more affordable for compliant taxpayers.  
📌 *If you're planning a property transaction, make sure your tax profile is up-to-date to benefit from the lower rate.*

---

**🌍 Carbon Levy Introduced to Promote Greener Energy Use!**  
To align with environmental goals, a Carbon Levy of Rs. 2.5 per liter has been introduced on Motor Spirit, High-Speed Diesel (HSD), and Furnace Oil for FY 2025–26. This rate will increase to Rs. 5 per liter in FY 2026–27. The levy is in addition to the existing Petroleum Levy and aims to encourage more sustainable energy consumption across the economy.  
🛢️ *With rising costs ahead, it's a good time to explore fuel efficiency and cleaner alternatives in your operations.*

---

**📦 E-Bilty System Mandated for Goods Transportation Nationwide!**  
A new digital cargo tracking requirement has been introduced under the Finance Bill 2025. All consignors, transporters, and freight agents must now generate and carry an e-bilty—a digital transport document—through FBR's Cargo Tracking System for every goods movement. Non-compliance may result in severe consequences, including fines of up to Rs. 1 million, confiscation of goods, and even imprisonment.  
📲 *Ensure your logistics systems are integrated with FBR protocols to avoid costly penalties and business disruptions.*

---

**🛒 E-Commerce Reforms: 2% Final Sales Tax on Online Sales!**  
A 2% final sales tax has been introduced on digitally ordered goods supplied within Pakistan. The tax is to be collected and deposited either by payment intermediaries (for digital payments) or by couriers (for cash on delivery). Sellers will not be allowed input tax adjustment on these supplies, simplifying the process for small businesses. This move enhances tax transparency in the growing e-commerce sector.  
💻 *If you operate online, make sure you’re tax-registered and compliant to keep your access to platforms and payment systems uninterrupted.*

---

**🚫 Bank Account Freeze for Sales Tax Non-Registration!**  
Under the proposed amendments, the FBR will now have the authority to bar operations of bank accounts for individuals or businesses that fail to register under the Sales Tax Act. This bar will only be lifted upon successful registration. The measure is intended to enforce broader compliance and discourage informal business operations.  
🔐 *Don’t risk your banking access—ensure timely registration to stay operational and avoid enforcement actions.*
