Under the proposed changes, individuals who are on the Active Taxpayer List (filers) will pay a stamp duty of 1% of the property’s value, while non-filers will be subject to a higher rate of 2%. This move is aimed at encouraging tax compliance and increasing revenue collection from real estate transactions.  
**Pro Tip:** 📌 Planning to buy or transfer property? Make sure you're a filer to enjoy the 1% reduced stamp duty rate and save significantly on transaction costs.

**🌍 Carbon Levy Introduced to Promote Greener Energy Use**

**📢 Major Income Tax Changes Introduced Through Finance Bill 2025 – Key Highlights You Should Know**

The Finance Bill 2025 proposes sweeping changes to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, especially in response to the rising digital economy, high-income earners, and documentation of transactions. A significant development is the introduction of **new definitions** such as “digitally delivered services,” “e-commerce,” and “online interfaces,” bringing services like video streaming, cloud computing, online marketplaces, and professional digital services (e.g., e-learning, telemedicine, online banking, etc.) formally into the tax ambit. Furthermore, a **new Section 6A** imposes a tax on gross receipts from digital transactions conducted on locally operated e-commerce platforms, while excluding export proceeds covered under section 154A. 

Another notable update is in **section 4AB**, where salaried individuals earning more than **Rs. 10 million annually** will now face a **9% income tax surcharge**, increasing the tax burden on high-income earners. In the case of commercial property, **section 15** introduces a minimum rental value benchmark — fair market rent must now be at least **4% of the property’s fair market value per annum**, unless the taxpayer provides contrary evidence to the satisfaction of the Commissioner. 

In an effort to promote documentation, **section 21 has been amended** to disallow 10% of purchases from non-NTN holders (excluding direct purchases from growers), and 50% of sales if payment exceeding **Rs. 200,000** per invoice is received other than through banking channels or digital means. Similarly, depreciation on capital assets under **section 22** will now be disallowed if the buyer fails to deduct and deposit tax under sections 152 or 153 — reinforcing compliance enforcement.

Taxpayers in the real estate and construction sector will note that the useful life of industrial buildings under **section 24** has been reduced from **25 to 15 years**, which will impact annual depreciation allowances. Likewise, **adjustment of business losses against income from property has been disallowed** under the revised section 56. For **group companies**, a key limitation is introduced under **section 59B**, where entities taxed under presumptive tax regimes will no longer be eligible to claim group relief.

On the relief side, the Bill introduces a new **section 63A**, allowing a tax credit on interest or rental share paid on **low-cost housing loans** for the acquisition or construction of one personal residence (house up to 2,500 sq. ft. or flat up to 2,000 sq. ft.), provided the taxpayer does not claim another credit for 15 years.

These amendments mark a clear policy shift — focusing on **broadening the tax base, documenting the economy, and taxing digital and high-income segments**. Businesses and individuals are encouraged to reassess their compliance strategies and digital transactions in light of these developments.

### 📌 Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 – Key Amendments Proposed in Finance Bill 2025

---

**1️⃣ Definition Overhaul for the Digital Age**  
The Bill expands the scope of tax definitions to catch up with the digital economy. “Digitally delivered services” now include everything from music streaming to cloud computing, e-learning, online banking, architectural design, and consultancy reports. Similarly, “e-commerce” has been defined to include transactions via websites, apps, or digital marketplaces — setting the stage for clearer taxation of digital players.

---

**2️⃣ Digital Platforms = Sellers**  
A pivotal change in the definition of “seller” now includes digital platforms that facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers — even if they don’t take ownership of goods or services. This affects online marketplaces, ride-hailing apps, and service platforms alike, bringing them within the income tax and sales tax net.

---

**3️⃣ New Tax on Local Digital Transactions**  
A new Section 6A proposes a tax on payments received via local digital platforms for goods/services ordered online. Whether you're running a website or an e-commerce app, if you're facilitating local deliveries and payments, you're liable to tax on your gross receipts — excluding export proceeds under Section 154A.

---

**4️⃣ Super Tax on High-Income Salaried Individuals**  
Under Section 4AB, a 9% surcharge has been introduced for salaried individuals earning over PKR 10 million. This move ensures progressive taxation but is likely to hit C-level executives, expats, and top professionals with a heavier tax burden.

---

**5️⃣ Disallowance of Cash-Based & Non-NTN Transactions**  
A stricter regime under Section 21 proposes disallowing 10% of expenses from purchases made from unregistered suppliers. Even harsher — 50% of expenses from sales over PKR 200,000 received in cash or non-digital means will be disallowed. This is a massive nudge toward digital payments and documentation.

---

**6️⃣ No Depreciation Without Tax Deduction Compliance**  
A new proviso in Section 22 states that depreciation won't be allowed on capital assets if the corresponding payments didn't comply with withholding under Sections 152 or 153. This could significantly impact companies with poor tax deduction practices, denying them long-term tax benefits.

---

**7️⃣ Minimum Rent for Commercial Properties Set at 4%**  
Commercial properties will now have a minimum benchmark rental value — set at 4% of the property’s fair market value per annum, as per Section 68. Rent lower than this is acceptable only if the taxpayer provides compelling evidence to the Commissioner.

---

**8️⃣ No More Set-Off of Business Loss Against Property Income**  
An amendment to Section 56 disallows the adjustment of business losses against property income. This restricts tax planning options for businesses holding rental properties or shifting losses across income heads.

---

**9️⃣ Group Relief Limited to Active Business Taxation**  
Section 59B has been tightened to restrict group relief to only those group companies whose income is taxed under “normal” business provisions — not under presumptive or minimum tax regimes. This narrows the benefits of group consolidation for large corporations.

---

**🔟 New Tax Credit for Low-Cost Housing Loans**  
A new Section 63A allows tax credit for individuals paying interest on loans taken for purchasing or constructing a single home or flat within specified area limits. The credit is allowed only once in 15 years and excludes loans claimed under Section 15A — a move aimed at middle-class housing promotion.

---

**1️⃣1️⃣ Industrial Tax Credit Eased Slightly**  
Section 65F has been revised by removing the word “exclusively,” allowing broader interpretation of eligible assets for industrial tax credit. This small change may significantly ease access to tax benefits for manufacturing and industrial businesses.

---

**1️⃣2️⃣ Minimum Tax Relief Duration Shortened**  
Section 113 now offers minimum tax relief for only two years (down from three) in loss or low-profit years. Companies with cyclical earnings will face tighter timelines for managing tax exposure.

---

### 💡 Sales Tax Act, 1990 – Major Proposals

---

**1️⃣ Real-Time POS Integration Expanded**  
The Finance Bill proposes to make real-time POS integration mandatory for a wider range of businesses under Section 3(9A) and 23(5). Penalties for non-compliance will apply, and transactions made outside the POS may not be admissible for input adjustment or even result in disallowance.

---

**2️⃣ Courier/Payment Gateways Now Withholding Agents**  
A game-changer in indirect enforcement: under the updated Eleventh Schedule, couriers and digital payment providers are now responsible for withholding 2% sales tax on behalf of sellers who are not registered. Cash-on-delivery transactions are no longer safe from the tax net.

---

**3️⃣ e-Bilty and Cargo Tracking Mandatory**  
Movement of taxable goods will now require mandatory e-bilty issuance and electronic cargo tracking. Non-compliance invites harsh penalties — including a Rs. 1 million fine and possible confiscation of goods. This targets under-invoicing and undocumented goods transport.

---

**4️⃣ Power to Arrest for Sales Tax Fraud**  
The Bill empowers FBR officers to arrest individuals involved in sales tax fraud without prior notice, expanding prosecution provisions. Directors, CFOs, and even consultants who aid or abet fraud could face imprisonment up to 10 years.

---

**5️⃣ New Return Filing Timelines and Penalties**  
New timelines for submitting returns and stronger default penalties have been proposed. Late filers could face automatic disallowance of input tax or enhanced scrutiny. Accuracy, timeliness, and digital compliance are now non-negotiable.

---

**6️⃣ Clarifications for Tier-1 Retailers & Service Providers**  
The Finance Bill further clarifies the scope and conditions for Tier-1 Retailers, including those supplying taxable services via digital platforms. This tightens enforcement of sales tax laws in the digital retail and service sectors.

Section 24 now sets the useful life of **leasehold improvements at 15 years**, down from 25. This accelerates depreciation but shortens the amortization period — especially relevant for retailers and manufacturers.

---

### 💳 **Post 11 | Rent Must Be Received Digitally or by Bank**  
Section 39 mandates that rental income (above Rs. 200,000) must be received via **bank or digital means**, or it won’t be considered for income tax purposes. Say goodbye to cash rent collection.

---

### ⚖️ **Post 12 | Business Loss Can’t Offset Property Income**  
Section 56 now restricts set-off of **business losses against rental income**. This blocks a previously used tax planning technique. Businesses owning property must plan segment-wise.

---

### 🏢 **Post 13 | Group Relief Denied for Presumptive Income**  
Section 59B introduces clause (ba), disallowing group relief where a group company is taxed under **non-standard provisions** (e.g., final tax regime). Full business taxation is now required to claim group benefits.

---

### 🏠 **Post 14 | Section 63A – Tax Credit for Low-Cost Housing Loans**  
A new section grants tax credit on interest paid on loans for one personal house (max 2,500 sq. ft. or flat of 2,000 sq. ft.). But:

✅ Claim can’t overlap with Section 15A  
A pro-housing move — with tight controls.

### 🏭 **Post 15 | Industrial Credit Relaxed Slightly – Section 65F**  
The word “exclusively” is removed from Section 65F, allowing broader scope for industrial undertakings to claim **investment tax credit**. This could boost spending on mixed-use capital assets.

---

### 🧾 **Post 16 | Section 75A – Digital Payments Now Recognized**  
Digital modes of transfer (e.g., online banking, payment gateways) are now equated to traditional banking instruments for tax purposes. Section 75A now accommodates modern fintech practices.

---

### 🧮 **Post 17 | Section 100C – Reference to Table II Removed**  
The wording "Table II" is removed from Section 100C, likely simplifying the eligibility conditions for tax-exempt entities and trusts — with clearer FBR oversight.

---

### 📊 **Post 18 | Section 113 – Minimum Tax Relief Reduced to 2 Years**  
The buffer time for using prior year tax losses to avoid minimum tax is now reduced from **3 years to 2** under Section 113(2)(c). Corporates must tighten tax planning timelines.

Here is a **detailed breakdown of the amendments made to the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001** through the **Finance Bill 2025**, structured by themes and sections for clarity:

---

## 🔸 I. **New Definitions Introduced in Section 2**
### ➤ Clause (17C) – Digitally Delivered Services:
Includes services delivered over the internet/electronic networks with minimal or no human involvement, such as:
- Audio/video streaming
- Cloud services
- Online software
- Telemedicine, e-learning
- Online banking, architecture, accounting, consultancy reports

### ➤ Clause (19AA) – E-Commerce:
Defined as sale or purchase of goods/services over computer networks using:
- Websites
- Mobile apps
- Online marketplaces
- Digital ordering features via smartphones, tablets, or automated systems

### ➤ Clause (38B) – Online Interfaces:
Expanded to include digital platforms facilitating transactions between multiple buyers and sellers, even if the platform does not take ownership of the goods/services.

---

## 🔸 II. **New Tax Imposed on Digital Economy – Section 6A**
A **new digital transactions tax** imposed on persons receiving payments for:
- Digitally ordered goods or services
- Supplied/delivered from within Pakistan
- Using **locally operated e-commerce platforms**, marketplaces, or websites

**Exclusion:** Export proceeds already taxed under Section 154A.

**Tax rates** detailed in **Division IVA of Part I, First Schedule** (e.g., 0.25% to 2% depending on transaction amount and mode – banking vs. cash-on-delivery).

---

## 🔸 III. **Surcharge on High-Income Salaried Individuals – Section 4AB**
A **9% surcharge** introduced for salaried individuals earning over **PKR 10 million** in a tax year.

---

## 🔸 IV. **Expenditure Disallowances and Compliance**
### ➤ Section 21:
- **Clause (q)**: 10% of expenditure disallowed if purchases are from persons without **NTN**, excluding direct purchases from growers of agricultural produce.
- **Clause (s)**: 50% of expenditure disallowed if payment exceeding Rs. 200,000 per invoice is made in **cash or non-digital means**.

### ➤ Section 22:
- No depreciation allowed on capital asset payments where withholding tax under **section 152 or 153** was not deducted and deposited.
- The asset cost will not be included for depreciation purposes.

---

## 🔸 V. **Rental Income Adjustments – Section 15(4)**
- For **commercial properties**, the **minimum fair market rent** is deemed to be **4%** of the property's fair market value per annum.
- Override allowed if taxpayer provides credible evidence to the Commissioner.

---

## 🔸 VI. **New Restrictions on Economic Transactions – Section 114C**
**Ineligible persons** (non-filers or those lacking sufficient declared resources) are restricted from:
- Booking/registering motor vehicles
- Purchasing immovable property above limits notified by the government
- Investing in securities or mutual funds
- Operating unrestricted bank accounts

They must:
- File a “**Sources of Investment and Expenditure Statement**” with **130% declared liquid assets**
- Immediate family is considered “eligible” with the filer

---

## 🔸 VII. **Tax Credit for Low-Cost Housing – Section 63A**
- Credit available for **interest paid** on loans used to acquire or construct **one personal residence** (max 2,500 sq. ft. land or 2,000 sq. ft. flat)
- Credit = **(A/B) × C** formula
- Restrictions:
  - Cannot be claimed for a second house within 15 years
  - Not applicable if deduction is claimed under section 15A

---

## 🔸 VIII. **Appeals Framework Restructured**
### ➤ Section 127:
- Taxpayer can **bypass Commissioner (Appeals)** and **directly approach Appellate Tribunal**.

### ➤ Section 131:
- Affirms taxpayer’s right to **appeal directly to ATIR** where CIR(A) is bypassed.

### ➤ Section 133:
- Time to file appeal before High Court **extended from 30 to 60 days**.
- Scope narrowed to **pure questions of law** (removes “mixed questions” of law and fact).

---

## 🔸 IX. **Immediate Recovery in Case of High Court/Supreme Court Rulings – Sections 138(3A) & 140(6A)**
Where a **legal precedent is set**, tax becomes **immediately recoverable**, irrespective of:
- Statutory timelines for appeal
- Procedural steps otherwise applicable

Applies **7 days after HC/SCP judgment in FBR's favor**.

---

## 🔸 X. **Taxation on Pension Income – Section 149(1A)**
For individuals **under 70 years of age**, pension income exceeding **Rs. 10 million/year** becomes taxable at **normal slab rates** (adjusted for credits and withholding).

---

## 🔸 XI. **Capital Gains on Debt Securities – Section 151A**
- **15% withholding tax** on gains from **debt securities** (including govt. securities) held in **IPS accounts**.
- Not applicable to securities traded on **registered stock exchange** and settled via **NCCPL**.

---

## 🔸 XII. **Withholding on Digital Sales – Section 153(2A)**
- **Payment intermediaries** and **courier companies** must **withhold tax** at the time of processing or cash collection for **e-commerce transactions**.
- Applies to:
  - Digital payments and COD transactions
  - Logistics services, ride-hailing, food delivery platforms

**Section 165C** mandates these entities to submit **detailed withholding and vendor statements**.

---

## 🔸 XIII. **Auditor Involvement & Digital Monitoring**
### ➤ Section 175AA:
- **FBR can share taxpayer data** (income, accounts, etc.) with **scheduled banks**.
- Banks must provide mismatched banking data for risk profiling.

### ➤ Section 175C:
- **FBR officers may be posted** at business premises to monitor **production, sales, and services**.

---

## 🔸 XIV. **Mandatory Registration for E-Commerce Sellers – Section 181(1A)**
- Online marketplaces must **verify registration** of all vendors with FBR under:
  - **Income Tax Ordinance**
  - **Sales Tax Act**

**Penalty**: Up to **Rs. 1 million** per default (Section 182).

---

## 🔸 XV. **Seventh Schedule Amendments for Banks**
- **Leasehold improvements** to be amortized at **10% per annum**.
- **IFRS 16 disallowed** for depreciation/finance cost on right-of-use assets; actual rent allowed instead.
- Adjustments for prior years required by 2025.
- **Detailed auditor certificate format** introduced for provisioning.

---

## 🔸 XVI. **Miscellaneous Key Amendments**
- **Section 59B**: Business income taxed under minimum tax not eligible for **group relief**.
- **Section 56(1)**: Business losses **cannot offset** income from property.
- **Section 120 & 124**: Appeal effect provisions updated for confirmed and remanded cases.
- **Section 216(3)**: Permits data sharing with auditors, policy offices, and anonymized data for universities/donors.
- **Section 231AB**: Advance tax on banking transactions for non-filers raised to **0.8%**.

# 25% Tax Rebate for Teachers: Terms and Scope  
The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to reinstate a *25% income‐tax rebate* on teachers’ salaries.  In practice, this means that full-time educators pay only 75% of the normal tax on their pay.  The relief applies specifically to **full‑time teachers and researchers** at approved institutions.  For example, media reports cite the Income Tax Ordinance (Second Schedule, Part III, Clause 2) which originally stated that “the tax payable by a full-time teacher or a researcher, employed in a non-profit education or research institution … shall be reduced by an amount equal to 25pc of the tax payable on his income from salary”【50†L90-L95】.  Business-Recorder analysis confirms the proposal targets “full-time teachers or researchers employed in a non-profit education or research institution duly recognized by [the HEC] or a Board of Education or University” (including government research bodies)【28†L149-L156】.  In short, **university and college teachers (and similar researchers)** working in HEC-approved public or private institutions would be eligible.  The rebate is applied at the source: eligible teachers’ income tax bills would be cut by one-quarter.  (In Islamabad’s Senate hearing, officials noted the clause is being added to the Finance Bill so that “once approved, it will come into effect immediately” for the new tax year【2†L76-L84】.)  

## Legislative Status and Process  
As of mid-2025, the proposal has Cabinet backing and is embedded in Pakistan’s budget legislation.  Reports indicate the federal cabinet approved the measure (via a tax-amendment bill) in early 2025【7†L191-L197】【43†L92-L100】.  The Senate Standing Committee on Finance and Revenue subsequently **unanimously approved** the Income Tax (Second Amendment) Bill 2025 – a bill specifically reinstating the rebate – in late May 2025【9†L64-L72】.  The clause has been formally included in the **Finance Bill 2025‑26** accompanying the federal budget.  Once Parliament (National Assembly) passes the Finance Bill, the rebate will be law again.  Officials have said the relief will take effect immediately for FY2025‑26 (beginning July 2025)【2†L80-L84】. In practice, this means the amendment will be tabled in the upcoming budget session (announced for June 10, 2025) and go into force upon enactment.  

## Government and Political Positions  
Government leaders have strongly signaled support for reinstating the rebate.  Ministry of Finance sources state the measure “will provide financial relief to thousands of teachers and researchers” nationwide【2†L83-L85】.  The Federal Cabinet’s decision to restore the rebate has been announced publicly【7†L191-L197】.  At the political level, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif personally directed the FBR to prepare the necessary legislation, approving a summary to restore the rebate【51†L1-L4】.  Finance Minister Aurangzeb has even petitioned the IMF for approval; reports indicate the IMF **granted** a waiver to allow the tax cut【23†L66-L72】【39†L109-L117】.  The Federal Tax Ombudsman has also intervened: in January 2025 it ordered the FBR to clarify that the 25% rebate *was* “lawfully available till tax year 2024” under the Income Tax Ordinance【27†L153-L161】.  In short, the executive branch is actively moving the bill forward.  (Private-sector education bodies have lobbied as well: the Association of Private Sector Universities and the Pakistan Private Medical Institutions Association wrote to the President, PM and Finance Minister asking to revert the 2024 Budget changes and restore the rebate【32†L147-L156】.) 

## Education Sector Reactions  
Educators and unions have been outspoken.  Many groups **welcomed** the reintroduction.  For example, the Joint Education Action Committee and college-teachers’ groups applauded the Senate’s move.  JEC Chairman Fazal-e-Maula called it a “positive step,” though he urged the government to offer even more (such as an education allowance)【9†L78-L87】.  Prof. Danish Yaseen of the Federal Govt. College Teachers’ Association (FGCTA) similarly noted that reinstatement merely restores the status quo, and he pressed for additional incentives so teachers aren’t “burdened with financial worries”【9†L78-L87】.  Meanwhile, advocates who had protested the initial withdrawal continue to press hard.  Punjab Lecturers’ Association leaders and the All-Gov’t Employees Grand Alliance (AGEGA) had launched street protests earlier, and as news of the reinstatement circulated they continued to demand swift action.  AGEGA’s Faiza Rana (also PPLA president) and colleagues condemned any delays, warning that abrupt tax deductions (without notice) were shocking teachers【33†L55-L63】【15†L73-L77】.  The university lecturers’ union (FAPUASA) issued an urgent letter to the Finance Minister, calling the January 2025 repeal “illegal” and stressing that the rebate was already approved by Parliament in the last budget【50†L53-L61】.  Private-sector university associations (APSUP) and hospital-educator groups (PAMI) similarly warned that removing the rebate would “undermine” educational quality and weaken the ability to attract quality faculty【32†L177-L185】. In summary, teacher and researcher associations have largely backed the restoration and sharply criticized its suspension; they are watching closely as the bill moves through Parliament. 

## Historical Background: Prior Availability and Discontinuation  
The 25% tax rebate is not new. It was first enacted in the 2001 Income Tax Ordinance and featured in every federal budget thereafter up to 2022【50†L90-L95】.  Under the original law, a teacher’s tax owed on salary was explicitly *reduced* by 25%【50†L90-L95】.  In practice this meant, for example, that a lecturer owing Rs. 100,000 in tax paid only Rs. 75,000. Thus by 2025 the issue had come full circle – with the new government now formally moving to reintroduce the rebate that its predecessor had deleted.

**Overview**  
The Finance Bill 2025 proposes to reinstate a **25% income tax rebate for full-time teachers and researchers** employed at **HEC-recognized or Board-affiliated non-profit education and research institutions**. This means eligible educators will pay only **75% of the tax otherwise due** on their salary income. **Sector Response**  
Educators and associations strongly support the reinstatement. Groups such as the **Joint Education Action Committee**, **FGCTA**, **PPLA**, and **FAPUASA** welcomed the measure but continue to call for further support, including education allowances. Protests erupted in late 2024 when the FBR resumed full taxation, prompting legal challenges and union-led demonstrations.

**Historical Context**  
First introduced in 2001, the rebate was consistently included in federal budgets until **its repeal via the Finance Act 2022**. Here’s an engaging, interactive **flyer layout** tailored for salaried individuals, highlighting the **key changes in Finance Bill 2025 (FY 2025‑26)** that impact your **salary, savings, and taxes**:

---

## 🎯 Top Highlights for Salaried Individuals

### 1. 💰 Salary & Pension Boost
- **10% salary increase** for government employees (Grades 1–16), plus a **30% special allowance** integrated into basic pay.citeturn0search6turn0search10  
- **Pension rise** of 5–7.5% for retired civil servants.citeturn0search6  

### 2. 🧾 Reduced Income Tax for Salaried Class
- New tax slabs effective **1 July 2025** offer broad relief across income groups:citeturn0search3turn0search10  

| Annual Salary (PKR)       | Tax Payable                                     |
|---------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Up to 600,000             | 0%                                              |
| 600,001 – 1,200,000       | 2.5% on amount over 600k                         |
| 1,200,001 – 2,200,000     | 15,000 + 11% on amount over 1.2 million         |
| 2,200,001 – 3,200,000     | 125,000 + 23% on excess over 2.2 million       |
| 3,200,001 – 4,100,000     | 355,000 + 30% on excess                        |
| Above 4,100,000           | 625,000 + 35% on excess                        |

- Compared to FY 24‑25, relief is significant, especially for middle-income earners.citeturn0search3  

### 3. 📉 Heavier Relief for Middle-Income Earners
- Some marginal rates halved: e.g., for a **PKR 100k/month salary**, the tax rate may drop from ~5% to ~2.5% monthly.citeturn0search16  

---

## 🔍 What These Changes Mean for You

- **More take-home pay**: Salary increments + lower taxes = real income gain.
- **Better savings potential**: Lower deductions free up funds for insurance, investments, or emergencies.
- **Pensioners benefit**: Pension adjustments help offset inflation.
- **Motivation for filing taxes**: Progressive slabs make compliance more beneficial.

---

## 🛠️ How to Make the Most of It

1. **Recalculate** your post-tax income using updated slabs.
2. **Adjust** your monthly budget—more disposable income means more saving or investing.
3. **Plan investments wisely**—e.g., tax‑efficient retirement schemes or TDRs.
4. **Stay compliant**—early filing avoids penalties and unlocks slab advantages.

---

✅ **1. Updated Tax Slabs for Salaried Income**
📊 The new progressive tax slabs for salaried individuals are as follows:

| Taxable Income | Tax Rate |
|----------------|----------|

---

🧾 **2. Surcharge on High-Income Salaried Individuals**
If your *salary income* exceeds **Rs. 10 million/year**, a **9% surcharge** is now applicable on the income tax payable under the regular tax slabs.

🔎 Example: If your regular tax is Rs. 2 million, you’ll now pay an additional Rs. 180,000 as surcharge.

🏠 **3. New Tax Credit: Interest on Low-Cost Housing Loans**
Building or buying your **first personal house** (up to 2,500 sq. ft.) or **flat** (up to 2,000 sq. ft.)? You can claim a **tax credit** on the interest portion of your loan repayment from a scheduled bank or SECP-regulated entity.

📐 Formula: (A/B) × C

- Total interest paid
- 30% of taxable income

💡 **Limitation:** This is a **one-time claim**, and can’t be availed again for the next **15 years**.

---

⛔ **4. Restrictions on Economic Transactions for Non-Filers**
🚫 Non-filers will be **barred** from:
- Registering **cars or property**
- Investing in **mutual funds**
- Opening **bank accounts**
- Withdrawing **cash beyond a limit**

📢 If you're a salaried person who hasn't filed a return, this could **directly freeze your financial freedom**.

---

📌 **Key Reminder:**
- Declare all **salary and savings** properly.
- File your **tax return** to stay eligible for investment and asset transactions.
- Consider availing the **housing tax credit** if you’re planning to own your first home!

💼 **Finance Bill 2025: What It Means for Salaried Individuals** 💡

The Finance Bill 2025 introduces significant tax changes for salaried individuals, directly affecting their take-home income and financial planning. Firstly, revised tax slabs have been proposed, with income up to Rs. 600,000 remaining tax-exempt. For income between Rs. 600,001 and Rs. 1.2 million, a 1% tax applies on the amount exceeding Rs. 600,000. The tax rate gradually increases, reaching 35% for annual salaries above Rs. 4.1 million. This progressive structure intensifies the tax burden on high earners.

Additionally, a new surcharge has been introduced: if your income under the salary head exceeds Rs. 10 million in a tax year, you’ll now be liable to pay an additional surcharge at 9% of your regular income tax. For example, if your calculated tax is Rs. 2 million, the surcharge will cost you Rs. 180,000—effectively increasing your overall tax liability.

On the savings side, a welcome measure has been introduced in the form of a tax credit for individuals who are building or purchasing their **first personal residence**. If you have taken a housing loan for a house (up to 2,500 sq. ft.) or a flat (up to 2,000 sq. ft.), you can now claim a tax credit for the interest paid on this loan. The credit is subject to a formula that considers your taxable income and interest paid, capped at 30% of your income. However, this benefit is a one-time opportunity and cannot be claimed again for the next 15 years.

In a major push toward documentation and financial discipline, non-filers (those who don’t file tax returns) will face severe restrictions. They will be barred from purchasing or registering property, buying vehicles above a certain value, investing in mutual funds, or even opening or operating regular bank accounts. Cash withdrawals above a notified threshold may also be disallowed. These restrictions are aimed at encouraging compliance and closing the gap between declared and actual incomes.

📢 In summary, salaried individuals should brace for higher tax burdens if they fall into upper income brackets, but also consider leveraging available tax credits—especially for housing. Filing your return on time is no longer optional; it is now crucial for maintaining access to basic economic rights.

If you’re earning between Rs. 2.2 million and Rs. 3.2 million, expect a tax hit of Rs. 116,000 plus 23% of the excess over Rs. 2.2 million. This makes proper salary structuring and investment planning more important than ever.

⚠️ **2. High-Income? Watch Out for the New 9% Surcharge!**
A new surcharge now applies if your salary income exceeds Rs. 10 million in a tax year. You’ll be required to pay an **additional 9%** of your already computed tax liability. For instance, if your tax is Rs. 3 million, expect to pay Rs. 270,000 more—just as surcharge. This measure tightens the net on higher earners and pushes for more equitable tax contribution.

🏡 **3. Planning to Buy or Build a House? You’re in Luck!**
There’s a **new tax credit** available for those who take a loan for constructing or purchasing their **first personal residence**—up to 2,500 sq. ft. for a house or 2,000 sq. ft. for a flat. You can claim a credit for the interest paid on your loan, subject to a formula. It’s capped at 30% of your taxable income and only available once—no double dipping for the next **15 years**. This is a golden opportunity to ease your tax burden while investing in your future.

🔒 **4. Haven’t Filed Your Return? Say Goodbye to Financial Freedom**
Non-filers will now face strict penalties. If you haven’t filed your return, you won’t be able to:
- Register or purchase a car or property
- Invest in securities or mutual funds
- Open or operate standard bank accounts
- Make large cash withdrawals

To regain these rights, you must either file your return or submit a **Source of Investment and Expenditure Statement** on FBR’s portal. This is part of the government’s major push for **tax compliance** and documentation.

💡 **Pro Tip:** Even if you earn under the taxable limit, file your return to remain eligible for financial transactions and loans.

📈 **5. Pensioners, Take Note!**
If you're under 70 and receiving pension income exceeding Rs. 10 million per year, your pension will now be taxed like salary income. This change impacts those with substantial retirement benefits and demands proactive tax planning.

Here is a structured website update containing interactive main headings and concise one-paragraph explanations for each proposed amendment in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, as per the Finance Bill 2025:

---

### 📌 Fair Market Rent of Commercial Properties  
Minimum fair market rent for commercial properties will be deemed at 4% of their FBR-assessed value. However, if a taxpayer can substantiate a lower rent with evidence, the actual rent will be accepted.

---

### 🚫 Disallowance of Purchases from Non-NTN Holders  
10% of business expenditure on purchases from non-NTN holders will be disallowed—except for direct purchases of agricultural products from growers or persons notified by the FBR.

---

### 💸 Disallowance on Unbanked Cash Sales  
50% of expenses will be disallowed if a taxpayer receives over Rs. 200,000 in cash (non-digital/bank mode) per invoice.

---

### 🏗️ Depreciation Disallowed Without Tax Deduction  
If withholding tax under section 152 or 153 is not deducted on the purchase of capital assets, depreciation on such assets will be disallowed.

---

### 🏢 Group Relief Tightened  
Companies taxed under minimum tax or special regimes will no longer be eligible for group relief on surrendered business losses.

---

### 🏠 Tax Credit on Low-Cost Housing Loans Restored  
A new section 63A allows tax credit on loans from banks and financial institutions for purchasing or constructing a house/flat (limited to 2,500 sq. ft. for houses and 2,000 sq. ft. for flats).

---

### 🚫 Restrictions on Ineligible Persons  
Economic transactions such as vehicle/property purchase or opening bank accounts will be barred for persons not filing returns or lacking sufficient declared resources.

---

### ❌ NPO Status Denied to Certain Clubs  
Recreational clubs charging over Rs. 1 million in membership fees will no longer qualify as Non-Profit Organizations under section 2(36).

---

### 📃 Tax Conditions Extended to Table 1 NPOs  
Institutions earlier exempt under Table 1 of Clause 66 will now be subject to section 100C conditions, bringing stricter oversight.

---

### 💡 Amortization Period for Intangibles Reduced  
Intangibles without a defined useful life will now be amortized over 15 years instead of 25.

---

### 🏘️ Business Loss Set-off with Property Income Reversed  
The ability to adjust business losses against property income is proposed to be reversed, restoring the pre-2021 position.

---

### 🏭 Broader Tax Credit for Coal Mining Projects  
Coal suppliers in Sindh will now be eligible for tax credit even if supplying to sectors beyond power generation.

---

### 📆 Minimum Tax Carryforward Period Shortened  
Minimum tax paid can now be carried forward for only 2 years (reduced from 3), though prior year benefits remain intact.

---

### 💳 Digital Means Recognized for Asset Purchases  
Payments made digitally (in addition to crossed cheques, etc.) will be valid for asset purchases above Rs. 5 million or Rs. 1 million, depending on the asset class.

---

### ⏳ Time Limit for Amendments Removed  
The 120-day time limit for issuing amendment orders after a show-cause notice is proposed to be removed.

---

### 🔁 Appeal Effect Orders Simplified  
Where tax orders are fully upheld, no appeal effect order will be needed; in partial modifications, a revised order will be required.

---

### 📜 Appeals Allowed Without Monetary Threshold  
Appeals before CIR(A) will now be allowed regardless of the amount involved. Taxpayers may opt to go directly to ATIR, waiving CIR(A) appeal.

---

### ⚖️ Reference to High Court – More Time, Clear Scope  
Time for filing a reference to the High Court is extended to 60 days, but only on pure questions of law—not mixed questions.

---

### 🏛️ ADR Reappointment for SOEs  
If the ADR Committee for a State-Owned Enterprise fails to resolve a case in 60 days, reappointment is allowed with another 60-day limit.

---

### 🔍 Banking Info Cross-Match with FBR  
Banks will be required to share account data with FBR when there’s a mismatch with tax profiles, overriding all other secrecy laws.

---

### ⌛ Time Condonation Limited to 2 Years  
FBR’s power to condone delays is capped at a total of two years. A Board committee may extend this for major revenue losses.

---

### 🏦 Higher Tax on Cash Withdrawal by Non-Filers  
Advance tax on daily cash withdrawals exceeding Rs. 50,000 by non-filers is proposed to increase from 0.6% to 0.8%.

---

### 👨‍🏫 25% Rebate for Teachers & Researchers Restored  
The 25% tax rebate for full-time teachers and researchers is reinstated retroactively from July 1, 2022, up to Tax Year 2025.

---

### 🌐 Tax on Pakistan-Based E-Commerce  
A new Section 6A introduces tax on digital transactions within Pakistan via e-commerce platforms. Withholding agents include payment intermediaries and courier companies.

---

### 🏦 Leasehold Expenses – Banking Sector  
Expenditure on leasehold improvements will be capitalized and amortized. Actual rent (with audit certification) will replace IFRS 16 adjustments.

---

### 💳 Revised Banking NPL Provision Rules  
Banks must furnish a detailed auditor certificate for provisions against non-performing loans (NPLs) starting from Tax Year 2025.

---

### 👨‍💼 Salaried Tax Slabs Adjusted  
Salaried tax slabs have been revised, with lower rates in certain brackets and the surcharge reduced from 10% to 9% for income above Rs. 10 million.

---

### 🧓 Tax on Pension Above Rs. 10 Million  
Individuals under 70 will pay 5% tax on pension/annuity exceeding Rs. 10 million unless such pension is their sole income.

---

### 💰 Super Tax Recalibrated  
The slab rates for super tax under section 4C are revised, reducing rates for income bands between Rs. 200–400 million starting Tax Year 2026.

---

### 📊 Dividend Tax from Mutual Funds Restructured  
Dividend from mutual funds will now be taxed at 15% (equity-based) or 25% (debt-based), depending on income source proportion.

---

### 💸 Profit on Debt – Higher Tax  
Withholding on profit/yield from banking companies is raised from 15% to 20%; non-ATL individuals face 40% tax rate.

---

### 🌍 Offshore Digital Services – Tax Increase  
Fee for offshore digital services will now be taxed at 15%, up from 10%, unless subject to the Digital Presence Proceeds Levy.

---

### 📈 Capital Gains – Debt Securities  
Banks managing Investor Portfolio Securities must withhold 15% tax on gains from debt security disposal (excluding exchange-based trades).

---

### 🌐 Foreign Company Gains – Tiered Tax  
Capital gains by non-resident companies will face 10% tax if held for over 12 months and 20% if under 12 months.

---

### 📦 Services & Contract Execution – Higher WHT  
Withholding tax rates on various services and contracts have been increased under sections 152(2A) and 153(1).

---

### 🏠 Property Transfer Taxes Revised  
Advance tax on sale and purchase of immovable property is revised—sale tax increased for sellers; purchase tax decreased for buyers.

---

### 📉 Tax on Securities – Higher for Non-Filers  
Tax on gains from securities (acquired before July 1, 2025) will be doubled for persons not on the Active Taxpayers List.

---

### 🏏 ICC Champions Trophy Income – Tax Exempt  
All income related to the ICC Champions Trophy 2025 by ICC, its staff, and affiliates is fully exempt from income tax.

---

### 💻 STZ & SEZ – Exemption Time Limit Imposed  
The 10-year exemption for STZ and SEZ enterprises will now expire on June 30, 2035, even if the full 10 years are not completed.

---

### 🏞️ Tribal Areas – Exemption Extended  
Tax exemption for residents of former Tribal Areas is extended until June 30, 2026.

---

### 🎥 Cinema Exemption Ends in 2030  
Income from cinema operations will remain exempt until June 30, 2030, or five years from operation commencement—whichever comes first.

---

### 💊 Section 148 – Pharma Imports Exempt  
Import of Cystagon, Cysta Drops, and Trientine capsules is exempt from advance tax under section 148.

---

### 📂 Audit Immunity Now for 3 Years  
Taxpayers audited in any of the preceding three tax years will be immune from audit selection under section 177 or 214C.

---

### 🏦 Voluntary Pension Fund Withdrawals – Taxable  
Withdrawals from Voluntary Pension Funds and transfer balances from provident to pension funds will now be fully taxable.
